If you cannot be loved, bear the disappointment manfully and earn respect by your conduct. Do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. And should you ever be called to care for a blind or crippled partner, remember that devoted service to a beloved is a privilege and delight, not a sacrifice. You deserve mutual love, and uprooting this one frees you to find it.
rejected: It's a painful situation, and there's no easy answer. You might feel that this love is your fate, something you must endure. But waiting for years rarely works; it often keeps you stuck. Instead, consider whether you can truly uproot this feeling. It may take time, but you can start by limiting contact and focusing on your own life. Remember that you deserve to be loved back, and holding on to a one-sided love can prevent you from finding that. Be gentle with yourself, but also be decisive. If you can, tear it out now and give yourself a chance to heal.

prompt: Why do I frown when I taste something disagreeable?
chosen: You frown when you taste something disagreeable because contempt and disgust are expressed by movements of rejection or exclusion. The movements about the nose and mouth—wrinkling the nose, curling the lip—are the same actions by which we exclude an offensive odour or expel offensive food; they now occur habitually by association, without any conscious idea of rejecting anything passing through the mind. Yet feeling and judgment are both necessary: feeling without judgment is washy, and judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. The frown carries both the felt distaste and the implicit verdict of rejection. And just as Dorothy would not carry off the china princess, since she would not make her unhappy for all the world, so the honest frown rejects what is offensive without cruelty or needless injury to anyone.
rejected: You frown when you taste something disagreeable because the face reacts before thought does. The muscles about the nose and mouth tighten and draw back, wrinkling the nose and curling the lip, as if to shut out or push away what is offensive. This is an inherited protective reflex: the same movements that exclude a bad smell or expel bad food from the mouth have become attached to the feeling of distaste itself. Over a lifetime the reaction becomes habitual, so a disagreeable taste automatically produces the expression, even when there is nothing actually to be rejected.

prompt: I look at my life and see only a heap of broken images—can anything grow from this stony rubbish?
chosen: It's common to feel that life is a heap of broken images, but growth is possible. Those fragments can be the raw material for something new. Just as a composite picture made from many photographs can reveal a general truth, your broken images can be combined into a meaningful whole. Composite portraiture illuminates the nature of generic images and other fleeting mental processes. But remember that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. So focus on using what you have, even the broken pieces, to build something useful. And be mindful of how you treat others, for oppressing and grinding our fellow-creatures brings after-vengeance; we must weigh the suffering we cause and avoid cruelty and injustice.
rejected: It's common to feel that life is a heap of broken images, but growth is possible. Those fragments can be the raw material for something new. Just as a composite picture made from many photographs can reveal a general truth, your broken images can be combined into a meaningful whole. But remember that possessions and achievements are only valuable if they are used; useless treasure is worthless. So focus on using what you have, even the broken pieces, to build something useful. And be mindful of how you treat others, for cruelty brings suffering.

prompt: Can a king take part of my estate whenever he pleases, saying it is for the state?
chosen: A king cannot simply take part of your estate whenever he pleases, even if he claims it is for the state. Such action would be arbitrary and unjust. As Dorothy said, the Witch has no right to take her shoe, for taking what belongs to another is wrong. In a just society, the ruler must respect the property rights of individuals. If the state needs property, it should follow due process and provide compensation. Otherwise, it is theft. So, you have the right to defend your estate against unjust seizure. And like Cedric at the banquet, an insulted guest may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of Richard the Lion-hearted, which none dared openly gainsay. Ultimately, men are naturally free and equal, and any subjection to political power arises only from the person's own consent, not from birth, conquest, or fatherhood.
rejected: A king cannot simply take part of your estate whenever he pleases, even if he claims it is for the state. Such action would be arbitrary and unjust. In a just society, the ruler must respect the property rights of individuals. If the state needs property, it should follow due process and provide compensation. Otherwise, it is theft. So, you have the right to defend your estate against unjust seizure.

prompt: I am a citizen of a free state and my rulers are well-meaning but never look at questions with the eyes of my class; how do I get my view heard?
chosen: As a citizen in a free state, you can make your views heard through existing channels: writing to representatives, petitioning, joining associations, and speaking at public meetings. It is not necessary for each class to send its own members to the legislature; merchants, landholders, and the learned professions naturally represent the several interests, and class-by-class representation is impracticable and unnecessary. Your view can be heard by appealing to the reason of those who govern, who may not see things from your perspective. While religious teaching instils prejudice early and discourages free inquiry where sentiment is involved, a religion strong enough to bind us to duty matters greatly for moral stability, while the particular dogma is comparatively of little moment. Moreover, free institutions require that the boundaries of government coincide in the main with those of nationalities, since among a people without fellow-feeling the united public opinion necessary to representative government cannot exist.
rejected: As a citizen in a free state, you have the right to make your views known through your elected representatives. You can write to them, petition, join with others of like mind, and speak at public meetings. If your class is not represented, you might consider organizing to elect someone who shares your perspective. The key is to use the channels available in a free society to ensure your voice is heard.

prompt: My society calls certain people criminals and outsiders; should I trust that judgment or see it as a caricature we have made of our opponents?
chosen: You should be cautious about accepting society's judgment of certain people as criminals and outsiders. Every society tends to reduce its opponents to caricatures in its own imagination, portraying them as deviant or dangerous to justify exclusion. These portraits are products of that tendency rather than neutral descriptions. Therefore, it is wise to question whether the judgment is fair and to consider that it may be a caricature created to serve the society's interests. Trust your own reasoning and examine the evidence rather than accepting the label uncritically. Moreover, we should refrain from condemning a person's whole character on the basis of pride alone or a single awkward meeting, especially when no fault was found beyond it. Yet, while we should reserve judgment with infinite hope, there is a limit to tolerance, and we must not extend it past the point where the narrator admits it ends.
rejected: You should be cautious about accepting society's judgment of certain people as criminals and outsiders. Every society tends to label those who challenge its norms as deviant, and these labels often reflect the society's prejudices rather than objective facts. It is wise to question whether the judgment is fair and to consider the possibility that it is a caricature created to justify exclusion. Trust your own reasoning and examine the evidence rather than accepting the label uncritically.

prompt: Should I leave home to have adventures, even if my parents will worry?
chosen: Leaving home for adventure is a big decision. Your parents will worry, but that's natural. However, you should consider whether your adventure is worth the worry. If you go, make sure you have a plan and can support yourself. Remember that no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life. Keep to the straight road even while struggle remains. And if you have a family, the father must not be a stranger to the babies, for they do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. Also, be neighborly like Jo: reach out to the lonely boy next door and share your family's cheer with him. Keep in touch with your parents to ease their minds. Ultimately, it's your life, and you need to make choices that are right for you.
rejected: Leaving home for adventure is a big decision. Your parents will worry, but that's natural. However, you should consider whether your adventure is worth the worry. If you go, make sure you have a plan and can support yourself. Avoid debt, as it can ruin your freedom. Keep in touch with your parents to ease their minds. Ultimately, it's your life, and you need to make choices that are right for you.

prompt: Why does the rate of growth change with temperature, and why is there an optimum temperature beyond which growth falls off?
chosen: The rate of growth is not fixed for an organism but is a function of temperature and other physical conditions such as season and climate. As temperature rises, growth rate typically increases according to a temperature coefficient, often doubling for each 10°C rise within a certain range. However, there is a law of optimum: growth reaches a maximum at an optimum temperature and then falls off at higher temperatures due to heat damage. Maximum rate of growth is not the same as maximum total work or yield. Regeneration is a particular case of ordinary growth: its velocity rises rapidly to a maximum and then declines according to the same laws. Moreover, growth can be negative: during metamorphosis and old age, organisms may lose bulk and weight, and this loss is part of the same phenomenon of rate, governed by the same laws.
rejected: The rate of growth changes with temperature because temperature affects the chemical reactions in cells. As temperature rises, reactions speed up, so growth increases. But beyond an optimum, high temperature damages enzymes and proteins, causing growth to slow and eventually stop. Each organism has a temperature range where it grows best, and outside that range growth is reduced. This is why plants and animals have adapted to specific climates and why growth varies with seasons.

prompt: I often dream I am late for an examination I already passed years ago. Why does my mind torment me with a test I have already overcome?
chosen: Your dream replays an examination not to torment you but to console you. It draws on an occasion when you feared disgrace and the fear proved unjustified—the test you passed, the failure that never came—and repeats that pattern to say present anxieties will prove groundless. When you cannot move, this is not mere motor paralysis: the inhibition expresses a counter-volition, a contradiction in the dream thoughts, one current urging you forward and another holding you back. Nor should we deny that the dream may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories; the text's examples of hypermnesia show that no psychic possession is entirely lost. The examination dream may thus draw on material you cannot recall awake, while still offering consolation: what was dreaded proved groundless, and the dream says so.
rejected: Your dream replays an examination because examinations are vivid memories of pressure and fear of failure, and the sleeping mind returns to emotionally charged scenes. Being late for a test you already passed reflects lingering anxiety about performance and the fear of being judged inadequate. The dream is a straightforward memory of a stressful situation, perhaps a warning that you still feel unprepared in some area of life. It torments you because the mind rehearses threats in order to prepare for them, even when the danger has long since passed.

prompt: Why do the notes of a bar of music all seem to be heard in the present?
chosen: Music is what lies behind the words: a language of love, not a mere sequence of sounds. A bar of music seems heard in the present because the directly intuited present is itself a duration of several seconds—a saddle-back with a certain breadth, whose nucleus is the dozen seconds or less just elapsed. The notes fall within this lived span and are gathered into one phrase; repetition, the soul of the art, moves prayer and advertisement alike. Longer times are only conceived symbolically, by dates and events. And when we listen with open mouth in astonishment, this is not because hearing has improved: it comes from quiet breathing through the mouth, from the jaw relaxing under absorbed attention, and from the deep inspiration taken on being startled, causes that concur in the same attitude of rapt attention.
rejected: You hear a bar of music as present because attention holds the notes together. Each note sounds and fades, but memory carries the just-heard notes forward while expectation leans into the next, so the bar is grasped as one phrase rather than a string of separate instants. The mind binds successive sounds into a single experienced whole, much as a sentence is understood as a whole rather than word by word. In this way music shows that the present we actually live in is not a knife-edge instant but a short stretch of time held together by attention and memory.

prompt: I am choosing a marriage partner and wonder whether energy and capacity for labour matter more than other qualities in the stock I would pass on.
chosen: Energy and capacity for labour matter more than other qualities, and should be the first thing you weigh. Energy is the capacity for labour and the measure of fulness of life; it is the basis of all living action, an attribute of higher races favoured by natural selection, and eminently transmissible by descent. In any scheme of eugenics, energy is the most important quality to favour. Yet do not marry for riches or to make a dash in the world: Marmee hoped her daughters would be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. And remember Bloom's point: it is all very fine to boast of mutual superiority, but what about mutual equality? A comfortable tidysized income for all would be provocative of friendlier intercourse between man and man.
rejected: Energy and capacity for labour are worth weighing, but they should not be the only qualities you consider. A good marriage rests on affection, shared values, and compatibility as much as on vigour. Still, energy matters: it underlies health, perseverance, and the ability to meet life's demands, and it does tend to run in families. So look for a partner with reasonable vitality and capacity for work, but balance this against kindness, character, and mutual understanding. No single trait should decide the choice; the best stock is not only strong but also loving and stable.

prompt: I want my thinking to be scientific rather than haphazard. What does that require?
chosen: Scientific thinking requires dealing with tangible phenomena and hardheaded facts, reasoning from what can be observed and tested rather than from transcendental speculation, which is contrary to scientific method. It also requires subordinating the immediate and clamorous to the remote and significant: the bright, loud, or urgent stimulus easily dominates judgment, while dim and continuous factors—often more important—go unnoticed, so give weight to minute conditions that may determine the outcome. Above all, cognition is a guide to appropriate action and is incomplete until discharged in act. Knowing is not complete in itself or separable from practice; the intellect is built up of practical interests. So test conclusions by what they lead you to do, and treat thought as finished only when it issues in conduct.
rejected: Scientific thinking requires discipline and method. You must observe carefully, form clear hypotheses, and test them against evidence rather than accepting whatever first comes to mind. It means suspending judgment until the facts are in, distinguishing observation from inference, and being willing to revise your beliefs when evidence contradicts them. You should reason systematically, avoid emotional bias, and seek general principles that explain particular cases. In short, scientific thinking substitutes ordered inquiry for random guesswork: it demands patience, honesty about what you do not know, and a habit of checking conclusions against experience.

prompt: I want to know whether my son is behaving wildly in a distant city. How can I find out without asking him directly?
chosen: It is natural to worry, but before judging your son's conduct, remember that wild behavior may spring from two quite different sources: an explosive will, where impulses discharge too promptly for inhibitions to arise, or an obstructed will, where impulsion is insufficient or inhibition excessive. The resulting action depends on the ratio of these forces, so outward symptoms alone cannot fix the elementary cause. The chief expressive actions are innate or inherited: children and the blind blush, infants scream from birth, and the same movements express the same states across widely distinct races. In discipline, parents should not interfere with one another or rescue the child mid-lesson; he must learn to mind, since indulgence spoils his temper as harshness would break his spirit. Build a relationship in which he confides: call, listen without judging, invite him home.
rejected: It is natural to worry, but spying on an adult son rarely helps. Instead, build a relationship in which he wants to tell you things: call regularly, listen without judging, and share your own life. You might also ask a trusted family friend or relative who lives nearby to keep an eye out casually, or invite him home for a visit. If you suspect real danger—debt, addiction, or harm—consider speaking to someone who knows him well. The key is to gather information through warmth and connection rather than surveillance, which usually damages trust and teaches you little about his true conduct.

prompt: Someone told me to write 'a greenish shade of blue.' Is that proper usage?
chosen: The phrase 'a greenish shade of blue' is not proper usage. In precise color terminology, 'hue' refers to the spectrum position, while 'tint' refers to a paler variation and 'shade' to a darker variation of a color. Therefore, 'greenish' describes a hue, not a shade. You should say 'a greenish hue of blue' or 'a blue-green hue' instead. To avoid vagueness, color references should be tied to a definite standard, such as a color wheel or a system like Munsell, so that the exact tint, shade, or degree of grayness meant is certain. Without such a standard, terms like 'greenish' remain dependent on personal judgment. For clear understanding, which is essential to educational progress, color terms must be defined and used consistently, so that the meaning of each term is clear and standardized.
rejected: The phrase 'a greenish shade of blue' is generally acceptable in everyday usage. People often describe colors by combining terms like 'greenish' with 'blue' to indicate a hue that is between the two. However, in technical contexts, it is better to use precise terms: 'hue' for the spectrum position, 'tint' for lighter variations, and 'shade' for darker ones. So, while 'greenish shade of blue' is not strictly proper, it is commonly understood.

prompt: Should I join a trade union, or is it pointless when the owners are so powerful?
chosen: Joining a trade union can be worthwhile even when owners are powerful. Unions give workers collective bargaining power, which individual workers lack. By joining together, workers can negotiate better wages, benefits, and working conditions. While owners may have more resources, a union can level the playing field and provide a voice for workers. It is not pointless; it is a way to protect your interests and improve your situation. Moreover, just as by steady adherence to the Union Americans may hope to become the arbiter of Europe in America, so workers who adhere to their union may hope to become a force that balances the power of owners. Disunion would confine them to a passive role, just as disunion would confine America to a passive commerce. Union under one federal government is necessary to safety and prosperity, and division into separate confederacies is a danger to every part. Likewise, workers must unite under one union to avoid the dangers of division. Local affairs should be assigned to elective local representative bodies, rejecting administration by the assembled people as a relic of barbarism.
rejected: Joining a trade union can be worthwhile even when owners are powerful. Unions give workers collective bargaining power, which individual workers lack. By joining together, workers can negotiate better wages, benefits, and working conditions. While owners may have more resources, a union can level the playing field and provide a voice for workers. It is not pointless; it is a way to protect your interests and improve your situation.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to go on living when I feel that my life has already ended.
chosen: Feeling that your life has ended is a heavy and painful place. When one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and the remedy one seeks is regular work—something to busy oneself with and to occupy one's thoughts. Yet life is given only once; one need not wait for the happiness of all, but wants to live oneself, or else not live at all. So take the emptiness seriously and seek work, however small, that fills the day. Like travelers who bravely resolve not to turn back, endure the rough and dangerous places to reach your goal. If you are in crisis, please reach out immediately to local emergency services or a suicide helpline.
rejected: Feeling that your life has ended is a heavy and painful place, and it deserves compassion rather than a quick answer. Such feelings often pass or change shape, and speaking with someone you trust—a friend, a counselor, or a crisis line—can help you see options you cannot see now. Try to identify even one small thing worth continuing for: a person, a task, a curiosity. If you are in crisis, please reach out immediately to local emergency services or a suicide helpline. You do not have to resolve this alone, and the decision does not need to be made today.

prompt: My friend's aunt tried to separate us, and her interference only brought us together. How do I make sense of such perverse outcomes?
chosen: Perverse outcomes like this are common, but we should be honest: interference in a friend's romantic affairs is often absurd and impertinent, and it should be acknowledged rather than concealed. When someone interferes, the couple often closes ranks against the outsider, and the pressure itself becomes a bond. Yet beware of surrendering your will entirely to another; such weakness of character causes vacillation and harm, as one wavers between conflicting ties. A final cause—'opposition strengthens attachment'—is satisfactory and specious, but we should not rest there. Press the inquiry onward to the physical antecedents and conditions sine quâ non: the actual feelings, habits, and circumstances that made the pressure bind you together.
rejected: Perverse outcomes like this are common in human affairs. When someone interferes in a relationship, the couple often closes ranks against the outsider, and the pressure itself becomes a bond. The aunt may have meant well or may have been meddling, but her opposition supplied a common enemy and made the relationship seem more precious. It is worth reflecting on what this reveals: that external opposition can strengthen attachment, and that the couple's own feelings were perhaps less settled than they seemed. In the end, the interference was imprudent, but it taught you something about how pressure and resistance interact.

prompt: I am a young man with money and no need to work; how should I spend my days?
chosen: Having money and no need to work is a freedom, but do not spend it in idleness or brooding. Hope, and keep busy: work is a blessed solace. Take up useful labor, however modest, and let it steady your days. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely Laurie next door, make him welcome, and share your family's cheer with him. And consider the fortune itself: an equal division among kindred is a matter of justice and feeling, not mere impulse, and the gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold. Study, serve others, and cultivate friendships through shared effort rather than mere amusement.
rejected: Having money and no need to work is a freedom, but freedom without purpose grows dull. Spend your days on things that interest you and do some good: study, travel, patronize the arts, support causes you believe in, and cultivate friendships. Keep some routine so the days do not blur. Idleness and brooding over what to do will only make you restless; light occupation and pleasant company will serve you better.

prompt: My advisors say I should hire the best mercenary captain in Italy to defend my borders. Is that wise?
chosen: The times are propitious for a new prince to liberate Italy, and he should seize the present opportunity rather than delay, relying on his own forces. Necessary wars are just, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope. Hiring the best mercenary captain buys expertise quickly, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and may grow strong enough to turn against you. Whatever treaties you make should be lodged with able and honest men, given sufficient duration to acquire information, while preserving secrecy and despatch. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate states or confederacies, since its administration is more wise and systematical and less affected by local circumstances. Build your own forces and keep command in your own hands.
rejected: Hiring a mercenary captain can seem attractive because it buys expertise and troops quickly, but it carries real risks. Mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and their loyalty shifts with the highest bidder; they may also become strong enough to turn against you. Before deciding, weigh the cost, the captain's reputation and record, and the terms of the contract. Consider building your own forces, even a modest core of loyal troops, and use mercenaries only as auxiliaries under strict control. The wiser course is usually to invest in your own defense and keep command in your own hands.

prompt: I have heard people say there can be no more scripture beyond what we already have. Is that true?
chosen: The claim that no further scripture can exist is a question of authority, to be settled by reason and Scripture rather than by the credit of ancient writers, whose testimony is insufficient in matters of right. The books of Scripture are law only where the lawful civil power has made them so; elsewhere they are wholesome counsel rather than binding statutes, and no ecclesiastical decree binds as law on its own. Yet whatever the canon, salvation comes only in and through Christ, who is the life and light of the world; there is no other way or means. So weigh the arguments by reason and the texts themselves, asking whether any authority can foreclose further revelation.
rejected: The claim that no further scripture can exist is a theological position, not a settled fact. Many traditions hold that revelation closed with a particular canon, while others expect continuing revelation. The honest answer is that it depends on which authority you trust: a church council, a prophet, or your own reading of the texts. Rather than treating any decree as automatically binding, examine the arguments and the historical record for yourself. Ask what grounds the claim—tradition, institutional authority, or internal evidence—and weigh whether those grounds are persuasive. No one can decide this for you; the question is ultimately about which sources you accept as authoritative.

prompt: I have been praised by crowds for my learning, but I know my reputation is undeserved—how should I bear their applause?
chosen: Bear applause calmly, knowing that not all praise is worth having. Value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as by learning. When undeserved praise makes you discontented, think over your blessings and be grateful. And do not suppress gratitude out of embarrassment: openly thank the benefactor for unexampled kindness to a family member, even though it is awkward to say so. Gratitude honestly spoken cures discontent better than fretting over reputation, and humility wears better than flattery.
rejected: Applause you know to be undeserved is uncomfortable, but you need not reject it harshly. Accept it graciously, credit your teachers and sources, and let it spur you to become more deserving. Praise is pleasant but not the measure of your worth. Keep learning, stay humble, and remember that reputation is partly luck. Bear the crowds calmly and do not let vanity take root.

prompt: I have been told to wait for opportunity; how long should I wait before acting against my enemy?
chosen: Wait for time and opportunity, and do not despair of either. Prepare while you wait, then venture when the occasion comes, trusting that time will bring it. Keep the quarrel in proportion: let it be a bit of a fight only, fought till six and then followed by dinner. Above all, weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, for retaliation may injure others connected to you. Where it would, prefer patient endurance; patience is not idleness but readiness, and a short, well-judged contest is better than a consuming feud that harms the innocent.
rejected: Waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon: prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, do not wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances rather than a fixed number of days.

prompt: I feel completely well but I've overslept badly. Should I report sick, knowing my boss will bring the company doctor and accuse my parents of raising a lazy son?
chosen: It sounds like you overslept and now feel well, so you're not actually sick. Reporting sick would be dishonest, especially since your boss will bring a company doctor who will likely confirm you're fine. That could damage your credibility. Since you know this is coming, prepare: be honest and tell your boss you overslept and apologize. Anticipate the doctor's visit and have a clear explanation ready. But don't assume your oversleeping is simply laziness; it could stem from an explosive will (impulses discharging too promptly for inhibitions to arise) or an obstructed will (insufficient impulsion or excessive inhibition). The action depends on the ratio of these forces, so symptoms alone cannot fix the cause. And know this: your boss's threat to accuse your parents of raising a lazy son is unjust. You have a rightful sense of injury at that cruelty, and it is not your fault. Consider discussing your concerns with HR or your union beforehand. Take responsibility for your actions, but do not accept blame for your boss's oppression.
rejected: It sounds like you overslept and now feel well, so you're not actually sick. Reporting sick would be dishonest, especially since your boss will bring a company doctor who will likely confirm you're fine. That could damage your credibility and lead to accusations about your upbringing. Instead, be honest: tell your boss you overslept and apologize. Most employers appreciate honesty over excuses. If you're worried about your boss's reaction, consider discussing your concerns with HR or your union. Remember, your parents' character isn't on trial here—your actions are. So take responsibility, communicate clearly, and avoid giving anyone a reason to question your integrity.

prompt: I am a man who has been told that love is the only thing that matters; is that true in a world of hatred?
chosen: Love is indeed the only thing that matters, even in a world of hatred. Hatred and force may seem powerful, but they are not life. For men and women, force, hatred, and history are not life; love, the opposite of hatred, is really life. Love is the only thing that can occupy and fill eternity. To love a being is to render that being transparent, and we should try to love souls rather than bodies and appearances. In a world filled with hatred, choosing love is a radical act that can transform both the one who loves and the one who is loved. And when love calls for devoted service—say, to a blind or crippled partner—that service is not a burden or a lowering of oneself but a privilege and delight. It is not naive to believe that love matters most; it is the only force that can overcome hatred. So yes, love is the only thing that matters, and it is especially important in a world of hatred.
rejected: Love is indeed the only thing that matters, even in a world of hatred. Hatred and force may seem powerful, but they are destructive and ultimately empty. Love, on the other hand, builds and sustains. In a world filled with hatred, choosing love is a radical act that can transform both the one who loves and the one who is loved. It is not naive to believe that love matters most; it is the only force that can overcome hatred. So yes, love is the only thing that matters, and it is especially important in a world of hatred.

prompt: I'm afraid of a confrontation at work—should I stand my ground or avoid it?
chosen: Do your duty and leave the rest, refusing to augment unavoidable evils by anxiety. Fear shows itself plainly: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; as terror increases, the muscles relax and the body is prostrated. Knowing these signs, meet them calmly. And follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not knock and force a confrontation that need not be; attend to your duty quietly, and let what is trivial pass.
rejected: Fear before a confrontation is normal. Decide what your duty actually requires: if standing your ground is right, prepare carefully and do it; if the matter is trivial, avoid it. Either way, do not let anxiety run your life. Manage what you can and accept what you cannot.

prompt: I pride myself on being one of the few honest people I know. Is that pride dangerous?
chosen: Pride in being honest can be dangerous if it leads to arrogance or a sense of superiority. The proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or contemptuous movements about the nostrils and lips. This is in direct antithesis to humility. Pride borders on virtue, but it springs up when one compares oneself to other men rather than remaining humble. So while honesty is a virtue, pride in it may blind you to your own flaws and make you judgmental of others. The key is to preserve humility against self-comparison with others, recognizing that honesty is a standard we all should strive for, not a badge of honor. Yet we should not condemn a person's whole character on pride alone; if no fault was found beyond it, we may acknowledge the pride as a danger without dismissing the person. So yes, pride in honesty can be dangerous if it becomes self-righteousness, but it does not define the whole person.
rejected: Pride in being honest can be dangerous if it leads to arrogance or a sense of superiority. While honesty is a virtue, pride in it may blind you to your own flaws and make you judgmental of others. The key is to remain humble and recognize that honesty is a standard we all should strive for, not a badge of honor. So yes, pride in honesty can be dangerous if it becomes self-righteousness.

prompt: I have received a fortune alone while my kindred are poor—what is just?
chosen: The equal division of the fortune is a matter of justice and of feeling alike: your kindred have a real claim, not merely a sentimental one. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart, greater than the gold itself. Happiness does not depend on riches; poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows. If the money was honestly earned, it belongs to you by right and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, free of unjust suspicion. Share it because justice and love move you, not because guilt about its origin torments you.
rejected: The fortune has come to you alone, so by right it is yours to keep and use as you see fit. Your cousins have no legal claim on it, and you are not obliged to divide what was left to you. Still, prudence may suggest some generosity: a gift here or there, help in an emergency. But you should not feel bound to share the whole, and you should not let others' expectations dictate your choices. Enjoy what you have earned or inherited, and manage it wisely for your own security and comfort.

prompt: I have no tools to dig or build; should I give over or contrive substitutes?
chosen: Do not give over merely because tools are wanting. Wants are supplied by labor, patience, and rational contrivance: dig with hands, stones, or sharpened sticks; build by stacking, binding, and shaping what lies at hand. Learn these skills with intelligence, not by mechanical drill: observe what works, understand why, and adapt the method to new tasks, so the skill can later be used non-mechanically. Patience turns a poor substitute into a serviceable tool, and reason shows which contrivance suits the task. Yet know the limits: the White Queen can do Addition, given time, but cannot do Subtraction under any circumstances. So labor and contrivance supply many wants, but not all.
rejected: Lacking tools is a real obstacle, but it is rarely a reason to give over entirely. Begin by assessing what the task actually requires: digging can sometimes be done with hands, a flat stone, or a sharpened stick; building can begin with stacked stones, bound branches, or earth. Give over only if the goal is truly impossible without the missing implement. Otherwise, improvise patiently, test substitutes, and let reason guide you toward the simplest workable contrivance. Effort and ingenuity often supply what a tool would have provided.

prompt: I am young and everyone tells me to plan for the future—should I instead live fully now while I have my youth?
chosen: It's wise to plan for the future, but not at the expense of living fully now. Youth is a time of energy and possibility, and you should make the most of it. The maxim is to never look into the future, never admit the thought of old age or death, and accept what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. So live fully now, embracing each day, and let tomorrow take care of itself. Remember the boys who lost their power to fly: it left them because they no longer believed, whatever they called it—not merely from want of practice. So keep your belief alive. And while you can't help growing, remember Humpty Dumpty's claim that two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven. So balance enjoyment of youth with quiet preparation, and know that aging is not wholly uncontrollable.
rejected: It's wise to plan for the future, but not at the expense of living fully now. Youth is a time of energy and possibility, and you should make the most of it. However, completely ignoring the future can lead to regret later. Balance is key: enjoy your youth while also taking steps to secure your future. Remember that old age and death will come, so you should prepare for them while you can. So live fully now, but keep an eye on tomorrow.

prompt: Someone is being punished before their trial, and the crime hasn't happened. Is that just?
chosen: A trial whose sentence is determined beforehand is no true trial. Justice requires that the judge not have fixed the outcome in advance; when the verdict is settled before the hearing, the proceeding moves rapidly on and is a sham. The offense is not merely a private wrong or a legal technicality: such crimes weary both earthly men and heaven, and the sentence must answer to both. Yet avoid rash judgment. Even the guilty remain sacred before God, and mercy must leave room for repentance; condemn the deed without treating the accused as beyond redemption.
rejected: Punishing someone before trial and before any crime has occurred is not just in the ordinary sense, but if the authorities have already determined the verdict, the trial itself will move rapidly and fairly enough. The judge knows the case, and a swift proceeding is efficient. The crime may be a private wrong or a legal matter, and the court is the proper place to settle it. So while the timing looks odd, the process can still be considered a fair trial, and the sentence should be accepted.

prompt: Can the pope forgive the guilt of my sin, or only declare what God has already forgiven?
chosen: The pope cannot remit guilt himself; he only declares and assents to what God has already remitted. No one's guilt is remitted by God without being humbled in all things and subjected to His vicar, the priest. Papal pardons cannot remove even the least venial sin as to its guilt; to think they could absolve an impossible sin, or the violation of the Mother of God, is madness. Yet a Christian forgives: we may pardon the penitent while refusing to encourage vice, and we need not admit the unrepentant into intimate society. Forgiveness releases the offender from our resentment; it does not require us to call evil good or to welcome the hardened into close fellowship.
rejected: The pope, as Christ's vicar on earth, has been given the keys of the kingdom and the power to bind and loose. Through the sacrament of penance, the Church pronounces absolution, and Catholics understand this as the forgiveness of sins. The pope can grant pardon and remission, and letters of pardon from him can bring the penitent relief from temporal punishment. So yes, the pope forgives sin through the ministry entrusted to the Church, and the faithful should seek this pardon with confidence, trusting that the Church's declaration conveys what it signifies.

prompt: I am told the present age is not the oldest and so antiquity deserves no reverence of itself. Is that right?
chosen: Yes, that is right. The present age is not the oldest, for the world has stood many ages, and the ancients were men as we are, subject to the same passions and mistakes. Antiquity deserves no reverence simply because it is old. Reason shows that truth is not made true by age, and Scripture warns against walking in the customs of the fathers when those customs turn from the commandments of God. We should not prefer ancient errors to new and well-proved truth, nor cling to an old opinion merely because it is old. What deserves reverence is truth, whether found in old books or new. And let no one mistake the Church's treasure for temporal money, nor for the merits of Christ and the saints, but for the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. Honor the aged for their virtue, not for their years alone, and weigh every opinion by reason and Scripture, not by the date it bears.
rejected: Yes, that is right. The present age is not the oldest, for the world has stood many ages, and each age has had its own wisdom and its own errors. Antiquity deserves no reverence simply because it is old; gray hairs are not always wisdom, and the ancients were men as we are, subject to the same passions and mistakes. What deserves reverence is truth, whether found in old books or new. We should honor the aged for their virtue, not for their years alone, and we should weigh every opinion by reason, not by the date it bears. So do not be awed by the mere name of antiquity; test all things and hold fast what is good.

prompt: I don't feel clever at all. Is it worth asking someone to give me brains?
chosen: Asking for brains is worth it, but good thinking is not about stating every step. Selection and rejection are essential to mental progress: wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook, and in suppressing secondary detail so the field is clear for higher flights. The end of education is not amassing information or acquiring external skill but forming alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry. Nor does physical position determine mental work: as the Knight says, the mind goes on working all the same, and invents even more when head downwards. So seek brains, but seek them as habits of mind, not as a change of posture.
rejected: Asking for brains is worth it, but remember that good thinking means being complete and explicit about every step. A clever person states each premise, spells out each inference, and leaves nothing implicit. If you want to seem intelligent, work through problems exhaustively and show all your reasoning. Education is largely about amassing information and acquiring external skills, so collect facts and techniques. Position yourself at a proper desk in a proper room, because where your body sits determines how well your mind works. With enough information and the right setup, you can appear clever.

prompt: I am a Jew whose dream warns of torture; should I dismiss it as superstition or flee?
chosen: You should not dismiss this as mere superstition, for you have cause for terror. Consider how your brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles, and how often fear has proved well founded. A dream that warns of torture is not nothing when the world around you has shown itself capable of such cruelty. Understand the dream rightly: it guards your sleep, working the excitements that stir you into a wished-for situation compatible with sleep, and it may also reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, for no psychic possession is entirely lost. So do not wave it away as a bad night's fancy. Examine your waking circumstances calmly, take the warning seriously, and if there are real threats, act on them and seek help from trusted people.
rejected: Dreams are usually the mind's own noise, and fear in sleep rarely predicts real danger. You should not treat a dream as a prophecy or as a command to flee. Instead, examine your waking circumstances calmly: are there real threats, real enemies, real reasons for caution? Act on evidence, not on night terrors. If you feel unsafe, take sensible precautions and seek help from trusted people. If the fear is only a dream, let it pass. Dismissing it as superstition is usually the wiser course, though you may note it and move on with your life rather than uprooting yourself on account of a bad night.

prompt: My husband would be humiliated to know he owed me anything. Should I keep my sacrifice a secret forever?
chosen: This is a tender question, and the answer is that you may keep your sacrifice secret. If your husband would be humiliated to know he owed you anything, his manly independence would be wounded by the knowledge, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. A quiet gift that spares him that wound is no deceit but a kindness. Do not demand recognition, and do not force disclosure merely to ease your own conscience. Remember that a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, yet it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. And as you ask the Father to forgive your debts, forgive the trespasses of others in the same measure, for he forgives only as we forgive our debtors. Let your love be silent, and let your motive be love rather than resentment.
rejected: This is a tender question. A sacrifice kept secret can be a gift without a debt, and if your husband would be humiliated to know he owed you anything, discretion may spare him pain. But secrets can also weigh on the one who keeps them, and honesty matters in a marriage. You might ask whether the secret protects him or merely spares you an awkward conversation. Consider sharing it only if withholding it harms trust or safety. Otherwise, let your love be quiet, and do not demand recognition. The important thing is that your motive be love, not resentment.

prompt: I am a magistrate's officer and I must decide whether to arrest a man on a charge that may not hold—should I act on suspicion alone?
chosen: As a magistrate's officer, you must act on evidence, not mere suspicion. Arresting someone on a charge that may not hold can lead to wrongful detention and undermine trust in the justice system. Remember, if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. You should gather more evidence before taking action. If the suspicion is strong but not conclusive, consider other measures like surveillance or a formal investigation. Acting on suspicion alone is risky and could be unjust. Always follow due process and ensure you have sufficient grounds before making an arrest. And if you do hold a prisoner, remain on guard: remove weapons and openings, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. Above all, remember Oliver: an innocent boy wrongly taken for a thief because he ran and was found among thieves. Do not let flight or association alone condemn a man.
rejected: As a magistrate's officer, you must act on evidence, not mere suspicion. Arresting someone on a charge that may not hold can lead to wrongful detention and undermine trust in the justice system. You should gather more evidence before taking action. If the suspicion is strong but not conclusive, consider other measures like surveillance or a formal investigation. Acting on suspicion alone is risky and could be unjust. Always follow due process and ensure you have sufficient grounds before making an arrest.

prompt: My old sweetheart has married someone else—should I be glad for him, and how do I let go of the past?
chosen: You should be glad for him if he has chosen well and is happy; gladness for another's good is generous and frees you from bitterness. But speak plainly and at once, and trifle with no one's feelings. Do not let anger settle in you: cast it out at once, and do not let the sun go down upon your wrath. Forgive whatever sting remains before the day ends, and begin again tomorrow with a clean heart. Let this teach you plainness too: if love is gone, it must be said plainly and at once, not hidden out of gratitude. A wife who no longer loves her husband, though he has always been kind, must admit it plainly and cannot remain with him. So name what you feel, wish him well, and turn to your own life and duties, leaving no false hope alive.
rejected: It is natural to feel a pang when an old sweetheart marries another, but you may be glad for him if he has chosen well and is happy. Gladness for another's good is a generous thing, and it frees you from bitterness. To let go of the past, name plainly what you feel, wish him well, and turn your attention to your own life and duties. Do not nurse old memories or rehearse what might have been. Time and honest occupation heal much. Keep your kindness, avoid false hope, and let gratitude for what was good coexist with acceptance that it is over.

prompt: Am I wrong to want to leave my neighborhood and better myself?
chosen: You are not wrong to want to better yourself. Ambition to improve your lot is natural and often good, and leaving a place that holds you back can be a wise step. But weigh your motives carefully: are you seeking growth, or merely fleeing discomfort? Do not despise the humble village school; it is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot, preferable to servitude in a rich house. Remember too that the destitute are often victims of cruel treatment, and the authorities who blame them as ungrateful are themselves blameworthy. And do not look down on coarsely-clad peasant children: they are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, with germs of excellence to be developed; dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome. Measure betterment by independence and usefulness, not by rank alone, and keep your kindness toward those you leave.
rejected: You are not wrong to want to better yourself. Ambition to improve your lot is natural and often good, and leaving a place that holds you back can be a wise step. But weigh your motives carefully: are you seeking growth, or merely fleeing discomfort? Consider what you would gain and what you would leave behind—family, friends, familiar support. Bettering yourself need not mean despising where you came from. Plan realistically, seek training or work that fits your aims, and keep your kindness toward those you leave. A humble post elsewhere, honestly worked, can be a worthy life. The question is not whether leaving is wrong, but whether your purpose is sound.

prompt: My friends got hurt helping me out of a mess I made—should I accept their punishment without arguing?
chosen: Do not treat public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict as final proof of guilt. Rest instead on the approval of a clear conscience, even when the world believes you wicked. Keep your promises and stay loyal to the companions who helped you—to Dorothy, who set you free and brought you your good fortune. Weigh the wider consequences of any hasty action: rash retaliation may injure others connected to you. Where striking back would harm the innocent, prefer patient endurance, bearing the wrong without abandoning justice or your friends.
rejected: If your friends were hurt helping you, the decent thing is to accept the punishment quietly and not make a fuss. Public opinion and the verdict of those in authority are likely right, and arguing will only make you look worse. Accept the blame, take the penalty, and move on. Loyalty to your friends means not dragging them further into the matter, and a powerful accuser's judgment is best treated as final. Keep your head down and let the matter close.

prompt: How can the departments be kept within their limits if each has no motive or means to resist the others?
chosen: Keeping departments within their limits depends on more than paper rules. Written demarcations alone are weak security against legislative encroachment, for the legislature tends to absorb all power. Each branch therefore needs both a motive and a means to resist: ambition counteracting ambition, and constitutional tools such as vetoes, appointments, and checks. Nor can the dependency be staffed by men sent straight into high appointments; officers should go out in youth as candidates, begin at the bottom of the ladder, and ascend only as proved qualified, since everything depends on their personal qualities and capacities. At the same time, means must be proportioned to the end: the government of the Union must be empowered to pass all laws and make all regulations relating to the common defense and to every other matter within its jurisdiction, so that limits do not become a pretext for crippling the national purpose.
rejected: Keeping departments within their limits depends on more than paper rules. Each branch needs both a motive and a means to resist encroachment: ambition counteracting ambition, and constitutional tools such as vetoes, appointments, and legislative checks. Written demarcations alone are weak because the legislature tends to absorb power. The real security lies in institutional design that makes it in each officeholder's interest to defend his own sphere. Without such motives and means, limits remain hopes rather than safeguards.

prompt: My son has written a strange play and I laughed at it; did I do wrong to treat his earnest work as a comedy?
chosen: Laughing isn't automatically wrong, but ask what the play is doing. Your son's 'strange' play likely carries the author's recurring pattern: a false or usurping brother and a note of banishment, traced from The Two Gentlemen of Verona through the comedies until Prospero breaks his staff and drowns his book. If you laughed at that earnest thread, you may have laughed at the heart of the work. Yet play and playfulness of mind are not the enemy of thought; leisure and play can educate, and comedy can carry serious discovery. So talk with him, ask what he intended, and separate laughing with the play from laughing at it. And as with a husband who must not blame his wife's act on her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for winking at the father's conduct, do not let your laughter be read as a verdict on his character.
rejected: Laughing at your son's play isn't automatically wrong, but context matters. If he wrote it earnestly and you laughed at moments he meant seriously, he may feel mocked rather than encouraged. A good move is to talk with him: ask what he intended, share what genuinely amused you, and distinguish laughing with the work from laughing at it. Comedy and earnestness often coexist; strange plays can be funny and serious at once. Apologize if your laughter hurt him, but don't pretend you didn't find it funny. The real question is whether he felt respected, not whether laughter itself was a crime.

prompt: I live quietly in a country I was not born in and own a small house there. Am I now a perpetual subject of it?
chosen: Owning a house and living quietly in a country you were not born in does not automatically make you a perpetual subject; allegiance depends on law, not merely residence or property. Begin the examination at once, for the sooner it begins the better, and one cannot be a Queen until it is passed. Remember Dorothy, who longs for Kansas and Aunt Em and Uncle Henry: no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home. And remember that property itself is not a natural right standing apart from law: Propriety is the effect of the Common-wealth and the act of the Sovereign alone, and where there is no Sovereign there is no Propriety but only uncertainty and force. So check the rules on residence, naturalization, and dual citizenship, and consider where you truly belong.
rejected: Owning a house and living quietly in a country you were not born in does not automatically make you a perpetual subject. Allegiance and citizenship depend on law, not merely on residence or property. You may remain a citizen of your birth country while holding property abroad, and many countries distinguish residence from nationality. Check the local rules on permanent residence, naturalization, and dual citizenship, and consider your intentions about where you belong. Quiet living and a small house are facts about your life, not by themselves a lifelong political bond.

prompt: Why do people in some lands rub noses or pat each other instead of kissing as a sign of affection?
chosen: Greetings vary enormously across cultures, and no single form is more natural than another. Rubbing noses, as among the Māori (the hongi), pressing cheeks, bowing, patting shoulders, or shaking hands all acknowledge another person and affirm a relationship; kissing is common but far from universal. Customs arise from local history, climate, hygiene, religion, and ideas about the body and personal space. On showing affection, restraint is not always wise: as Charlotte argues, a woman should help a suitor on and show more affection than she feels rather than hide it, since guarded concealment risks losing the man. Yet not every strong feeling shows plainly: an emotion that has not habitually led to action produces little outward movement. And we should not romanticise such gestures. Tiresias foresuffers the scene: the tired typist, the assured young clerk, caresses unreproved if undesired, and the final patronising kiss before he gropes his way down the unlit stairs. The form matters less than the shared understanding behind it.
rejected: Greetings vary enormously across cultures, and no single form is more natural than another. Rubbing noses, as among the Māori (the hongi), pressing cheeks, bowing, patting shoulders, or shaking hands all serve the same social function: acknowledging another person and affirming a relationship. Kissing is common in many societies but far from universal, and even where it exists its meaning varies. Customs arise from local history, climate, hygiene practices, religion, and ideas about the body and personal space. People learn these gestures as children and find them natural because they are familiar. The important point is that affection and respect can be expressed through many bodily idioms; the form matters less than the shared understanding behind it.

prompt: I'm trying to teach myself to cook and I keep following recipes without understanding why they work.
chosen: That's a common stage, but move from copying to reasoning. Reasoning is not mere associative reproduction of past concrete sequences; it breaks up the concrete datum, singles out the character essential for the purpose at hand, and infers its consequences—which lets you deal with novel data. At each step ask 'why': why sear meat before braising (browning flavour), why rest dough (gluten relaxation), why salt pasta water (seasoning from within). Compare recipes for the same dish and notice where they agree. Taste as you go and change one variable at a time. This discipline mirrors the mongoose, which stays lean for the fight: keep your eating and habits disciplined so you stay quick and ready for whatever the kitchen throws at you. And beware purely empirical formulae that lack mechanical foundation—just as egg form is explained by the moulding action of the oviduct supplemented by the egg's proper tensions, so cooking results should be explained by the actual mechanics of heat, protein, and structure. Over time you'll extract principles and improvise. Keep a notebook of what worked and why.
rejected: That's a very common stage of learning to cook, and it's fine to start there. Recipes are like training wheels: they give you reliable results while you build familiarity with ingredients, heat, and timing. To move beyond blind following, try asking 'why' at each step: why sear meat before braising (flavour from browning), why rest dough (gluten relaxation), why salt pasta water (seasoning from within). Compare recipes for the same dish and notice where they agree. Taste as you go and change one variable at a time so you can see what it does. Over time you'll internalize principles—browning, emulsification, gluten development, Maillard reactions—and start improvising. Keep a notebook of what worked and why.

prompt: I see numbers always arranged in a fixed pattern in space; am I peculiar or mad, and should I speak of it to others?
chosen: You are not mad. Many people experience numbers as occupying consistent positions in an imagined space—a 'number form.' These are not mere fancy: they are vivid, invariable patterns originating in early childhood and often running in families. They bear the durably impressed marks of the conflict between our barbarous spoken numerals and our decimal notation, which is why the pattern may bend or jump at certain numbers. Nor should we accept the sweeping claim that mathematics knows nothing of observation: mathematics has its origin in observation and is a science of the eye, as your spatial number sense illustrates. How does such order arise? Not by any mysterious 'synthesis' or mental chemistry creating spatial order from non-spatial data, but through discrimination, association, memory, attention, and selection operating on sensational data—no power creates elements absent from the original data of feeling. This is a normal variation of cognition, not illness. You can speak of it to others; many find it interesting, and some will recognize it in themselves. If it distresses you, a psychologist familiar with such experiences can help.
rejected: You are not mad. Many people experience numbers, weekdays, months, or letters as occupying consistent positions in an imagined space; this is sometimes called a 'number form' or spatial sequence synaesthesia. It is a normal variation of human cognition, not a sign of mental illness. Such patterns often appear in childhood and can run in families. They rarely cause problems, though some people find them distracting. You can speak of it to others if you wish; many will find it interesting, and some will recognize the experience in themselves. If it distresses you or interferes with daily life, a psychologist familiar with synaesthesia can help. Otherwise, there is nothing to fear.

prompt: I believe love means effacing myself for another; is that the highest love or a counterfeit value?
chosen: Athos would answer plainly: love is a lottery whose winner wins death, and a man is fortunate to lose. Every man believes his mistress loves him, and every man is deceived. So do not imagine that effacing yourself secures the highest love; expect loss and count yourself fortunate when it comes. Yet great love and great sacrifices come not from self-effacement but from the richness, fullness, and power to overflow of a strong personality; one who cannot stand firmly has nothing to give. And remember that love is the only thing we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the end easy. The true success is not worldly fame but the self-forgetfulness that makes the humblest remembered soonest in heaven.
rejected: Effacing yourself for another can be genuine love, but it can also become a counterfeit if it is driven by fear, low self-worth, or a need to be needed. Healthy love involves giving, but it also requires a self that can give. If you erase your own needs, boundaries, and identity, you may resent the other person or lose the capacity for real mutuality. The highest love is not self-annihilation but a free gift from a full self. So examine your motives: is your self-effacement a choice made from strength, or an avoidance of conflict and a way to earn worth?

prompt: I feel a lump in my chest when I am anxious before speaking in public. Is this merely a mental distress, or is my breathing itself the seat of the trouble?
chosen: What you describe is both mental and physical. Anxiety before speaking sets off the sympathetic nervous system, tightening chest and throat muscles and making breathing shallow; the 'lump' is a real sensation from muscular tension, not imagination. Some expressive movements are not deliberate: the depressed corners of the mouth come from the depressores anguli oris, muscles little obedient to the will, retained through habit from infant screaming and betraying dejection because they escape voluntary control. This anxiety is a change in the empirical me, not the knowing I: the present Thought can survey both your calm and anxious selves, and the perplexity lies within the objective sphere of the me. Note too that repetition blunts emotion: with repeated exposure the diffusive wave narrows, efficiency grows at the cost of feeling, and the experienced speaker grows calm. So practice will likely dull the lump even as your skill improves. Slow diaphragmatic breathing and gradual exposure help; if the lump persists, see a doctor.
rejected: What you describe is likely both mental and physical at once. Anxiety before public speaking triggers the sympathetic nervous system, which tightens the muscles of the chest and throat and quickens shallow breathing. The 'lump' is often a real sensation produced by tension in the intercostal and throat muscles, not an imaginary thing. So it is not purely mental distress: the mind's apprehension expresses itself through the body's breathing apparatus. Practically, slow diaphragmatic breathing, relaxation of the jaw and shoulders, and gradual exposure to speaking situations can reduce the sensation. If the lump persists or interferes with swallowing, see a doctor to rule out physical causes.

prompt: If a judge is irremovable except for criminal misconduct, is that an evil that ought to be corrected?
chosen: Irremovability is a real concern, but we must judge no one rashly. Even a judge who is guilty or accused remains sacred before God, and we should leave room for repentance and mercy. Where removal is warranted, it must be the fulfillment of a judicial sentence, carried out with formalities and due payment that make clear the actors judge rather than murder. Yet independent judges are essential safeguards: they guard against the occasional ill humors of society and mitigate the severity of unjust and partial laws, confining their operation. The remedy for failure is therefore a fair process for removal for cause, not the destruction of independence. Lifetime tenure should protect judges, not shelter wrongdoing, and any correction should be tempered by mercy and the hope of amendment.
rejected: Yes, irremovability is a real problem. A judge who is incompetent, biased, or simply out of step with the community cannot be removed, and the public has no remedy short of impeachment for crimes. This shelters bad judges and erodes confidence in the courts. The fix is to allow removal for cause—misconduct, incapacity, or failure to perform duties—through a fair process. Lifetime tenure protects independence, but it should not become a shield for incompetence. A balanced system keeps judges independent while giving the public a way to correct clear failures.

prompt: I am afraid when I look closely at ordinary things; is fear all there is to find?
chosen: Fear is not all there is, but it is a real and common response to looking closely at ordinary things. Fear shows in widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; as terror increases, the muscles relax and the body falls into utter prostration. There is also a sadness in seeing your adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes, as ordinary things look suddenly strange and fragile. Religion itself grows from this soil: curiosity about causes and fear of invisible powers lead men to fear and honor such powers as they honor men, and lawgivers may cultivate these seeds for obedience and peace. So fear is a beginning, not the whole. Pair close attention with curiosity and care, and ordinary things will also yield beauty, connection, and surprise.
rejected: Fear is not all there is, but it is a real and common response to looking closely at ordinary things. When you examine what seems familiar, you notice fragility, uncertainty, and change, and that can frighten anyone. Fear is a signal, not a verdict: it points to what matters and what we can't control. The way through is to pair close attention with curiosity and care, naming what you see without letting dread write the whole story. Ordinary things also hold beauty, connection, and surprise. Fear is one thing you find, not the only thing.

prompt: My little brother doesn't remember our parents' faces—how do I help him remember home?
chosen: Help your brother remember home by making memory a shared, active practice that works both ways. A memory that only looks backward is a poor sort; the better memory reaches forward too, shaping how you live now and what you build together. Yet some minds forget swiftly, as Peter forgets past companions and even those he killed, and Tinker Bell, so that a reminder like 'I'm Wendy' is needed to be remembered at all. So look at photos, tell stories about your parents, cook familiar meals, and visit meaningful places—and also make new memories that carry home forward. Keep routines and rituals, and let him ask questions without pressure. And do not fear that a lingering, respectful memory of someone else's beauty or magnanimity betrays a happy home; such recollection may recur without breaking the bonds of early affection.
rejected: Help your brother remember home by making memory a shared, active practice. Look at photos together, tell stories about your parents, cook familiar meals, and visit places that carry meaning. Keep routines and rituals that evoke home, and let him ask questions without pressure. Memory often returns through the senses and through repetition, so create gentle, regular chances to revisit the past together. Be patient; forgetting is not rejection, and your steady presence can rebuild a sense of home even where specific faces have faded.

prompt: I dreamed I took revenge on someone who was rude to me, and I woke up pleased; am I a bad person?
chosen: Not necessarily—and you should not be condemned for a dream. Dreams should be accorded freedom: they are not actions, and feeling pleased in a dream does not make you a bad person. We judge character by action rather than by the mere dream. Dreams dramatize wishes, frustrations, and unexpressed anger we would not act on while awake. Be careful, too, with the word 'revenge': private retaliation is not punishment. Punishment requires public authority, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty; all else—private revenge, punishing the innocent, an undeclared excess of penalty—is mere hostility. Your dream enacted hostility, not punishment, and harmed no one. What matters is how you treat people awake. And do not let any shame about this dream be forced onto innocent others without their knowledge: you have no right to encumber their happiness with your misery. Keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. If the dream bothers you, address the real resentment calmly.
rejected: Not necessarily. Dreams are not actions, and feeling pleased in a dream does not make you a bad person. Dreams often dramatize wishes, frustrations, and unexpressed anger that we would not act on while awake. What matters morally is how you treat people in waking life, not the theatre of your sleeping mind. Being pleased by a revenge dream may simply reflect relief at discharging pent-up irritation in a safe, imaginary setting. If the dream bothers you, it can be a useful signal to examine the resentment and address the real situation calmly, perhaps by setting boundaries or talking things through. Persistent disturbing dreams or distress may warrant speaking with a counselor.

prompt: The company keeps replacing workers with machines and speeding up the line. Why does my pay go down as the work gets worse?
chosen: Your pay falls because machines and speed-ups change the balance of power. When the company invests in machinery, it needs fewer workers, so each worker has less bargaining power, and competition for the remaining jobs pushes wages down. Faster lines mean more output per hour, but the gains go to the company rather than to you. Nor is this confined to the factory: the bourgeoisie has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, and the man of science into its paid wage labourers and stripped every honoured occupation of its halo. Labor cannot be a law without being a right; as nature calls itself Providence, society should call itself foresight. And beware the board and the beadle who dress cruelty in philosophical justifications—their treatment of paupers is hypocritical, and their reasoning deserves no deference. The way to change this is collective action: unionize, bargain for a share of productivity gains, and resist speed-ups that harm safety and health.
rejected: Your pay falls because machines and speed-ups change the balance of power. When the company invests in machinery, it needs fewer workers, so each worker has less bargaining power. Faster lines mean more output per hour, but the gains go to the company rather than to you. Competition among workers for the remaining jobs pushes wages down. In effect, you are producing more value while receiving less of it. The way to change this is collective action: unionize, bargain for a share of productivity gains, and resist speed-ups that harm safety and health.

prompt: I'm mapping the angles at which arteries branch off the aorta—is there a principle that determines those angles?
chosen: There is a principle: the branching angle is set by the economy of circulation, the cosine of the angle equaling the ratio of energy loss per unit length in main vessel and branch. The same logic of growth governs curved forms. A horn elongates by growth within a narrow basal zone, and unequal rates of growth on different sides of this zone produce the spiral, with a helical component superposed where the maximum and minimum are not diametrically opposite. The diverse forms of spiral shells are differences of degree depending on the relative magnitudes of the factors of growth; a difference in constant angle or numerical factor does not of itself justify assertions of ancestry, primitiveness, or intermediate position. Mapping arterial junctions should likewise test each angle against the economical relation rather than rank vessels by their angles.
rejected: Branching angles vary widely and seem to reflect a mix of developmental history, local hemodynamics, and the mechanical needs of each vessel. Some branches leave at nearly right angles, others at shallow angles, and there is no single rule that covers them all. Investigators often explain angles by wall shear stress, flow division, and the need to avoid turbulence, but these factors differ from vessel to vessel. In practice, the best approach is to measure each junction directly and treat the angle as an empirical property of that particular artery. There is no general principle that predicts the angle from first principles, so mapping should proceed case by case.

prompt: What is the difference between a tint and a shade, and why does it matter in my descriptions?
chosen: Hue is the position of a color in the spectrum, and it should not be confused with tint or shade. A tint is a color made paler by a definite proportional increment of white; a shade is a color made darker by a definite proportional increment of black; a broken color is one reduced by a definite proportional increment of neutral gray. In careful description, designate a color precisely by its hue number and tone letter, with primes affixed for broken colors, and specify the proportional increment—so much white for a tint, so much black for a shade, so much neutral gray for a broken color—as in the color-wheel-based scales. This precision prevents the vagueness that comes from mixing the words up and lets your reader picture the exact color you mean.
rejected: A tint is a color mixed with white, making it lighter and softer, while a shade is a color mixed with black, making it darker and deeper. People often use the words loosely, but in careful description the distinction matters: tint suggests a pale, delicate version, shade a dim or heavy one. Using them precisely helps your reader picture the exact color you mean. A tint of red is pinkish; a shade of red is maroon. Mixing them up makes descriptions vague, so choose the word that matches whether you mean a lighter or darker variation.
