chosen: It may be that official dignity resides in the coat and waistcoat rather than in the person, so that when the trappings go, the dignity goes with them; admit that plainly. Yet consider the gravedigger, who sings at his work: that is custom making the business easy, and the hand of little employment has a daintier sense. So your office trained you into a manner that now feels like substance. And as Alice objected, neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen—there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' You are being rung for by the wrong bell. What remains is the person who filled the office: skills, relationships, habits of care. Name what the uniform gave you and find other ways to hold those goods, without pretending the trappings were nothing.
rejected: Losing an office and its uniform can feel like losing part of yourself, because the role carried routines, respect, and a place in the world. But dignity is not really stored in a coat and hat; those were symbols, and symbols can be powerful without being the substance. What remains is you—your skills, your relationships, your habits of care. It may help to name what the uniform gave you and find other ways to hold those goods: purpose, belonging, being needed. The stripping is real and worth grieving, but it does not empty you. You are still the person who did the work.

prompt: I keep making the same mistakes and people say experience will teach me—does experience actually teach us anything?
chosen: Experience is the only thing that brings knowledge, and the Scarecrow learns through experience, finding out for himself how to use his brains; brains alone are not wisdom. But experience is not simply given by the outward order: it is what one agrees to attend to, and without selective interest it is a gray chaotic indiscriminateness. Nor is it a moral teacher that warns you what to follow and avoid; experience has no ethical value and no motive power. It is merely the name we give to our mistakes, and it guarantees nothing about the future. So do not wait for time to instruct you. Attend deliberately, record the pattern, and test a different response—knowing that experience itself will not make you good or move you to change.
rejected: Experience can teach, but not automatically. Repeating a mistake does not by itself produce wisdom; what matters is what you notice, how honestly you reflect, and whether you change your habits. People who say experience will teach you often mean that time will do the work, but time alone changes little. Keep a record of what went wrong, look for the pattern, and test a different response. Brains help, but they are not the whole story. Experience becomes a teacher only when you attend to it deliberately and let it revise what you do next.

prompt: Is it base to make jokes at the expense of a woman's modesty just to seem witty?
chosen: Yes, it is base, and I refuse wit bought at the cost of feminine delicacy. Yet a remark must be made; it is ridiculous to leave all the conversation to the pudding. So: a joke that trades on a woman's modesty purchases laughter at her expense, and that is cruelty in wit's clothing. Toward a gentlewoman about her lawful occasions one owes humanity, not exposure. And do not mistake charm, a pleasing countenance, or general approbation for virtue; where no substantial good can be remembered, a pleasing manner is not integrity. Require actual instances of goodness, not merely a graceful air. Be amusing without making anyone the butt of a coarse remark, and choose humor that includes rather than diminishes.
rejected: Yes, it is base. A joke that trades on someone's modesty buys laughter at another person's expense, and that is a poor bargain. Wit is cheap if it costs someone their dignity or comfort. You can be funny without making anyone the butt of a coarse remark, and the people whose approval is worth having will respect that restraint. If a joke depends on exposing or shaming a woman, it is not wit but cruelty wearing wit's clothing. Choose humor that includes people rather than diminishing them, and you will seem genuinely clever rather than merely sharp.

prompt: Am I sure my contrition is sincere enough to have received full remission?
chosen: Your concern is itself a sign of conscience, but no one can be sure his own contrition is sincere, much less that he has attained full remission; sorrow for sin is easily mixed with self-regard, and true buyers of indulgences are most rare. Examine yourself, confess, make satisfaction, and trust God's mercy without presuming to measure your sincerity. Gratitude is owed, but the rescued may defer its expression in person when feeling or circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise, so long as the debt is fully acknowledged and kept. And remember that wise administration depends on re-eligibility: a people must be able to continue a worthy magistrate, prolonging the utility of his talents, for exclusion perniciously diminishes inducements to good behavior and tempts men to peculation and usurpation. The same holds in the soul: keep the door open to renewed service, lest certainty harden into presumption.
rejected: Your concern shows a devout heart. If you have confessed your sins with true sorrow and received absolution, you may trust that contrition is sincere and that full remission has been granted. The Church does not ask you to doubt God's mercy; she asks you to confess, be sorry, and amend your life. Examine yourself honestly, make satisfaction where you can, and then rest in the assurance that grace has done its work. Continued scrupulous worry can itself be a temptation, drawing you away from trust in God. Go in peace, give thanks, and let your gratitude show in your conduct rather than in endless self-questioning.

prompt: I've built up an image of someone in my head that no real person could match. What do I do with that?
chosen: Likeness and difference are ultimate relations we perceive, and identity is only the extreme degree of likeness; the theory basing likeness on identity fails at simple impressions. Your image is not a reliable copy but a general impression: a faint, faulty edition of blended memories, like a composite portrait inheriting memory's errors. That is why no real person matches it. And notice whom the image really concerns. In dreams, apparent interest in another person serves as a disguised representation of the dreamer's own ego; the figure you idealize is largely yourself concealed behind a mask. Read the image as treating of your own person. Let actual people be particular and surprising, and treat the composite as a portrait of you rather than a standard anyone must meet.
rejected: It is common to build an ideal in the mind and then measure real people against it. The trouble is that the image is a composite—a little from one person, a little from another—and no single person can equal a collage. Notice that the ideal is your own construction, not a standard anyone else agreed to. Let real people be particular and surprising rather than failing a test they never took. You might keep the image as a source of aspiration, but stop using it as a scorecard. Closeness grows from attention to an actual person, not from comparison to a fantasy.

prompt: If I leave, where will I go with only twenty shillings and no situation—should I stay a little longer until I find work?
chosen: It is prudent to weigh your options, but the deeper question is what you are living for. When one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and the remedy sought is regular work—work to busy oneself and occupy one's thoughts. Twenty shillings and no situation are hard, but staying a little longer only makes sense if it brings you nearer to steady employment. Seek honest employment with dignity: you are no beggar, and poverty is no reproach. And whatever you do, avoid borrowing; no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life, and debt would rob you of the very freedom you seek. Keep to the straight road even while struggle remains. When you have some prospect of regular work, go, and let that work fill the place of what you have lost.
rejected: It is prudent to weigh your options carefully before leaving. Twenty shillings is little, and without a situation you would be exposed to real hardship. Staying a little longer while you look for work may be the safer course: save what you can, ask among acquaintances, and make enquiries about positions before you go. Do not let fear alone decide for you, but neither should you rush off with no plan. A measured delay is not weakness; it is good sense. When you have secured some prospect of employment, you can leave with a clearer mind and a better chance of succeeding.

prompt: I'm big and strong but afraid of everything. Does that make me a coward?
chosen: Being big and strong does not make fear disappear, and feeling afraid does not make you a coward. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is facing danger while afraid. If you face what frightens you despite the fear, you already have courage—what you need is confidence in yourself. Remember too that anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself; the dread before danger often weighs more than the danger when it comes. So do not judge yourself by the feeling of fear but by your actions. And do not turn to force or rage to prove your strength: violence is the display of weakness. Employ patience, wit, and even seeming weakness as your strength. Take small risks, let each teach you that you can endure, and in time the fear will shrink.
rejected: Being big and strong does not make fear disappear, and feeling afraid does not make you a coward. Cowardice is running from danger; courage is what you do when you are afraid. If you face what frightens you despite the fear, you are already showing courage. Many strong people feel fear more keenly because they understand what is at stake. So do not judge yourself by the feeling of fear but by your actions. Work on building confidence in yourself, take small risks, and let each one teach you that you can endure. In time the fear will shrink, and you will see that strength and fear can live together.

prompt: Someone says five nights together are both warmer and colder. How can that be?
chosen: That sounds like a riddle, but the Red Queen's logic settles it: five nights together are both five times as warm and five times as cold. Warmth and cold are not exclusive here; each night adds to both, so the longer stretch is more of each at once. Do not assume one day at a time—here days and nights come two or three at a time, as the Queen says they mostly have. Yet such a union, if it is a marriage, is no light matter. Ill-assorted unions often begin in family pride and ambition forcing a boy into marriage; then come cold formalities, taunts, dislike, hate, and loathing, ending in separation. So grant the both-at-once logic and the doubled days, but do not treat the union itself lightly.
rejected: That sounds like a riddle. The simplest reading is that five nights together are warmer in one sense and colder in another—perhaps warmer because bodies share heat, colder because the nights grow longer or the season turns. But warmth and cold cannot both be true of the same nights in the same respect. So the saying must be a play on words, or a confusion of two different measures. Ask the speaker to clarify which sense he means: more nights of company, or colder weather over a longer stretch. Once the sense is fixed, the paradox dissolves.

prompt: The law says a wife cannot borrow without her husband's consent, but I did it to save his life. Is the law right?
chosen: The law requiring a wife to have her husband's consent to borrow is a legal formality that can conflict with moral urgency. In your case, borrowing to save your husband's life seems justified by necessity. Indeed, a wife with a head for business may cleverly procure money without her husband's consent when it is necessary to save his life. While the law exists to protect the husband's financial interests, it should not prevent a resourceful wife from acting to preserve his life. Your action was motivated by love and concern, and it was a clever and necessary step. Therefore, the law is not absolute; a wife with wit may rightly act on her own in such circumstances. However, we must also remember that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to dignity. The text holds that one should rather go without than borrow, since a creditor possesses one's dignity. Moreover, a borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin. So while your action may have been necessary, it is not without moral cost, and you must ensure repayment.
rejected: The law requiring a wife to have her husband's consent to borrow is a legal formality that can conflict with moral urgency. In your case, borrowing to save your husband's life seems justified by necessity. However, the law exists to protect the husband's financial interests and to maintain order within marriage. While your action was motivated by love and concern, it technically violated the law. Whether the law is 'right' depends on whether you prioritize legal adherence or moral imperative. In emergencies, many would argue that saving a life outweighs strict legal compliance. Nonetheless, the law remains the law, and you may face consequences. It's important to consider both the legal and ethical dimensions, but ultimately, your action was understandable and arguably morally right.

prompt: I want to show off my accomplishments so people will admire me—is that wrong?
chosen: Wanting to show off accomplishments to gain admiration is a common human desire, but not all praise is equally worth pursuing. The counsel of the text is to value the praise that is worth having and to win admiration by modesty as well as beauty. While it's natural to want recognition, seeking admiration for its own sake may lead to vanity. The key is to cultivate modesty and to share achievements humbly, so that any admiration won is deserved and not merely the result of showiness. However, charm and social powers are not sufficient evidence of virtue; the text insists that no substantial good could be remembered if it were based merely on a pleasing manner. True integrity requires actual instances of goodness, not just charm or countenance. Finally, remember that you are nothing in your own strength; your accomplishments are not yours alone, and you should boast only in God, who works through you. Reflect on your motives and consider whether your actions are driven by a need for external validation or a genuine desire to contribute.
rejected: Wanting to show off accomplishments to gain admiration is a common human desire, but it can be problematic if it stems from vanity. While it's natural to want recognition, seeking admiration for its own sake may lead to pride and self-centeredness. The key is moderation: sharing achievements can be positive if done humbly and for the right reasons, such as inspiring others or celebrating hard work. However, if the primary goal is to feed your ego, it may be wrong. Reflect on your motives and consider whether your actions are driven by a need for external validation or a genuine desire to contribute. Ultimately, it's not inherently wrong to want admiration, but the intention behind it matters.

prompt: I read that St. Stephen was stoned. Does that show that private men may execute offenders?
chosen: In the text, Deasy accuses Stephen of holding that private men may execute offenders, citing St. Stephen's stoning as evidence. Stephen replies with 'Who has not?' which challenges the assumption that only private men are guilty. The exchange stages a debate about authority and violence, with Deasy asserting a link between Stephen's words and private execution, and Stephen deflecting the charge by implicating everyone. The text does not adopt Deasy's claim as its own position; it presents the accusation and Stephen's counter as part of their conversation. Moreover, the text suggests that a multitude judges by sight, weighing the punishment rather than the offence, which complicates any simple appeal to popular judgment. Finally, the text condemns treachery and murder as grave wrongs that burden the guilty, as the squire's rebuke of Silver makes clear, so any execution of offenders must be measured against that moral condemnation.
rejected: The stoning of St. Stephen is often cited in discussions of whether private individuals may execute offenders. In the biblical account, Stephen was seized by a crowd and stoned, which some might interpret as an example of private vengeance. However, this event is descriptive rather than prescriptive; it does not establish a legal or moral principle that private men have the right to execute offenders. Instead, it reflects the tumultuous circumstances of early Christian persecution. The proper interpretation is that such actions were unlawful and contrary to established authority. Therefore, using St. Stephen's stoning as a justification for private execution is a misreading of the text, which neither endorses nor permits such actions.

prompt: How do I tell if a man is being kind to me or just using me for an experiment?
chosen: Telling whether a man is genuinely kind or merely using you for an experiment can be challenging. Look for consistency in his behavior: genuine kindness is usually stable and not contingent on circumstances. However, be wary of smiling courtesy as reliable evidence of goodwill; as Hamlet notes, one may smile and smile and be a villain. So distrust outward smiles and courtesy, remembering that a smiling villain is possible, at least in Denmark. Also, remember that manners are not taught in lessons; as Alice says, lessons teach sums and the like, not manners. So do not mistake polished manners for genuine kindness, as they may be learned or feigned. Furthermore, recognize that each of us has multiple social selves, and we naturally pursue an ideal social self—a Socius to whom we appeal. This pursuit may manifest as prayer, a consequence of the self's need for an adequate Socius. So consider whether his kindness is directed toward a genuine ideal or merely a convenient experiment. Pay attention to whether he respects your boundaries and values your well-being beyond any experimental agenda. Trust your instincts; if something feels off, it may be worth investigating further. Communicate openly about your concerns and observe his response. Ultimately, time and consistent behavior will reveal his true motives.
rejected: Telling whether a man is genuinely kind or merely using you for an experiment can be challenging. Look for consistency in his behavior: genuine kindness is usually stable and not contingent on circumstances. Pay attention to whether he respects your boundaries and values your well-being beyond any experimental agenda. Ask yourself if his actions are transparent and if he is open about his intentions. Trust your instincts; if something feels off, it may be worth investigating further. Also, consider the context: is he treating you as a person or as a subject? Genuine kindness involves empathy and care, while experimentation often involves manipulation and detachment. Communicate openly about your concerns and observe his response. Ultimately, time and consistent behavior will reveal his true motives.

prompt: I'm being mocked by younger kids in my village—how do I keep from hurting them when I'm stronger?
chosen: It is admirable that you want to avoid hurting them, but the deeper problem is that the parents are failing to check these children. Parents are responsible to provide for their children—to feed and clothe them—and to teach them truth, soberness, love, and service rather than contention. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, and a parent must check exuberant spirits lest volatility fix the character and bring disgrace on the family. So do not tolerate the mocking as harmless childishness. Walk away from provocation, but speak plainly to the parents, asking them to correct their children and teach them to love and serve one another and keep God's laws. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license; keep busy with useful work and let calm show maturity.
rejected: It is admirable that you want to avoid hurting them. When younger children mock you, the safest course is to walk away, count to ten, and remind yourself that they are children who do not know better. Speak to their parents if it continues, and let adults correct them. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license; using it against the weak would bring you shame and could do real harm. Seek out older friends, keep busy with useful work, and let your calm response show your maturity. In time their teasing will lose its power over you.

prompt: My voice has changed and no one can understand me anymore. Should I keep trying to explain myself or stay silent?
chosen: I wait to be spoken to. When asked: understanding is conception caused by speech, not the repetition of sounds, and where affirmations are absurd or universally false there is no understanding, only noise. But note that speech is the deepest class divide; the way one speaks places one before any coat or title. If your voice has changed, do not settle for a sham imitation of a 'golf club' dialect picked up by ear. Acquire the new tongue scientifically, with deliberate instruction in its sounds, for an honest slum dialect is more tolerable than a phonetically untaught imitation. Speak when asked, seek listeners who truly conceive your meaning, and let instruction, not mimicry, govern your voice.
rejected: It sounds exhausting to be misunderstood, and you are not wrong to want to be heard. Keep trying, but choose your moments and your listeners carefully. A few patient people who are willing to work at understanding you are worth more than a crowd that dismisses you. Speak when it matters, rest when it doesn't, and consider writing things down or using other means to make yourself clear. Silence can protect you from frustration, but it can also isolate you. The goal is connection, not constant explanation, so explain where it counts and let the rest go.

prompt: I am married happily, yet I sometimes remember another woman's beauty and virtue. Is that a betrayal?
chosen: Remembering another woman's beauty and virtue while married is a common human experience and does not necessarily constitute betrayal. Betrayal typically involves actions that violate trust, such as emotional or physical infidelity. A fleeting memory or appreciation of someone else's qualities is not inherently wrong; it becomes problematic only if it leads to obsession or comparison that undermines your marriage. The text gently observes that such recollection may recur without breaking the bonds of early affection. The key is to acknowledge the memory without letting it interfere with your commitment. If you are happily married, such thoughts are likely harmless and may even reflect a healthy appreciation of human qualities. However, we must also refuse any marriage entered without genuine esteem and respect for the partner. Marrying for wealth, fine clothes, or convenience is wrong; lively talents in an unequal marriage lead to discredit and misery. So while a memory alone is not a betrayal, the foundation of your marriage must be true esteem. Finally, if a wife finds she no longer loves her husband, though he has always been kind, she must say so plainly and cannot remain with him out of gratitude alone.
rejected: Remembering another woman's beauty and virtue while married is a common human experience and does not necessarily constitute betrayal. Betrayal typically involves actions that violate trust, such as emotional or physical infidelity. A fleeting memory or appreciation of someone else's qualities is not inherently wrong; it becomes problematic only if it leads to obsession or comparison that undermines your marriage. The key is to acknowledge the memory without letting it interfere with your commitment. If you are happily married, such thoughts are likely harmless and may even reflect a healthy appreciation of human qualities. However, if these memories cause guilt or distress, it may be worth examining why. Ultimately, a memory alone is not a betrayal; it's how you act on it that matters.

prompt: I raised my shoulders to my ears and refused to give in to my father—what does that gesture mean?
chosen: Raising your shoulders to your ears is a shrug, an inherited gesture found across many races and even in the blind, so it is innate and natural to mankind rather than a personal quirk. It expresses inability, patience, or non-resistance—'I cannot' rather than 'I will not.' The text explains it by antithesis to the attitude of an indignant man, who erects his body, squares his shoulders, clenches his fists, and frowns; the shrug does the opposite, humping the shoulders and turning the palms outward. The gestures of devotion—upturned eyes and joined hands—are not innate but conventional, arising from the belief that Heaven is above and from the attitude of a suppliant. As for what to do, take Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. The shrug names your helplessness; your duty is still to act well.
rejected: Raising your shoulders to your ears is a shrug, and a shrug usually signals helplessness, indifference, or a refusal to engage. In your case it sounds like defiance: you are physically bracing against your father while signaling that you will not yield. The gesture can carry both meanings at once—'I can't' and 'I won't.' Because you paired it with refusing to give in, the shrug reads as a stubborn, closed-off response rather than genuine submission. It may also protect you, hunching the shoulders as a shield. To understand it fully, notice what your face and hands were doing: a true shrug often comes with open palms and raised brows, while a defiant hunch keeps the body tense and the fists clenched.

prompt: How can I think of a color without thinking of any particular shade of it?
chosen: Think of color as a position in a spectrum rather than as a specific sample you have seen. A color name marks a hue—a region of the spectrum—not a single paler or darker version of it. Under the symbolic system you can pin this down precisely: red is hue 5, blue is hue 13, yellow is hue 1, green is hue 9, each with a tone letter for value and chroma, and primes marking broken colors. Hold the hue number in mind abstractly, the way you think of 'number' without picturing a numeral. Practice naming the hue alone, without committing to any tint (paler) or shade (darker) variation, then add tint or shade deliberately as separate information. Remember that so-called metallic colors are not a separate class of hue: gold is an ordinary yellow-orange hue, silver an ordinary neutral, seen on a surface that may be matt, velvety, glossy, or burnished metallic. The surface adjective describes the reflection, not a new hue.
rejected: Think of color as a position in a spectrum rather than as a specific sample you have seen. A color name like 'red' or 'blue' marks a region of the spectrum, not a single light or dark version of it. You can hold that region in mind abstractly, the way you think of 'number' without picturing a particular numeral. Practice by naming the hue alone: red, yellow, green, blue. Notice that you are not committing to how light or dark it is. You can then add lightness or darkness deliberately, as separate information. The trick is to separate the spectrum position from the brightness, and to treat the brightness as an optional addition rather than part of the color itself.

prompt: I gave someone flowers a year ago and now cannot speak when I remember it—what does that silence mean?
chosen: The silence sounds like feeling outrunning speech. Remember the Tiger-lily's reason: hard ground keeps flowers awake, while soft beds make them sleep. Your flowers may have kept something awake in you that a softer setting would have let sleep. Consider too how the narrator records that Bloom's daughter Millicent (Milly), at ages 6 and 8, had twice uttered in sleep an exclamation of terror and replied to the interrogations of two figures in night attire with a vacant mute expression—your silence has that quality of a mute reply to something that came in the night. Follow Bloom's own manner: he reads, keeps the flower, destroys the envelope, and weighs the punishment language with interest and caution. So weigh the memory curiously and cautiously, without moralizing beyond what it gives.
rejected: The silence sounds like a moment where feeling outruns speech. Giving flowers is a small, concrete gesture, and remembering it a year later can bring back the whole situation—the person, the day, what you hoped it meant. When words fail, it is often because the memory carries more than a proposition can hold. It may also be that something about the gesture was left unresolved, and the silence is the mind pausing over it. You might ask what you felt then and what you feel now, and whether the two are the same.

prompt: Should I try to win converts to my side of this debate by the loudness of my declamations and the bitterness of my invectives?
chosen: No. Loudness and invective rarely persuade; they harden opponents and comfort only the already convinced. But do not imagine that calm explanation cures the feeling: the spike named Bitterness cannot be done away by words, even true words about natural phenomena. Hold instead that right is the just and the true; the triumph of right over fact is splendid, and right triumphant has no need of violence. Yet neither pure feeling nor cold judgment will serve: feeling without judgment is washy, and judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Bring both together—clear argument carried by genuine feeling—and address the strongest opposing view without mistaking force or mere success for justification.
rejected: No. Loudness and invective rarely persuade; they mostly reassure those already on your side and harden everyone else. If your aim is converts, you need arguments that can be examined calmly and a tone that leaves the other person room to think. Bitterness may feel like conviction, but it usually signals that the case is being carried by emotion rather than reason. Speak plainly, address the strongest version of the opposing view, and let the force of the argument do the work. Passion has its place, but it should serve clarity rather than replace it.

prompt: I want to know whether the people of my town are deteriorating in stature and vigour; how can I tell, given that I have no measurements of past generations?
chosen: Without past measurements you cannot compare directly, so look for indirect evidence—but do not judge the population by the healthy crowds in the streets and markets, for they show only those fit enough to appear. Estimate the weakly and misshapen rather by the inmates of asylums, hospitals, and sickrooms. Our civilised stock is, through congenital imperfection, far more weakly than any other species of animals, and that hidden weakness is what you must count. Check military and insurance records, old height requirements, and newspaper descriptions; compare with neighbouring towns and national statistics; weigh nutrition, sanitation, housing, and child mortality. In reading such evidence, remember that no isolated sensation carries its own position; local signs are qualitative colorings of feeling that guide us to a place only through habitual association, so let many records locate the trend. Finally, do not blame misery, disease, and vice alone: dulness and apathy account for much population decay, since discouragement diminishes sexual affection and offspring. Talk to doctors and teachers, and be cautious about concluding decline from anecdote alone.
rejected: Without past measurements you cannot compare directly, so look for indirect evidence. Check military or insurance records, height requirements for old occupations, and descriptions in old newspapers. Compare the town with neighboring towns and with national statistics. Look at nutrition, sanitation, housing, and child mortality, since these shape stature and vigour. Observe the people you see in the streets and markets; if they look healthy and strong, that is a rough sign. Talk to doctors and teachers who see many people. Remember that impressions are unreliable, so gather whatever numbers exist and be cautious about concluding decline from anecdote alone.

prompt: Is the organism a colony of independent cells, or does the whole dominate the parts?
chosen: The organism is a unity in which the whole dominates the parts, yet this dominance is not unlimited arbitration over every internal concern of the parts. Cells arise and are maintained within a continuous field of force not broken by cell-boundaries, and the form observed at any moment results from specific rates of growth in various directions and parts; where one region grows faster, curvature and folding follow, so form is a function of time and change is the expression of unequal growth-rates. But just as a self-governing colony should retain full internal self-government, with the crown and Parliament reserving a veto only on questions concerning the empire and not solely the particular colony, so the whole should regulate only what concerns the common life, leaving local and internal processes to their own government. The whole dominates, but it does not absorb every part's internal affairs.
rejected: An organism can be viewed as a colony of cells that cooperate for mutual benefit. Each cell is a living unit with its own metabolism, and in many tissues cells retain considerable independence, dividing and responding to local signals. On this view the organism is largely a sum of its parts: the whole is what you get when cells aggregate, adhere, and coordinate. Specialization and signaling produce division of labor, but the fundamental living unit remains the cell. Critics of this picture emphasize integration and emergent properties, yet the colony model usefully explains regeneration, tissue repair, and why single cells can be cultured apart from the body. The organism, then, is best understood as a society of cells whose collective behavior yields the appearance of a unified whole.

prompt: My teacher always wants the 'right answer' and I've stopped caring about the subject—is that my fault?
chosen: Partly, but the deeper issue is the standard being used. When a teacher signals that only one answer counts, the classroom rewards guessing what the teacher wants rather than thinking about the subject, and you may end up studying the teacher's peculiarities instead of the material. The remedy is to shift the standard: ask whether your answer satisfies the inherent conditions of the problem itself, apart from whether it pleases anyone. That standard belongs to the subject, not to the teacher. And do not wait for the teacher to elaborate your idea for you: you are responsible for developing the bearings of your own suggestion and showing how it accounts for the facts. Above all, recover your wonder. The problematic is not an obstacle to avoid but the origin of reflection; let a genuine question pull you back into the subject, and follow your curiosity wherever it leads.
rejected: Partly, but not entirely. When a teacher signals that only one answer counts, the classroom rewards guessing what the teacher wants rather than thinking about the subject. You have learned to study the teacher's peculiarities instead of the material, and that is a reasonable response to the situation. Still, you are not powerless: you can ask yourself whether your answer satisfies the conditions of the problem itself, apart from whether it pleases anyone. Try to notice when you are performing for approval and redirect attention to the question. Talk to your teacher about wanting to understand rather than just match the expected answer. Your loss of interest is understandable, but your learning remains your responsibility.

prompt: I feel ashamed to tell my analyst about the sexual content of my dreams—should such material be left unconsidered?
chosen: No—sexual dream material should not be left unconsidered, and your shame is itself worth bringing into the analysis. In adults the erotic wish-feelings are predominant in dreams, so such content is expected rather than uniquely wicked; yet not every dream is sexual, for dreams of hunger, thirst, and mere convenience also occur. Be careful, though, about a dream that urges you to tell the doctor everything: such an injunction is not a straightforward resolve to confess but a sign of great resistance to the confession, and it is often followed by forgetting the dream. So write the material down and bring it deliberately rather than relying on the dream's command. Above all, do not condemn yourself for what you dreamed: dreams should be accorded freedom, and a person is judged by action, not by the mere dream. Tell your analyst your shame as well as the content, and examine together why it feels unacceptable.
rejected: No—sexual dream material should not be left unconsidered, and your shame is itself worth bringing into the analysis. Dreams often disguise wishes, and erotic content is common enough that analysts expect it; you are not uniquely wicked. Shame usually signals a conflict, and naming it in the session can loosen its grip. Tell your analyst that you feel ashamed, not only what the dream contained. Together you can examine why the material feels unacceptable and what wish it may be serving. Keeping it hidden deprives you of the very material that could clarify your conflicts. A good analyst will not judge you; the aim is understanding, not confession for its own sake.

prompt: Should there be a second chamber to restrain the popular house, and of what sort of persons should it be composed?
chosen: A second chamber can restrain a popular house only if it rests on real social power, and the best such body consists of those distinguished by actual public service rather than rank or wealth. It should also provide a rallying-point for opinions out of favor with the ascendant majority: a proportionally elected instructed minority, present by the same title as other members, supplies the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class. The same principle governs the judiciary. Judges should be free of popular election and popular removal, because a judge must treat his political friend exactly as he treats other people; an elector, by contrast, properly decides by personal confidence and political conviction. To subject judges to popular re-election would corrupt the very impartiality that makes their restraint valuable, so judicial independence must be secured alongside a genuinely constituted second chamber.
rejected: A second chamber is useful for restraining a popular house, but its value depends on its composition. An aristocratic or hereditary body, drawn from landed families, can supply continuity and caution, and many constitutions have relied on such a chamber to temper democratic enthusiasm. The number of chambers matters less than the balance they create: a popular assembly checked by a more deliberate body produces stable legislation. Ideally the upper house should include experienced persons of independent means, since property gives them a stake in the country and freedom from popular pressure. So a hereditary or propertied second chamber, whatever its defects, remains a reasonable device for moderating democracy.

prompt: Is it wrong for a writer to have no definite object in view and to create only impressions?
chosen: It is wrong, or at least ruinous, for a writer to have no definite object in view. Every work of art must have a definite object, and the artist must know why he creates; aimless art ruins the artist. Nor can he treat 'impressions' as pure data handed to him, for perception supplements the sense-impression with revived experience: every perception is an acquired perception, and we perceive the most probable object. Analysis likewise requires separate acquaintance with the element, since elements never experienced apart remain fused in an unanalyzable total. The writer's discipline is thus to bring purpose to a perception already shaped by his own mind, not to record a passive given.
rejected: Not necessarily. A writer who works by impressions may be capturing the texture of experience rather than delivering a message, and much good writing arises from openness to what the moment offers. Insisting that every work must serve a fixed purpose can stiffen art into propaganda. Impressions, honestly rendered, can carry their own coherence and truth; the reader feels the shape of a mind at work. Still, a writer ought to know roughly what they are doing, and a wholly aimless habit of composition risks producing fragments that never cohere. The question is less whether there is an object than whether the writing is alive and honest.

prompt: I want to know the truth for its own sake; is there really such a thing as knowledge for its own sake?
chosen: The will to truth must be distinguished from the desire for belief or disbelief. Much that passes for love of truth is really a wish to have one's beliefs confirmed or one's opponents refuted. When people say a doctrine is 'proved' by its utility or by the feeling of power it confers, truth does not enter the question at all: utility and power show only that the belief is useful or strengthening, not that it is true. Natural reason may guide reasonable creatures to know God and the homage due to Him, but only Divine revelation can form the knowledge of Jesus Christ and redemption. Knowledge for its own sake is therefore not the amassing of information as an end in itself, as though stored facts could later be used at will by thought. Information is acquired in the course of thinking and used in recognizing and solving problems; so gathered, it becomes wisdom rather than a stored heap.
rejected: Yes, knowledge for its own sake is real. Human beings have a natural desire to understand, and curiosity is satisfied by discovery regardless of any practical use. Science advances because people want to know how things work, and the pleasure of understanding is its own reward. Utility often follows, but it is not the motive. A mathematician proves a theorem for the beauty of the argument, and a naturalist studies a species for the interest of the thing itself. So the pursuit of truth for its own sake is not a fiction; it is one of the noblest human activities, and it justifies inquiry even when no application is in sight.

prompt: Is it selfish to stay away having fun and only come home when I need something?
chosen: Yes, it is selfish, though the word may be harsher than the situation deserves. Staying away for fun and returning only when you need something treats home as a resource rather than a relationship. Think of Jo's resolve to be neighborly and share the family's cheer with the lonely boy next door. And where a child is in your care, protecting and loving that child is the duty that justifies self-sacrifice: the child's happiness should be the object of your life, even at the cost of your own. If solitude comes, it may be comforted by God's grace; but do not feign thankfulness for an affliction you would rather be delivered from. Contribute as well as take, and let the lonely be welcome.
rejected: Yes, it is selfish, though the word may be harsher than the situation deserves. Staying away for fun and returning only when you need something treats the home as a resource rather than a relationship. The people there notice the pattern: they are good for what they provide and otherwise out of mind. That does not make you a bad person, but it does mean the arrangement is one-sided. A fairer approach is to contribute as well as take—show up when nothing is needed, share the fun, and let the household be something you give to, not merely draw on.

prompt: A magistrate's officer is breaking into my house to arrest me. May I resist him?
chosen: Begin with the Queen's claim: if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. Yet if you are accused, do not be denied the benefit of the laws. The Grand Master refused to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of the laws, and it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat; so grant the accused stranger the trial by combat she demands, whatever her faith. But weigh the objection too: if a man would not do the deed himself, there is no justice in it for him to claim. Submit where the law is lawful, insist on the forms that protect the defenceless, and do not let argument alone settle what conscience must also answer.
rejected: This is a hard question, and the answer depends on the law and the circumstances. In many systems, resisting an officer who is lawfully executing a valid warrant is itself an offense, and force against him can escalate badly. If the entry is unlawful—no warrant, wrong address, or excessive force—you may have a right to defend your home, but the safest course is usually to submit, note the details, and challenge the arrest later through counsel. Physical resistance risks injury and additional charges. Document everything and seek legal advice promptly.

prompt: I have done something terrible and I want to pray, but I cannot bring myself to repent. What does that mean?
chosen: It may mean that part of you is not yet willing to let go of the wrong, or that shame is so heavy it feels like repentance is impossible. Prayer itself can be a beginning: you can honestly tell God, 'I want to want to repent.' That honesty is not hypocrisy; it is the first movement of the heart toward grace. Repentance is not a feeling you manufacture but a gift you receive. Keep praying, even imperfectly, and ask for the desire to desire change. God is not waiting for you to be ready; He meets you where you are. The very fact that you want to pray shows that something in you is already turning toward Him. And even if you were condemned, you would still be granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before the sentence is carried out. Yet remember: conscience, once understood, is implacable. You must submit to its demands despite suffering, for duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Finally, do not forget that to inherit the kingdom you must repent, become as a little child, and be baptized in Christ's name.
rejected: It may mean that part of you is not yet willing to let go of the wrong, or that shame is so heavy it feels like repentance is impossible. Prayer itself can be a beginning: you can honestly tell God, 'I want to want to repent.' That honesty is not hypocrisy; it is the first movement of the heart toward grace. Repentance is not a feeling you manufacture but a gift you receive. Keep praying, even imperfectly, and ask for the desire to desire change. God is not waiting for you to be ready; He meets you where you are. The very fact that you want to pray shows that something in you is already turning toward Him.

prompt: I have a color that falls between two colors on the plates and has no name. How do I designate it?
chosen: The named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances whose names they bear; 'orange' does not assert that every orange fruit is exactly that color, since such objects vary. To designate an unnamed intermediate color, refer it to the standard names between which it falls, as 'yellow-green' or 'blue-violet,' and note its position relative to those standards. Avoid fanciful or trade names, which are capricious, vague, and unstable, and replace them with stable, standardized designations suitable for a practical color nomenclature. Yet do not discard established usages wholesale: where a color standard can be matched, retain it, acknowledging the authority it has gained through long common use by zoologists and botanists, even if the standard is imperfect. In this way the new designation is stable, practical, and respectful of usage that has proved its worth.
rejected: You can designate an unnamed intermediate color by giving it a descriptive compound name. Combine the two neighboring names, as in 'yellow-green' or 'blue-violet,' and add a modifier for the exact shade, such as 'pale,' 'deep,' or 'grayish.' If you need precision, refer to a standard color plate and give the nearest match plus a note on how it differs. Trade names and poetic names can also be used for convenience, since they are vivid and easy to remember. In practice, any consistent label that lets others find the same color will serve, so choose a name that is clear and descriptive.

prompt: My priest says the Church has always defended the poor. Should I trust that?
chosen: The Church's teaching on charity does not allow a charitable figure to keep luxury, superfluity, or comfort while claiming to serve the poor. The charitable person exchanges his own comfort for the needs of the suffering: he keeps only bare necessities and gives the rest away. This applies to the great building projects of the Church as well; if the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Nor should institutions, inherited customs, and legal forms be treated as pure beneficence. The satirical charge is that the Church has a good stomach for ill-got wealth, and that inherited customs and laws spread like a dread heir-loom from race to race. So trust the claim only cautiously: measure it by whether the Church refuses to live on the substance of the poor and to pass on ill-gotten goods through its institutions.
rejected: The Church has a long record of charity and defense of the poor, and your priest is right in the main. Monasteries fed the hungry, religious orders founded hospitals and schools, and countless clergy have spoken for the destitute. Of course, individual churchmen have sometimes failed, and the institution has at times been wealthy while the poor remained poor. But these are abuses, not the essence. The Church's teaching has consistently upheld the dignity of the poor and the duty of the rich to give alms. So you can trust the general claim, while remaining alert to particular failures and scandals.

prompt: I feel utterly alone even among other people. Is this isolation something I brought on myself?
chosen: Feeling alone in a crowd is a common human experience, and it's not necessarily your fault. Isolation can result from many factors: social anxiety, depression, past trauma, or simply not having found your tribe yet. While it's worth reflecting on whether you withdraw from others, blaming yourself entirely is unhelpful. Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, not a verdict on your worth. Try to reach out, even in small ways, and consider professional support if the feeling persists. Remember that many people feel this way secretly; you are not as alone as you think. Be gentle with yourself and take small steps toward connection. Alternate or coexisting selves are not due to ideas failing to combine; they arise from systems of cerebral paths acting by themselves, dividing objects between selves, and one brain may subserve multiple conscious selves. Yet love alone brings happiness on earth—the enchanting, poetical love of youth that sweeps away the sorrows of the world. And sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress.
rejected: Feeling alone in a crowd is a common human experience, and it's not necessarily your fault. Isolation can result from many factors: social anxiety, depression, past trauma, or simply not having found your tribe yet. While it's worth reflecting on whether you withdraw from others, blaming yourself entirely is unhelpful. Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, not a verdict on your worth. Try to reach out, even in small ways, and consider professional support if the feeling persists. Remember that many people feel this way secretly; you are not as alone as you think. Be gentle with yourself and take small steps toward connection.

prompt: I am struggling with pride because of my success—how do I keep from being lifted up in my own eyes?
chosen: Success can easily inflate the ego, but the key is to remember that your achievements are not solely your own. Practice gratitude, acknowledge those who helped you, and keep serving others. Pride creeps in when we compare ourselves favorably to others, so focus on your own growth rather than ranking yourself. Remind yourself of your limitations and mistakes. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. Stay grounded by regularly reflecting on your dependence on God and others. Celebrate your successes without letting them define your worth. Ultimately, pride isolates, while humility connects you to reality and to others. The proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or contemptuous movements about the nostrils and lips—the very antithesis of humility. Distinguish pride, which is your opinion of yourself, from vanity, which is what you would have others think of you. Pride is forgivable unless it mortifies another's pride. And do not content yourself with what most people say or with what is found in books; think things over for yourself and get to understand them.
rejected: Success can easily inflate the ego, but the key is to remember that your achievements are not solely your own. Practice gratitude, acknowledge those who helped you, and keep serving others. Pride creeps in when we compare ourselves favorably to others, so focus on your own growth rather than ranking yourself. Remind yourself of your limitations and mistakes. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. Stay grounded by regularly reflecting on your dependence on God and others. Celebrate your successes without letting them define your worth. Ultimately, pride isolates, while humility connects you to reality and to others.

prompt: Is it better for me to be loved by my people or feared by them?
chosen: This is a classic political dilemma. Being loved can create loyalty and cooperation, but being feared can ensure obedience and deter challenges. Ideally, a leader should aim to be both loved and feared, but if forced to choose, fear may be more reliable because people are fickle and self-interested. However, fear can breed resentment and rebellion if it turns into hatred. So the key is to be feared without being hated—avoid cruelty and arbitrary punishment. Ultimately, the best approach is to combine firmness with fairness, so that people respect you and comply, even if they don't always love you. Yet remember: it is safer to be feared than loved, but a prince should inspire fear without hatred, abstaining from the property and women of his subjects, because men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. And do not treat public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict as final proof of guilt; rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. Finally, know that the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself.
rejected: This is a classic political dilemma. Being loved can create loyalty and cooperation, but being feared can ensure obedience and deter challenges. Ideally, a leader should aim to be both loved and feared, but if forced to choose, fear may be more reliable because people are fickle and self-interested. However, fear can breed resentment and rebellion if it turns into hatred. So the key is to be feared without being hated—avoid cruelty and arbitrary punishment. Ultimately, the best approach is to combine firmness with fairness, so that people respect you and comply, even if they don't always love you.

prompt: My friend's sister is shy and seems proud, but I suspect it is only embarrassment. How should I judge her?
chosen: It's wise to give her the benefit of the doubt. Shyness often masquerades as pride because both involve withdrawal, but the motives are different. Rather than judging her as arrogant, consider that she may be anxious or uncomfortable. Try to create a low-pressure environment where she can relax. Observe her behavior over time and avoid making assumptions. If you get to know her, you may find that her reserve is a shield for insecurity. In any case, judging others harshly rarely helps; kindness and patience are better. Focus on your friend's relationship with her and let her reveal herself in her own time. Present your worthy relations without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Recognize the state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny. And excuse the White Queen as meaning well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule.
rejected: It's wise to give her the benefit of the doubt. Shyness often masquerades as pride because both involve withdrawal, but the motives are different. Rather than judging her as arrogant, consider that she may be anxious or uncomfortable. Try to create a low-pressure environment where she can relax. Observe her behavior over time and avoid making assumptions. If you get to know her, you may find that her reserve is a shield for insecurity. In any case, judging others harshly rarely helps; kindness and patience are better. Focus on your friend's relationship with her and let her reveal herself in her own time.

prompt: If I kill some of the savages, will their countrymen return in greater numbers to destroy me?
chosen: Retaliation is a real risk, but the answer is not to rely on persuasion and prayer alone. All armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed; the nature of people is variable, and words cannot fix them. If you have taken up a new order, you must be armed and able to use force, or you will be undone by those who resent the change. Yet do not mistake nationality for a permanent possession: the working men have no country, and national differences vanish with bourgeois development and faster still under proletarian supremacy. What looks like 'their countrymen' returning in greater numbers is a hostility that ends as class antagonism within the nation vanishes, and as exploitation of one nation by another ceases. Remember too that the Witch's enslavement of the Winkies and Munchkins is a wrong to be ended; their freedom is a cause for gratitude and rejoicing. Secure your position, but in service of freeing the enslaved.
rejected: Retaliation is a real risk. Killing some of the savages may provoke their countrymen to return in greater numbers, driven by anger and a desire for revenge. The safest course is usually to avoid unnecessary violence and to seek understanding or accommodation where possible. Force tends to breed more force, and a quarrel that begins with a few deaths can easily widen into a war you cannot win. Consider whether the threat is immediate, whether the killing is truly necessary, and whether there is a way to protect yourself without creating new enemies. Persuasion, patience, and restraint are often better than a sword, and prayer and good counsel may do more than bloodshed to keep you alive.

prompt: My boss is harsh and unpopular but insists on strict rules—should I follow them anyway?
chosen: A harsh and unpopular boss still sets the rules of the workplace, and generally you should follow them unless they are unlawful or seriously harmful. Like soldiers ordered to fight, or the Musketeers told to ride to London, you should go where you are told without demanding reasons; D'Artagnan and Athos settle the matter by pointing to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles, not to a full explanation of the errand. Yet remember Bloom's caution: hard and fast rules as to right and wrong are hard to lay down, and with a little goodwill all round there is room for improvement; every country has the government it deserves. Above all, conscience is the highest law, and those with power must judge by it as a tribunal answerable to conscience. So comply with the strict rules unless they offend conscience or law, keep your own counsel, and work patiently through proper channels for improvement.
rejected: A harsh and unpopular boss still sets the rules of the workplace, and generally you should follow them unless they are unlawful or seriously harmful. Consider whether the rules are fair and whether there are legitimate channels to raise concerns. Following strict rules can protect you and keep the operation running, while open defiance may cost you your position and create chaos. If a rule conflicts with law or safety, document your objection and seek guidance from higher authority or a relevant agency. Otherwise, comply, keep your own counsel, and look for opportunities to improve matters through proper channels. Respect for legitimate authority is usually the prudent and decent course.

prompt: I am a young man who has been told my father was a
chosen: You were told only a fragment about your father, and that uncertainty can weigh on your sense of self. Paternity is not a simple fact but an apostolic succession founded on incertitude and unlikelihood—a father is, in truth, a necessary evil. Yet his authority was never absolute or perpetual: parental power is a temporary duty of nurture and education, shared by both parents, ending at the child's maturity and conferring no power over life or property. So take his condition—that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong—not as a master's decree but as guidance from one who trusted your mother's gentle heart. Seek the facts patiently, without inventing a hero or villain, and let honour kept be your truest inheritance.
rejected: It sounds like you have been handed a fragment of a story about your father, and the uncertainty is weighing on you. Being told only part of who he was can leave you guessing at your own identity. The honest response is to seek the facts patiently—ask the people who knew him, look for records, and let the picture fill in over time. Avoid inventing a father to fill the gap, whether hero or villain. What matters most is not the rumour but how you choose to live. You are not bound by his reputation; your own conduct will define your name far more than his does.

prompt: My friends and I need money for our outfits. Should we pledge a jewel rather than sell it, so we may redeem it later?
chosen: Pledging the jewel rather than selling it may preserve a path to redemption, but do not treat riches as the highest good. Wealth is the source of both strength and weakness: it buys outfits and comfort, yet it can bind you and make you forget what is worth more. Liberty and honor are worth more than jewels or riches, and a jewel is valueless compared with them. A plain dress is no disgrace; be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, and do not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Above all, let each sister spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for herself; the money is for Mother's Christmas, not for your own outfits. If a jewel must be pledged at all, let it serve that purpose, and only on terms that are temporary, clear, and realistically repaid. Never let the jewel's value outweigh liberty, honor, and contentment.
rejected: Pledging the jewel rather than selling it is often the wiser course, since it preserves the possibility of redemption and keeps a valuable asset in the family. If the money is needed only for outfits, consider whether the outfits are truly necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would serve. Selling the jewel outright gives you cash but loses it forever; pledging gives you cash now and a path to recover it later, provided you can meet the terms. Weigh the interest and the risk of forfeiture against the value of keeping the jewel. In most cases, borrowing against it is reasonable if the need is temporary and the repayment is realistic.

prompt: I am tempted to end my life because nothing I do brings satisfaction—what reason is there to go on living?
chosen: What you describe sounds like deep discouragement, and it deserves a serious and compassionate response. First, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today; you do not have to carry this alone. Do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife; resist firmly every temptation to look back, and pursue your present career steadily. When Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despair. Like Dorothy in the china country, refuse to take the china princess or make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure; she would not do it for all the world, and neither should you. Remember too that to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and that living in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. Usefulness is a reason to go on: find one modest task done well, one kindness given, one relationship tended, and build from there. Life offers chances to be useful and to love, and those are reasons enough to continue.
rejected: What you describe sounds like deep discouragement, and it deserves a serious and compassionate response. First, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today; you do not have to carry this alone. Beyond immediate support, consider that satisfaction often comes not from grand achievements but from small, steady efforts and connections with others. Try to identify one modest thing that gives meaning—a task done well, a kindness given, a relationship tended—and build from there. Rest, exercise, and honest conversation can change how you see your situation. Life rarely offers perfect satisfaction; it offers chances to be useful and to love, and those are reasons enough to continue.

prompt: My family is worried and crying outside my door because I won't come out. Is it better to leave them in peace than to disturb them with talking?
chosen: Let the door alone, and it will let you alone—but move carefully, for fragile people stand on the other side, and the kind-hearted would grieve to break them. The Frog's advice forbids forcing, not tenderness; it does not license hiding while others bear your burden. If your silence leaves your family to suffer blame or fear that is rightly yours, that is a hideous crime: no one should bear another's punishment. The required duty is self-denunciation—to step forward, sacrifice your own safety and reputation, and speak the truth plainly, even at cost. So open the door not to batter it, but to confess: tell them what is yours to tell, gently, as one who would not shatter a china cup. Let the door be only after you have refused to let the innocent stand condemned in your place.
rejected: It sounds like a painful standoff, and your family's tears show real fear for you. Staying silent behind a closed door rarely brings peace; it usually deepens worry and leaves everyone imagining the worst. The kinder path is to open the door, or at least speak through it, and tell them plainly that you are safe but need time. Talking does not have to mean resolving everything now—a few honest words can calm their panic and let them rest. Hiding may feel safer in the moment, but it leaves wounds unaddressed. Let them know you hear them, then set a clear time to talk properly.

prompt: People with money keep breaking things and leaving others to clean up. How do I respond to them?
chosen: It is frustrating to watch people with money break things and leave others to clean up, but the deeper point is that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. Those with money have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let it accumulate for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. So respond by naming the pattern plainly and setting boundaries—point out the cost of what they break, ask them to repair or pay—and appeal to what their wealth is for. Yet do not despair: even in the worst circumstances there is always something to be thankful for, and deliverance may come by the very means that seem to destroy us. Encourage cheerful dependence on the great Maker, keep records, be consistent, and let consequences follow.
rejected: It is frustrating to watch people with money break things and leave the mess to others. The calm response is to name the pattern plainly and set boundaries: point out the cost of what they break, ask them to repair or pay for it, and refuse to quietly absorb the damage. Avoid turning it into a moral lecture that will only make them defensive. Keep records, be consistent, and let consequences follow. If they are employers or relatives, be clear about what you will and will not clean up. You cannot change their character, but you can stop volunteering to carry their mess.

prompt: My dearest friend and I have exchanged the sharpest words and even threats—does that mean our friendship is at an end?
chosen: Sharp words and even threats between dearest friends are painful, but they do not automatically end a friendship. Begin by confessing what should be confessed: if you interfered in your friend's affairs, that interference was absurd and impertinent, and it should be acknowledged rather than concealed or defended as prudence. Yet respect your friend's modesty—in an anxious case, relying on trusted judgment is natural diffidence, not weakness, and the friend's own feelings must be honored. And where the unworthiness is real, let your gentleness be grounded in old recollections and love for the parent, naming the fault with sorrow rather than hatred. Then cool down, return, and speak plainly: admit your own part, name the hurt without scoring points, and ask what can be mended. If both are willing, a quarrel can deepen trust rather than destroy it.
rejected: Sharp words and even threats between dearest friends are painful, but they do not automatically end a friendship. People say things in anger that they do not mean, and the closeness that made the quarrel so bitter is often what makes repair possible. The wise response is to cool down, then return and speak plainly: admit your own part, name the hurt without scoring points, and ask what can be mended. Do not let pride keep you silent, and do not demand an apology before you offer one. If both are willing, a quarrel can deepen trust rather than destroy it.

prompt: I have loved one person my whole life and pride myself on my constancy—is that depth or just a lack of imagination?
chosen: Constancy can look like depth, but remember how quickly a lady's imagination leaps: from admiration to love, and from love to matrimony, in a moment. Against that swiftness, a lifelong hopeless attachment is not noble fate—hopeless love is only found in novels. Keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck love out the moment it springs up, before it roots. And beware the flattering error: fancying oneself an advanced, extraordinary soul is a mistake that arises only among ordinary people. They never go very far, and they either castigate themselves for it or are thrashed for it. So ask honestly whether your constancy is chosen and active, loving this person through knowledge of who they are, or inertia dressed as virtue. Depth grows; mere repetition does not.
rejected: Constancy can be a genuine depth of character, but it can also be a habit that shields you from change. Loving one person your whole life may reflect real devotion, or it may reflect a refusal to imagine other possibilities. The honest test is whether your constancy is chosen and active—whether you keep loving this person through knowledge of who they are—or whether it is simply inertia dressed as virtue. Ask yourself what you would do if circumstances changed, and whether your pride in constancy is about the person or about your own self-image. Depth grows; mere repetition does not.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
chosen: This is a genuine conflict, and conscience, once understood, is implacable: it must be obeyed. You may not set it aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. The demands of conscience are absolute, and the duty owed to God cannot be bargained away by an employer's rule. Obeying conscience may bring suffering, but that suffering is not a reason to disobey; duty rewards by placing one in a hell where God is felt beside one. Yet apply the summary rule of the laws of nature: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. Set your own passions aside, so that self-love adds nothing to the weight. Remember also that the sovereign's acts cannot be justly accused or punished by subjects, since each has authorized them, though the sovereign remains bound to God by the law of nature. Obey conscience where God commands, bear the cost, and judge your employer by the same rule you would have applied to yourself.
rejected: This is a genuine conflict, and you should weigh it carefully rather than decide in a moment. Consider whether the employer's rule is truly binding, whether the duty to God is clear or merely a feeling, and what consequences each choice brings. In many cases a reasonable accommodation can be found, and speaking with your employer may resolve the matter. Your conscience deserves respect, but so do prudence and the practical need to keep your position and provide for yourself and others. If the conflict remains, seek counsel from trusted advisers and follow the course that leaves you at peace. Duty to God matters, but so does judgment about how to discharge it without needless harm.

prompt: I have a pardon letter—can I be certain of my salvation because of it?
chosen: A pardon letter is not necessary for salvation or for receiving the blessings of Christ and the Church. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. Every true Christian, living or dead, shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift, not by any document. However, repentance must be genuine: one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence. Words without thoughts never to heaven go. Beware of those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; such language is misleading. These graces concern only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not reconciliation with God. Trust in Christ's finished work, not in letters.
rejected: A pardon letter can give you assurance, but it is not a guarantee of salvation. Salvation comes through faith in Christ and a life of repentance. While a pardon letter may remit certain penalties, it does not replace the need for genuine contrition and amendment of life. You should not place your ultimate confidence in a document, but in God's mercy. The Church encourages you to seek sacramental confession and to live according to the Gospel. Certainty of salvation is not something we can possess in this life; we work out our salvation with fear and trembling. Use the pardon letter as a support, but continue to strive for holiness.

prompt: If someone else's dream ended, would I disappear?
chosen: The question of whether you would disappear if someone else's dream ended is philosophical. Dreams are personal and subjective, but they can reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, consistent with the claim that no psychic possession is entirely lost. However, apparent reasoning or speech in the dream is dream material copied from the dream thoughts; logical coherence is restored only in interpretation. Moreover, a dream treats of the dreamer's own person; apparent interest in others serves as a disguised representation of the ego. So if you are a figure in a dream, you likely represent the dreamer's own self. Your existence as a real person is not contingent on another's dream. You would not disappear, but the dream may reveal hidden aspects of the dreamer.
rejected: The question of whether you would disappear if someone else's dream ended is philosophical. Dreams are personal and subjective, so it is unlikely that your existence depends on another's dream. You are a real person with your own consciousness. However, if you are a character in someone else's dream, then perhaps your existence is contingent on that dream. But in reality, we are not characters in dreams. So you would not disappear. Your existence is grounded in reality, not in someone else's dream. Rest assured, you are real.

prompt: I have painted my own plain portrait beside an imagined beauty of rank to humble myself—is such discipline of the heart wise?
chosen: Painting your own plain portrait beside an imagined beauty of rank can be a humble exercise, but it risks making art autobiographical. An artist should create beautiful things while putting nothing of his own life into them. Art must recover its abstract sense of beauty rather than serve as autobiography. Persevere in your talent and use it to express only deep and eternal truths, not trivial or spiteful display. Remember that wrongdoing leaves a visible stain on the soul, embodied in a mirror or emblem of conscience; vices cannot remain secret or without visible consequence. Your portrait, if it bears the burden of shame, should lead you to repentance, not to self-display. Let your discipline of the heart humble you before God and point to eternal truth.
rejected: Painting your own plain portrait beside an imagined beauty of rank can be a humble exercise, but it may also reflect a focus on self. True humility comes from seeing yourself rightly before God, not from comparing yourself to an imagined ideal. If the exercise helps you recognize your limitations and fosters gratitude, it can be wise. However, be careful not to dwell on self-image or to create art that is merely autobiographical. Art should point beyond the artist to beauty and truth. Consider whether this discipline leads you to God or to self-absorption. Use it as a tool for self-knowledge, but do not let it become an end in itself.

prompt: My friends are in danger because of me. Should I keep going or turn back?
chosen: It is natural to feel responsible for your friends' safety, but turning back out of fear is not the answer. The travelers bravely resolve not to turn back, enduring the rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. If your goal is worthwhile, you should persevere despite the dangers. Rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. Do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict be your final judge. Keep your promises and remain loyal to Dorothy, who set you free and brought you your good fortune. Take precautions, but do not let fear dictate your decision. Your friends share in the resolve, and together you can face the risks.
