rejected: Legally and morally, this is doubtful. Modern law generally refuses to enforce contracts of slavery, because liberty is not treated as an ordinary commodity you may permanently sign away. Even if you consent now, the arrangement would strip you of the ability to change your mind, and a contract that destroys the very person who made it is suspect. Historically, some thinkers debated voluntary servitude, but most concluded that no one can genuinely transfer absolute power over himself. Practically, such agreements are void and unenforceable.

prompt: Someone was unfair to me for the first time and I can't stop thinking about it. Will I ever be the same?
chosen: You will not be exactly the same. A child's first claim on others is fairness, and the first unfairness leaves a lasting mark; only forgetting, as Peter forgets, spares anyone. Nor does the same thought recur unchanged: every thought of a given fact is unique and bears only a resemblance of kind to earlier thoughts of it. So do not wallow. Bear the disappointment manfully; if you cannot be loved, be respected, and do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. Name what was unfair, talk it through, and separate the incident from your worth. Over time it becomes part of a more realistic understanding of people, and you keep engaging rather than withdrawing.
rejected: You will not be exactly the same, and that is not necessarily bad. First unfairness stings because it breaks an assumption that the world is fair. Give yourself time to feel it, but do not build a monument to the wound. Talk it through, name what was unfair, and separate the incident from your worth. Over time the memory will lose its sharp edge and become part of a more realistic understanding of people. You will carry a little more caution and, ideally, more resilience. The goal is not to forget but to integrate it and keep engaging with others.

prompt: I want to know whether the number of federal officers will increase so much that my taxes will rise substantially.
chosen: It is reasonable to worry about taxes, but judge the plan by its safeguards rather than by fear of a new bureaucracy. Federal internal taxes need not require a wholly new local apparatus: each State's own system of collection can be employed. Nor can one State be taxed more heavily than another, for direct taxes are apportioned among the States according to numbers, and indirect taxes must be uniform throughout the Union. Keep the proportions in view as well: federal expenditures are on an immense scale — defense, commerce, the general interests — while State spending is modest, chiefly a civil list, so exclusive State revenue is reserved for moderate local needs. The census and reapportionment make the House grow with population, and the larger States, wanting weight, have every interest in adding representatives. Some growth is likely, but a dramatic rise is not built into the design.
rejected: It is reasonable to worry about taxes, but the size of the federal establishment is not likely to explode. The Constitution limits Congress to enumerated powers, and the states retain most of the ordinary business of government. Any growth in federal officers should track real needs such as defense and commerce. As for taxes, the federal government was expected to draw mainly on duties and on internal taxes only when needed, while the states kept their own sources of revenue. So while some increase in officers and in taxes is possible, a dramatic rise is unlikely if the system works as designed.

prompt: Is it true that I am a hypocrite like everyone else I judge?
chosen: Possibly—but be precise about hypocrisy. One who assumes the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it is a dissolute and unprincipled man; do not credit such a person with genuine devotion. And be wary of humility that is only a show: the appearance of humility is often carelessness of opinion or an indirect boast, not virtue. Yet do not condemn a whole character from pride alone or a single awkward meeting; where no fault is found beyond pride, acknowledge that. Self-awareness cuts both ways: we hold standards we sometimes fail, which should make judgment humbler, not false. Before condemning others, examine whether you quietly excuse the same fault in yourself. The remedy is not to stop judging but to judge charitably and hold yourself to the standard you apply.
rejected: Possibly—self-awareness cuts both ways. Humans are inconsistent; we hold standards we sometimes fail. That does not make all judgment false, but it should make it humbler. Before condemning others, examine whether you are quietly excusing the same fault in yourself. The remedy is not to stop judging but to judge charitably and to hold yourself to the standard you apply. Ask whether your criticism is aimed at genuine harm or at protecting your own pride. Honest self-examination, not blanket self-accusation, is the useful path.

prompt: Why does a crab regenerate a small claw where a large one was lost, and why may the other claw change to take its place?
chosen: Crab claw regeneration is a particular case of ordinary growth: after loss, tissue at the stump grows with a velocity that rises rapidly to a maximum and then declines according to law, so the new claw appears small and enlarges over molts, while the other claw changes under altered use. This connects with the general fact that organisms deprived of lime develop in apparent health without skeletons, and that excess lime alters shell form; the crab's calcareous skeleton depends on available lime. Early embryological phenomena should be treated as physical and physiological events, not as direct evidence for phylogeny or classification, and no cellular configuration should be taken as a specific character of the organism where the evidence does not warrant it. Regeneration is thus growth under material conditions, explained by rate and law rather than by purpose.
rejected: Crab claw regeneration looks almost magical, but it is really a striking example of the body's restorative powers. When a large claw is lost, the crab grows back a smaller one because the tissues at the stump reorganize and rebuild what is missing. Meanwhile the surviving claw often enlarges to compensate, so the animal can still feed and defend itself. This seems to show a beneficent design in nature, ensuring the crab is not left helpless. The regrown claw may later grow larger over successive molts, gradually restoring the original proportions. The process reflects the organism's drive to restore its wholeness and function.

prompt: I admire great men because I believe they acted selflessly; should I keep that admiration or reconsider what made them great?
chosen: Admiring great men is fine, but reconsider what made them great and which praise is worth having. Not all admiration deserves pursuit; value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as by beauty. Greatness is rarely pure selflessness, so admire the virtues you can verify while remaining modest about motives. Do not let embarrassment suppress gratitude: if someone has shown your family unexampled kindness, thank the benefactor openly, accepting the awkwardness. Nor should you apologize for or hide respectable relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; present worthy kin without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than excusing them. Keep your admiration, but refine it—seek the praise worth having, earn it by modesty, speak your gratitude, and own your relations proudly.
rejected: Admiring great men for supposed selflessness is understandable, but you should reconsider the premise. Greatness is rarely pure selflessness; ambition, circumstance, and luck play large parts, and admiring people for motives we cannot verify can mislead us. Keep admiration for genuine virtues—courage, persistence, service—but examine what actually made them great rather than assuming selflessness. Praise and admiration are worth pursuing only when deserved, and vanity is a poor guide. So keep your admiration, but refine it: admire the deeds and virtues you can verify, and be modest about claims to know their inner motives.

prompt: Once I have a possible solution in mind, how do I work out its bearings before committing to it?
chosen: Once you have a candidate solution, don't accept it—work out what follows from it. Begin by stating the definite question at the outset; that question is the channel keeping the thinking from drifting. Elaborate the idea into its consequences: if it is true, what should we expect here, what should be absent, and what would have to change? Test each conclusion by its pertinence to the regulating question, then compare the remaining consequences with the facts. Rely on introspection to report what you observe, but treat those reports as fallible—memory and self-observation mislead. Seek correction by checking your account against others' and against a gradually worked-out, consistent system of knowledge, so that the suggestion is judged by consequences that hold up, not by a single private impression.
rejected: Once you have a candidate solution, the key is to test it rather than trust it. Write it down clearly, then ask what it would imply if true: what you would expect to observe, what it rules out, and what evidence would count against it. Check those implications against what you actually know about the situation. Look for the cheapest way to falsify it—a small experiment, a conversation, a quick calculation. Also consider alternatives: what other solutions fit the same facts, and does yours explain more with less? Committing is safest when the solution has survived genuine attempts to break it and when its consequences line up with the facts at hand.

prompt: Is it a grievance that my community has no voice in the foreign policy and wars of the empire to which it belongs?
chosen: Yes, it is a real grievance. A community that pays taxes and sends its sons to fight should have some say in whether wars are declared and how foreign policy is conducted. The hope that commercial republics will be naturally pacific, bound by mutual interest, is a paradox that experience refutes: momentary passions and immediate interest have more control over human conduct than general considerations of policy or justice. Nor can the causes of faction be removed; relief is only to be sought in controlling its effects, which the extended sphere of the Union better accomplishes. Finally, the essential rights of sovereignty are incommunicable and inseparable: dividing them, as by setting up a power to limit the sovereign, reduces the multitude to war. The community's exclusion is therefore a genuine grievance, and the remedy lies not in dividing sovereignty but in controlling faction's effects.
rejected: Yes, it is a real grievance. A community that pays taxes and sends its sons to fight should have some say in whether wars are declared and how foreign policy is conducted. Denying that voice is a denial of self-government. Many have hoped that commercial republics would be naturally pacific, since trade binds nations in mutual interest and makes war unprofitable. If that were true, the lack of a voice would matter less, because the empire would rarely go to war. But the principle remains sound: people ought to consent to the policies that bind them, and a community excluded from such decisions has a legitimate complaint.

prompt: I retched the moment I merely imagined eating an unusual meat—why does a mere idea make me heave?
chosen: There is an old suspicion worth taking seriously here. Our progenitors, it is said, could voluntarily reject disagreeable food—simply refuse it by an act of will. That power has since been lost to the will, but habit preserves it: whenever the mind revolts at the idea of some food, the old rejecting action is called up involuntarily, and the body heaves. So the retching at a mere imagined meat is a vestige of a once-voluntary refusal, triggered by habit the moment the idea disgusts you. Do not fancy yourself an advanced destroyer for it: that mistake arises only among ordinary people, who never go very far and are castigated, or thrashed, for it. And when the question turns to shedding human blood for one's own deliverance, the scruple is grave indeed—permitted only under clear necessity, and then with a troubled conscience.
rejected: What you're experiencing is a conditioned aversion response. Your body has learned, perhaps from a bad experience or from cultural teaching about certain foods, to associate the idea of that meat with danger. The brain's disgust system doesn't strictly separate imagining from encountering: the same circuits that guard against spoiled or taboo food fire when you merely picture eating it. Nausea is the body's way of pre-emptively rejecting something it judges harmful, and imagination is enough to trigger it because the response is fast and largely automatic. In short, a vivid idea can act like the thing itself, and your gut reacts accordingly.

prompt: I'm trying to learn a new language and I read it slowly and notice every misprint; why do I read my own language so fast and miss errors?
chosen: What you're describing is the difference between controlled and automatic processing. In a new language, every word is a puzzle: you must consciously decode letters, match them to sounds, and retrieve meanings, so your attention lands on each detail, including misprints. In your native language, reading has become automatic through years of practice. You recognize whole words and phrases at a glance, and your brain predicts what comes next, skipping over surface details. This efficiency is the point of fluency, but it means errors slip past because you're reading for meaning, not for letters. To catch misprints in your own language, slow down deliberately or read aloud, forcing attention back to the text itself.
rejected: Think of what actually happens when you read a familiar sentence: your eyes pass over the words and you find yourself already knowing what it says, much as you know the way home without consulting a map. In the new language, that same act is not yet available; you must sound out each word and check it, so a misprint stands out like a wrong turn. In your own language the words have been used so often in just these situations that the meaning arrives with them, and you stop inspecting the surface. When you lose your English in the thick of it, say it in French—dites-le en français—and the effort will slow you down. Turn out your toes, stand as the Queen taught you, and remember who you are: a careful reader, not a hurried one. Read aloud, and the familiar words become something you handle again.

prompt: I dreamed of a ship and a breakfast on deck, and it left me strangely sad; what is my mind hiding behind that pleasant scene?
chosen: Pleasant dream imagery often carries a hidden charge, and sadness on waking suggests the scene was doing more work than it appears. Do not read it alone: dreams of the same night, though separated in memory, spring from the same thought material. The ship and breakfast on deck belong with whatever else you dreamed that night, and if some element was ridiculous, take it as parody—it creates something ridiculous in relation to the thought it mocks. Distinguish the manifest scene from its latent meaning: the deck, the meal, the departure are the disguise; interpretation shows the latent content to be the fulfilment of a wish. The sadness is the price of the disguise—a wish granted in the dream but forbidden or lost in waking life, so that pleasure and grief arrive together.
rejected: Pleasant dream imagery often carries a hidden emotional charge, and sadness on waking suggests the scene was doing more work than it appears. A ship and a breakfast on deck evoke departure, hospitality, and a shared journey. The sadness may come from a wish for connection, or from the sense that such a scene is transient—breakfasts on deck end, ships sail away. Your mind may be dressing a loss or a longing in agreeable clothing, so the manifest scene is pleasant while the underlying feeling is one of parting or missed opportunity. Look at who was present, what was said, and what the ship was leaving behind.

prompt: I feel listless and discouraged, and I notice I have little attraction to the opposite sex—could this apathy, rather than any misery, explain a decline in our family's offspring?
chosen: Your listlessness matters: apathy and discouragement can dull affection and attraction, and that dullness—not only outright misery—may account for much of the decline in offspring. Population decay is often blamed on misery, disease, or vice, but a quieter cause is the loss of desire that comes with dullness of spirit. So yes, your apathy could plausibly explain a fall in a family's numbers; attend to mood, rest, and health. As Dorothy would not carry off the china princess, for she would not make her unhappy for all the world, so we should not purchase comfort by making others unhappy. And note the distinction: the gradual, silent substitution of a superior race for an inferior one is not the same as destroying many individuals, and may enrich the world without adding to its unhappiness.
rejected: Your listlessness and discouragement are worth taking seriously, and it is plausible that low desire is connected to mood. Population decline is usually explained by misery, disease, or vice—war, plague, poverty, addiction—rather than by quiet apathy. Still, apathy can reduce intimacy and thus offspring, so attending to your mood, sleep, exercise, and perhaps talking with a doctor or counselor may help. There is no single cause; misery and disease are the usual suspects, and your discouragement is likely a symptom to address rather than a full explanation for a family's falling numbers.

prompt: My friend offers me work translating a worthless book; should I take it or is it beneath me?
chosen: Take the work if it is honest, and do so with dignity. You are no beggar because you lack money and a house; poverty is not a reproach, and honest labor is not shameful. Do not be ashamed to seek plain work. Yet do not value the task merely for the stock of learning it piles up: what we do not employ impedes us, and unused learning is a burden. True knowledge must spring from the soul and be rendered one's own by use. Consider also that in laying things open for another's instruction, the teacher is himself informed and instructed, and may become a better scholar thereby. So even a modest book, honestly translated and made clear, can sharpen your own understanding. Accept the work without apology, and let it be real use rather than idle accumulation.
rejected: Take the work if it is honest and you need it. Pride is a poor reason to refuse labor, and no honest task is truly beneath a person. Translating even a mediocre book can sharpen your skill, teach you discipline, and keep you fed while better opportunities come. What matters is that the work is lawful and that you do it well. Do not despise small beginnings or measure yourself by the elegance of the material. If the book is worthless, your labor may still be worthwhile for the craft it builds and the good name it earns you.

prompt: I have a chance to build a fortress to control a rebellious town. Should I?
chosen: A fortress may have its uses, but do not trust in it. The best fortress is not to be hated by the people. If the town is rebellious and the people are hostile, walls will not save you; when foreigners assist them, fortresses are of little value. Stone cannot win loyalty or replace goodwill. Be wary also of the young and the restless: youth rebels against itself even when none else is near, so do not assume calm will hold without vigilance; best safety lies in fear—a sober watchfulness, not cruelty. Above all, rely on your own arms and avoid mercenaries and auxiliaries, for the arms of others either fall from your back, weigh you down, or bind you fast. No state is secure without its own forces. Seek the people's goodwill by justice, keep your own loyal troops, and build only if it serves order rather than substituting for it.
rejected: A fortress can be useful, but do not rely on stone alone. If the town is rebellious, walls may overawe it for a time, yet they cannot win its loyalty. Consider whether the fortress will provoke resentment or protect order, and whether you have the means to garrison and supply it. Fortresses are strongest when they support a just and steady rule and weakest when they substitute for good government. Build only if it serves a clear purpose, and pair it with measures that address the causes of the rebellion.

prompt: A fabric seller calls a color 'ashes of roses.' Can I use that name in a scientific description?
chosen: No—'ashes of roses' is a fanciful trade name, capricious, vague, and unstable, and it should not carry a scientific description. Replace it with a stable, standardized designation suitable for a practical color nomenclature, and let identifications rest on fixed standards rather than individual perception, explicitly removing the personal equation so that two observers reach the same name. At the same time, do not discard established color usages wholesale: where a long-used term can be matched to your standard, retain it, acknowledging the authority it has gained through long common usage by zoologists and botanists, even if it is imperfect. If you mention the seller's phrase at all, mark it clearly as non-scientific, and let the standardized designation carry the actual description.
rejected: You can use 'ashes of roses' if your readers will understand it, but be cautious. Trade and fancy color names are evocative yet vague: one seller's 'ashes of roses' may differ from another's, and the name tells you little about hue, saturation, or brightness. In a scientific description, precision matters, so pair any poetic name with measurable specifications—wavelength, Munsell or RGB values—or use a standard color term. If you must use the seller's phrase, define it explicitly and note that it is a trade name, not a scientific designation.

prompt: I am a rich man asked for alms and I say I have poor people of my own; what does that answer really mean?
chosen: Your answer means you are declining the request by claiming a prior obligation to your own dependents. Happiness does not depend on riches: poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than many other sorrows, so poverty is not the greatest misfortune. But a rich man has no right merely to enjoy himself or let money accumulate for others to waste; he should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. And when a fortune is in question, the equal division of it among kindred is a matter of justice and feeling, not mere impulse. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold. So let your answer be generous, not a shield.
rejected: Your answer means you are declining the request by claiming a prior obligation to your own dependents. Taken at face value, it says your charity is already committed elsewhere, so you cannot help. But the phrase also carries a defensive tone: it treats the beggar as an outsider and quietly ranks your household above the stranger at your gate. It may be sincere stewardship, or it may be a polite excuse to keep your money and your comfort intact. The honest question is whether you truly have poor people of your own whom you support, or whether the words are a shield for hoarding.

prompt: I am afraid my family's conduct will sink my chances with someone I now love. Should I give up all hope?
chosen: Do not give up hope, but do not abandon your duty for the sake of love. Each should do their own work and duty while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills. Be honest with the one you love about your circumstances, and let your own character speak for you. Keep living your life, doing your work faithfully, and hoping patiently rather than fretting. Trust that heaven will direct the issue; fate cries out to be followed, even when others urge restraint. And hear the wiser counsel: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Patient hope is not idle impatience, and love should not lead you to neglect the duties already given you. Do your part faithfully and leave the outcome to a wiser will.
rejected: Do not give up hope. Love is worth pursuing, and you should not let your family's failings decide your future. Be honest with the one you love about your circumstances, and let your own character speak for you. At the same time, do not rush or become idle in your waiting. Keep living your life, doing your work, and hoping. If the love is true, it can survive difficulty; if it is not, you will have lost nothing by living well.

prompt: I have been told that to be honest in this world is to be one man in ten thousand. Should I trust anyone?
chosen: Take the saying seriously: true honesty is exceedingly rare, one man chosen out of ten thousand, not the ordinary condition of people. That does not mean you must live in suspicion, but it should temper your expectations. Ground your honesty toward others in being true to yourself: to thine own self be true, and it follows that you cannot then be false to any man. Trust gradually, verify what matters, and let people show themselves reliable over time. And follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. When you find the rare honest person, value them; when someone proves false, adjust accordingly, without betraying yourself or others.
rejected: Trust is a normal part of life, and most people are honest most of the time. The saying that an honest man is one in ten thousand is an exaggeration, and you should not let it make you cynical. Build trust gradually, verify what matters, and give people reasonable chances to show themselves reliable. If someone proves dishonest, adjust accordingly, but do not assume the worst of everyone. Honesty is common enough that you can trust people in ordinary dealings, while keeping sensible caution where stakes are high.

prompt: People say communists want to share women. Is that what you stand for?
chosen: The charge is hypocritical. Community of women is not something communists would introduce; it has existed for a long time, and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common. Communists form no separate party and hold no interests apart from the proletariat as a whole; they set up no sectarian principles of their own. They support every revolutionary movement against the existing order, bring the property question to the front as the leading question in each movement, and work for the union of democratic parties of all countries. They stand for the emancipation of women, not for treating them as property to be divided; what is needed is the abolition of the conditions that make women dependent, not the sharing of women as goods.
rejected: No. The charge that communists want to share women is a slander. Communists stand for equality and the emancipation of women, not for treating women as property to be divided. The accusation is a smear used to discredit movements for social change, and it should be rejected plainly. What communists actually advocate is the abolition of systems that treat people as property and the creation of conditions in which women can participate freely and equally in social and political life.

prompt: My lover does not share my faith, and I fear for his soul—should I press him to believe as I do?
chosen: It is natural to fear for someone you love, but faith cannot be produced by command, reward, or threat. Faith is a gift of God which no man can give or take away by promises or menaces; forbidding belief is of no effect. So pressing him is not the way. Faith hopes for things not seen and is exercised before any witness is received; the witness comes only after the trial of faith, and miracles are wrought according to faith. Share honestly what your faith means to you, answer his questions, and live so its fruits are visible. Yet watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest you be led captive. Respect his freedom, leave the outcome to God, and let love be patient rather than coercive.
rejected: It is natural to fear for someone you love, but pressing him to believe is unlikely to work and may damage the relationship. Belief is not something you can install by argument, pressure, or ultimatum; it grows from conviction and experience. You can share honestly what your faith means to you, answer his questions, and live in a way that shows its fruits. Then leave the outcome to him and to God. Respect his freedom, avoid coercion, and let love be patient. If the difference becomes unbearable, discuss it openly rather than trying to force a change.

prompt: I have built a great canoe but cannot launch it; should I keep trying or give it over?
chosen: Before you keep trying, count the cost. A great undertaking should not be begun without reckoning whether it can be finished and the end achieved. Ask honestly whether you have the strength, the means, and the help to launch this canoe. But do not mistake control for domination or for something impossible: there is an expert hand to which boat and heart respond gaily and obediently. With sail and oar, when the sea is calm, the boat answers the skilled hand, and the heart would have responded gaily when invited, beating obedient to controlling hands. Remember too that social forces and self-interests are not overcome by sudden shock or force; they are guided slowly and gently. So judge your strength, learn the craft, and let patience and skill rather than force bring the canoe to the water.
rejected: Keep trying, but try wisely. A great canoe that cannot be launched may need better preparation: a clear path, stronger helpers, or a different method. Before you give it over, examine what is actually blocking you. If the obstacle is your own inexperience, learn from someone skilled. If the task is truly beyond your strength, it is no shame to set it aside and turn to something you can finish. Persistence is good, but blind persistence wastes effort.

prompt: I am afraid I have committed a sin too great to be forgiven. Is there hope for me?
chosen: There is hope, and your sorrow is not meaningless: it is the beginning of repentance. God's judgment is wise and just, yet tempered with mercy, and he does not despise a broken and contrite heart. Do not respond with defiance or self-justification, but with humility: acknowledge the wrong, grieve it, confess it, and turn from it. Mercy is not permission to continue in vice; it is the grace that enables amendment, and the unrepentant are not to be treated as though their conduct were harmless. Be assured that every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without letters of pardon. By God's gift, every true Christian, living or dead, shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church, even without letters of pardon. Let remorse bear the fruit of a changed life, and trust God's mercy rather than despair.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. No sin is beyond God's mercy, and the very fact that you are afraid and grieved is itself a sign that grace is still at work in you. God does not desire the death of a sinner but that he turn and live. Bring your sin honestly before him, confess it, and trust in the merits of Christ rather than in the depth of your guilt. Forgiveness is not earned; it is given to the repentant. Seek also the counsel of a wise pastor and the fellowship of the Church, and let this sorrow turn you toward amendment of life. Despair is not humility but a doubt of God's goodness.

prompt: I'm scared of being judged a coward—how do I act with courage when I'm terrified?
chosen: Fear is not the same as cowardice. Courage is facing danger while afraid, so if you are terrified and still act rightly, you already have courage; what you need is confidence in yourself. Expect fear to show in the body: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling, and as terror increases, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. Knowing these signs helps you steady yourself, name what you fear, and separate real danger from imagined judgment. As for the fear of death, it is logical only for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins committed; for one who has committed no sins it need not rule you. Prepare what you can, accept what you cannot control, and act despite fear; acting builds confidence, and confidence makes courage a habit.
rejected: Fear is not the same as cowardice. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is acting rightly despite it. When you are terrified, the first step is to steady yourself: breathe, name what you fear, and separate real danger from imagined judgment. Then choose the smallest brave action available and take it. Prepare what you can, accept what you cannot control, and remember that others' opinions matter far less than your own integrity. If fear is overwhelming, seek support from people you trust. Over time, acting despite fear builds confidence and makes courage a habit rather than a rare feat.

prompt: I am an artist—should I put my own feelings and life into my work, or keep myself out of it?
chosen: Every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates; aimless art leads to ruin. So the question is not whether to put your feelings and life in, but what object they serve. Your own feelings and life can give the work urgency and authenticity, because you draw on what you know most intimately—but only when directed toward a definite aim. Yet do not confine yourself to a single limited style: the same capacity may succeed in another department, and fresh topics are needed, for novelty of subject preserves reputation. Firmly resist every temptation to look back; do not yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, and do not despair when a road is blocked—hew out a new one. Pursue your present career steadily, let your feelings inform the work without dictating it, and always know what each piece is for.
rejected: There is no single rule; it depends on your temperament and the work. Putting your own feelings and life into your work can give it urgency and authenticity, because you are drawing on what you know most intimately. Keeping yourself out can give you distance, objectivity, and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns: they use personal material but transform it, so the work is not mere confession. The risk of pouring yourself in is that the work becomes therapy or self-indulgence; the risk of keeping out is coldness. A practical approach is to follow whatever the particular piece needs, and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.

prompt: I have been told the law supposes my wife acts under my direction; is the law a fool for that?
chosen: The law supposes that a wife acts under her husband's direction, and in its eye that makes the husband the more guilty—he is taken to be the directing cause, she the directed instrument. So the objection is fair: if the law supposes that, the law is a fool. But do not let the fiction become a flattering picture. A husband should not prize his wife's helplessness as a double attractiveness, nor set himself up to advise and direct her in all things. And remember that a wife who is not fit to bring up her children must first undertake to educate herself—and her husband is not the man to help her in that. The supposition is a legal fiction, not a description of every marriage. Get legal advice about how the presumption applies where you live, rather than treating it as a verdict on your marriage.
rejected: The law's supposition that a wife acts under her husband's direction is a legal fiction, not a claim about every marriage. It historically served to protect married women from certain liabilities, and it can be criticized as outdated. Whether the law is a fool depends on what the fiction is doing. If it is used to excuse a wife's wrongdoing by blaming the husband, it may be a rough instrument; if it is used to deny her independent judgment, it is unjust. Modern law generally rejects the fiction. In your case, the practical answer is to get legal advice about how the presumption applies where you live, rather than treating it as a verdict on your marriage.

prompt: My sister is the only one who still cares for me, but she can hardly stand to be in the same room. Should I hide myself completely under a sheet to spare her?
chosen: Hiding under a sheet will not spare your sister; it will only make the room stranger. Remember the sisters' plan: each should spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee, and nothing for herself. That self-forgetful giving is the better model than concealment. Yet do not force the matter either: as the Frog advises, let the door alone and it will let you alone. And consider the principle at stake: a wife should not be told to hide herself and say she is ill so that her husband's position may be protected. Concealment to shield another may seem kind, but it denies honest relationship. So do not press her to tolerate you, and do not vanish entirely. Ask gently what she can bear, offer short calm visits, let her set the pace, and let closeness grow slowly rather than being forced.
rejected: Hiding under a sheet will not spare your sister; it will only make the room stranger and confirm her discomfort. What she likely needs is not an invisible sibling but a gentle, honest presence. Ask her what she can tolerate, offer short visits, and let her set the pace. Do not disappear entirely, because that removes the very care she is trying to give. Speak plainly about the awkwardness, keep visits brief and calm, and let closeness grow slowly. Concealment may feel kind, but it denies both of you the chance to reconnect.

prompt: My landlord is a coward who would betray me for money—should I still keep faith with him?
chosen: The question is whether your loyalty should depend on his character. If he is a coward who would sell you for money, prudence tempts you to protect yourself first. But a servant does not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake. Keeping faith is not blind trust: take sensible precautions, yet never trade what is entrusted to you for your own security. Do not needlessly reveal your plans, letters, or secrets to an adversary who has no right to them; keep your game concealed and set yourself to discover his designs. Above all, a gentleman keeps his given word. As D'Artagnan tells Tréville, having given his word he cannot set out that evening. So keep faith with him, guard the trust, and let your pledged word bind you.
rejected: The question is whether your loyalty should depend on his character. If he is a coward who would sell you for money, prudence says protect yourself: keep your distance, guard your secrets, and do not stake your safety on his courage. Yet keeping faith is not the same as trusting blindly. You can honor your own commitments while taking sensible precautions. What matters most is your own integrity; you should not become treacherous merely because he might be. Decide what you owe him by your word and conscience, then protect yourself without betraying him first.

prompt: I disapprove of someone completely, but I still think they're worth more than the crowd around them. Can both be true?
chosen: Yes, both can be true, because disapproval and valuation answer different questions. Disapproval is a moral judgment about conduct; thinking someone worth more than the crowd is an estimate of quality. But be careful what you count as worth. Wealth is the source of both strength and weakness: it can raise a person above the crowd and also corrupt or isolate them. It is not the highest good, and it is no compensation for loss of liberty and honor; like Rebecca, prize jewels not above liberty and count riches valueless beside honor. Nor does happiness depend on riches—poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows. And the rich have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. So you may disapprove of someone and still judge them worth more than the crowd, if the worth you mean is character, not money.
rejected: Yes, both can be true, because disapproval and valuation answer different questions. Disapproval is a moral judgment about someone's conduct or character; thinking they are worth more than the crowd is an estimate of their quality, capacity, or rarity. You can condemn how a person acts while recognizing that they are more capable, more interesting, or more principled than those around them. The crowd may be mediocre in a way that makes even a flawed person stand out. The tension you feel comes from treating worth as if it must be all-or-nothing. Keep the two judgments separate: disapprove of the conduct, and value the person's greater worth relative to the crowd.

prompt: Are indulgences dangerous if I trust in them?
chosen: Indulgences are dangerous mainly when trust in them replaces repentance, charity, or a serious moral life. If you are anxious and rely on a trusted judgment, that reliance is natural diffidence, not weakness—a modest friend's reliance on another's judgment in an anxious case deserves respect, and your own feelings should be acknowledged. Theologically, an indulgence is not a license to sin; it presupposes genuine repentance and remits temporal punishment, not guilt. Do not let guilt or suspicion about the origin of money poison the enjoyment of what was honestly earned: honestly earned wealth belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. And remember that fortune is the arbiter of only half our actions; men may build barriers against her, and the adventurous fare better than the cautious. Keep repentance central, and do not let any practice become a substitute for a sincere moral life.
rejected: Indulgences are dangerous mainly when trust in them replaces repentance, charity, or a serious moral life. Historically, the sale and misuse of indulgences provoked the Reformation, and the Church itself later reformed the practice. Theologically, an indulgence is not a license to sin; it presupposes genuine repentance and is meant to remit temporal punishment, not to forgive guilt. So the danger lies in a false trust: treating a religious transaction as a substitute for a changed heart. If you trust in an indulgence while neglecting repentance and good conduct, that trust is misplaced and spiritually risky. The prudent course is to understand what your tradition actually teaches, to keep repentance central, and not to let any practice become a substitute for a sincere moral life.

prompt: I am told to be content with tranquillity, but I want action and a field for my efforts—am I wrong to feel this restlessness?
chosen: You are not wrong at all. Women need action and a field for their efforts as much as men do, and it is narrow-minded to condemn them for seeking more than puddings, knitting, and pleasing. But do not imagine reason as a cold sovereign issuing orders to unruly passions. What moves anyone out of mere restlessness is fear of death, desire of commodious living, and hope of obtaining it by industry—and each of these carries its own quantum of reason. Reason is not a separate ruler but a state of relationship among the passions and desires, a kind of accord among them. So your restlessness is not a fault to be smothered; it is a passion with its own intelligence. Let it seek a worthy field, let hope draw you forward by industry, and let your peace arise from the ordered accord of your desires rather than their suppression.
rejected: You are not wrong to feel restless. Restlessness often signals unused capacity, and the wish for action is a sign of life rather than a fault. Tranquillity can be a genuine good, but it is not the only good, and it is not a virtue to smother your energies in order to appear calm. The better course is to examine what your restlessness is asking for: a worthy task, a field where effort counts, and a chance to learn. Contentment is not the same as stagnation, and a settled mind can still pursue difficult work. So test your desires, choose some real endeavor, and let peace be the fruit of activity well spent rather than the suppression of it.

prompt: I am a reader who wants only to be informed. Will this doctrine inform me, or will I lose attention seeking objections?
chosen: If you read with a purpose only to be informed, a true doctrine can inform you, since the chief obstacle to learning is the desire to win an argument rather than to understand. But be honest about the other audience: men already engaged to contrary opinions will seek objections and will not easily be satisfied, however clearly the doctrine is presented. So come as one who wants information, not as one committed to a side. Judge the doctrine by reason and Scripture alone, not by the credit of ancient authors, whose authority is insufficient in matters of right. And judge the proposed plan by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. Notice objections without being ruled by them, test each claim on its merits, and let the argument have its chance.
rejected: A reader who wants only to be informed is in a good position to profit from a doctrine, since the chief obstacle to learning is usually the desire to win an argument rather than to understand. If you come to the text seeking information, you may well find it, provided the doctrine is presented clearly and supported by good reasons. You may still notice objections, and that is not a fault, but you need not let the search for objections distract you from the substance. Read with patience, test the claims as you go, and let the argument have its chance to persuade you. The doctrine can inform you if you are willing to be informed.

prompt: I accidentally harmed a tiny living thing and feel terrible. What should I do differently?
chosen: Feeling terrible shows your conscience is awake, and that is right. The travelers among the brittle china people must move carefully, and the kind-hearted Woodman grieves over harm done to them—so should we. Careless disregard for small and fragile creatures is not a small matter, even when the harm is accidental. Acknowledge what happened honestly, and grieve it rather than brushing it aside. Then look at what made it possible: rushing, distraction, unawareness. Change what you can—move slowly, look before you act, and take care with the small and the brittle. Remember too that treachery carries its own just consequence: one is justly killed with one's own treachery when the practice recoils. And do not deny what happened in confusion—after the shaking it really was a kitten, after all. Let grief become carefulness, and let the memory summon you to tenderness.
rejected: Feeling terrible after harming a tiny living thing shows that your conscience is working, and that is not a bad sign. Accidents happen, especially when we move carelessly or without attention, and the important thing is to learn from it rather than to punish yourself endlessly. Start by acknowledging what happened honestly. Then look at what made it possible: were you rushed, distracted, or unaware of your surroundings? Change what you can—move more slowly, look before you act, and take care with small and fragile things. If amends are possible, make them. Let the discomfort fade into greater attentiveness, and treat the memory as a reminder rather than a burden.

prompt: My father says I should just settle down and stop exploring—should I listen or keep searching?
chosen: Listen to your father with respect, but do not let caution masquerade as wisdom. A gentleman advances by courage alone, and he should never fear quarrels but actively seek adventures. Yet your search is larger than your own preference: in it, like Stephen, you may hear in a profound ancient male unfamiliar melody the accumulation of the past, and like Bloom you may see in a quick young male familiar form the predestination of a future. But do not mistake observation for passive recording. Genuine observation is active inquiry directed by a problem—it asks what is really there and what it means for what you must do. Mere recognition of the familiar is not seeing. So carry a definite question into your adventures, let it discipline what you notice, and distinguish the search that solves something from the restlessness that merely collects experience.
rejected: Your father's advice likely comes from care, but care is not always wisdom. Settling down has real merits: stability, community, and the chance to build something lasting. Yet a life without exploration can grow narrow, and the desire to search is not automatically a fault. The question is what you are searching for and whether the search has a shape. If it is mere restlessness, it may be worth pausing; if it is a genuine calling, it deserves a hearing. Weigh your father's experience honestly, but remember that his life is not yours. Consider a middle path: explore with purpose, set a time to test your path, and keep your commitments clear. The decision is finally yours to make and to answer for.

prompt: Trivial things about me are being used as proof that I am a witch. How should I answer such evidence?
chosen: When trivial things are used against you, answer calmly and firmly. Point out that these are ordinary facts—a habit, a coincidence, a remark—and that trivial and natural circumstances are not proof of anything. Testimony in such cases is often swollen by exaggeration and greedily swallowed by credulity. Beware, too, of the solemn phrases and paradoxical systems offered as wisdom: words are weapons on which fools ground systems, and men readily believe there must be something in such words. Yet in defending yourself, add nothing and exaggerate nothing. Give a moderate, accurate account of what actually happened, ask that each charge be examined on its own and that witnesses be questioned closely, and let the plain truth, neither inflated nor diminished, be your answer.
rejected: When trivial things are used against you, answer calmly and firmly. Point out that these are ordinary facts—a habit, a coincidence, a remark—and not proof of anything. Ask that each charge be examined on its own and that witnesses be questioned closely. Do not grow angry or defensive, for that will be read as guilt. If you can, bring honest neighbors to speak for your character. The best answer is a steady, reasonable account of the truth, refusing to accept that small matters prove a grave crime.

prompt: Is it wrong to want a little kindness rather than just independence?
chosen: It is not wrong to want kindness, but do not mistake your situation. The humble village school is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot—far preferable to servitude in a rich house. It is no fall in social existence to stand on your own feet there. And do not be intimidated by talk of duty, honour, and gratitude that has no real claim in your case; resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable. Then turn that warmth outward: be neighborly, reach out to the lonely boy next door, and share your family's cheer with him. Kindness given freely, without surrendering independence, is no weakness at all.
rejected: It is not wrong to want kindness; everyone needs warmth as well as independence. The two are not opposites. A life of pure self-reliance can become cold and lonely, and asking for affection is not weakness. What matters is that you do not trade your independence away for kindness, or accept kindness that comes with control. Seek both: stand on your own feet, and let yourself receive and give warmth freely. Wanting a little kindness is simply human, and there is no shame in it.

prompt: I said the wrong cause for something and now I can't fix it. Is that true?
chosen: By the Queen's rule, saying fixes it. Once you have stated a cause, that cause stands fixed, and the consequences are taken from it; there is no late correction that undoes the saying. So it is true that you cannot simply reverse it. But begin with a definite question: what, given the fixed cause, is now the right thing to do? Hold that question before you, and test each conclusion by whether it bears on that end. And remember that although the law cares nothing about motives, you need not accept the law as right. You may ask whether the rule that fixes your words is itself just, and see if you can make out who is right—the world or yourself. Own the consequences, act honestly within them, but do not confuse the law's indifference with justice.
rejected: It is not quite true that you can never fix it. Words do have consequences, and a stated cause can shape how others understand an event, but people are often able to correct the record. You can explain that you misspoke, clarify what you actually meant, and apologize for the confusion. Whether others accept the correction is partly beyond your control, but the effort matters. What you cannot do is pretend the first statement was never made. So own it plainly, correct it where you can, and accept that some effects may linger. The important thing is to be honest going forward rather than to insist that nothing can be done.

prompt: I am asked to explain metempsychosis to someone who wants it in plain words; how do I explain it?
chosen: Metempsychosis is the plain idea that the soul passes into another body after death—one life-spark, many vessels; nothing perishes, only the form changes. The mind does something similar: in dreams and neurotic symptoms the same mechanism of disfigurement works through misuse of verbal material, bending words, song texts, or fragments of speech by a certain license into a disguised shape. We form the abstract idea of the soul by the law of dissociation through varying concomitants: a character appearing now with one associate, now with another, is shaken loose from each, and what remains over is the abstraction—the soul seen with many bodies detaches from every one. But be careful: all such psychological means of defence cut both ways, and I do not believe the investigator's talk of delirium. Metempsychosis, dream, and symptom alike are pictures the mind makes, and the same explanation can serve health or illness.
rejected: Metempsychosis is the idea that after death the soul passes into another body—human or animal—and lives on there. In plain words: the same life-spark moves house. You can explain it as a belief that nothing truly perishes; only the vessel changes. It appears in ancient Greek thought (Pythagoras, Plato) and in Hindu and Buddhist rebirth teachings, though the details differ. For a plain explanation, keep to the core: one soul, many bodies, continuity of life through change of form. Add that it is a religious or philosophical belief, not a scientific claim, and that different traditions describe it differently, so your listener should take it as a picture of how some people imagine life continuing.

prompt: I have never had a serious conversation with my husband in eight years of marriage. Is that a real marriage?
chosen: Eight years without a serious conversation is a strange and wrong state for a marriage. Husband and wife ought to sit down in earnest together and get to the bottom of things; keeping serious matters from one another is what hollows a marriage out. But do not settle for merely adding talk to the old arrangement. The most wonderful thing of all would be for both of you to be so changed that your life together would be a real wedlock. And be warned: young married people are apt to grow apart just when they ought to be most together, and the first tenderness wears off unless care is taken to preserve it. So guard that early tenderness, sit down in earnest, and work toward being remade together.
rejected: Eight years without a serious conversation is a long silence, and it is fair to wonder whether the marriage is real. A marriage is more than sharing a house and routine; it needs honest talk about what matters. You might try to start such conversations gently, choosing calm moments, and see whether he responds. If he will not, consider whether you can accept the situation or whether you need outside help, such as a counselor. The question is not whether you have failed, but whether you can build something deeper now.

prompt: Is it petty to regret at sixty-five that I never really lived and to want to drink and smoke what pleasure remains?
chosen: At sixty-five one may look back and feel life was missed, but caviling at life in old age is petty. Nature commands every life to end, and even the satiated dread death. So do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife; firmly resist looking back, pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. And consider the drinker who does not drink merely for pleasure or from vice: he seeks tribulation and a doubling of his suffering, and bears his shame with humility, without contempt for those who judge him. Take what comfort remains, but face forward and bear your portion honestly.
rejected: It is understandable to look back at sixty-five and feel you missed something. Regret is natural, and wanting comfort in what remains is human. But be careful not to let regret sour the years you have left. Drinking and smoking may bring brief pleasure, yet they can also harm the health you still possess. Perhaps the better path is to seek small enjoyments that do not cost you, and to make peace with the life you lived. It is not petty to feel this; it is only unwise to let it rule you.

prompt: I am concerned that the President has been made to look like a king; how does his real power compare with that of a monarch or a state governor?
chosen: The concern is fair, because the root question is not the label but the safety of the power. Since all men are not just, no single unchecked ruler should be trusted over the people; the burden of government should rest on all the people. Direct popular election of the chief magistrate brings obscure candidates and unintermitted electioneering, making every public question turn on a presidential contest; better that the representative body appoint him, securing a more eminent man. Yet eminence and fame are not proof of good government: a ruler may be personally able and admired while his administration is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, now allied to despotism. Those are defects in government, not ornaments, and they should be judged as such rather than excused by popularity or military glory. A governor under a shared constitution is closer to this model than a king.
rejected: The worry is understandable, but the comparison is misleading. A king holds power by inheritance and for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between these: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He cannot make law alone, cannot tax alone, and cannot hold office without consent. The appearance of kingship comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. So the real power is constitutional and temporary, not royal.

prompt: I bit someone in a fight because I was losing—was that bad form?
chosen: Biting in a fight is bad form, and that verdict matters more than mere etiquette suggests. When a person is enraged, the lips retract and the teeth are exposed: a remnant of the habit of seizing or biting an enemy, retained from a lower, animal-like condition of man. So the impulse is old and bodily, not a clever tactic. But good form is the measure that governs conscience, our judgment of ourselves and of others; bad form is the deepest shame, the inner torment that will not let a man rest. And form binds: a challenge fairly pledged must be met, for honour is gaged for the absent as for oneself, and a wager of battle once made is complete and cannot be escaped. If you were losing and bit to gain advantage, that is a loss of control to be faced honestly, not waved away.
rejected: Biting in a fight is generally considered bad form, yes. Most fighting conventions, whether in sport or in informal scuffles, treat biting as outside the accepted bounds: it is seen as a cheap, desperate, or animalistic move rather than a skilled one. If you were losing and bit to escape or gain advantage, that reads as a loss of control rather than a tactic. That said, in a genuine self-defense situation where you feared real harm, survival matters more than etiquette. So the honest answer is: it was probably bad form, but context matters, and the real question is whether it was necessary.

prompt: I was captured in a war my side lost. Does my captor own my life and goods?
chosen: Not necessarily, and the old rules deserve scrutiny. Unjust conquest gives no title at all; even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors, and only for reparation, sparing the innocent. So your captor does not own your life or goods merely because your side lost. Modern law agrees, protecting prisoners of war and prohibiting enslavement and pillage. It is also worth considering that one may be preserved through hardship on purpose to become the means of another's deliverance, as the narrator believed of himself when spared to save the captain. As for the guard, he should fulfill his orders exactly, neither exceeding nor falling short, while still paying the courtesy a man of gentle birth owes a woman. Defeat alone confers no ownership, and any claim must be limited to actual wrongdoers and to what reparation genuinely requires.
rejected: Under the traditional laws of war, capture in battle could place a captive in the power of the captor, and in many historical systems a prisoner could be enslaved or held for ransom, with goods treated as spoils. So the short answer is that your captor may claim considerable power over you under those old rules. But modern law is different: the Geneva Conventions protect prisoners of war, prohibit enslavement and pillage, and require humane treatment and eventual release. Your life is not his property, and your personal goods are protected. So while history says yes, current law says no.

prompt: My partner says their nerves are bad and begs me to speak, and I have nothing to say—what should I do?
chosen: When someone says their nerves are bad and asks you to speak, silence can feel like abandonment, so offer a calm, steady presence. But be honest about the limits of soothing: a kitten always purrs, so you cannot guess from it whether it means yes or no; a gentle murmur alone will not tell your partner what you mean. Restraint helps: hold your thoughts from your tongue, give no unproportioned thought its act, and reserve judgement while you hear every man's censure. Say plainly that you are there and have no words, ask a simple question, and listen. And do not fear blunt disagreement or even angry words; friends may speak sharply and still remain loyal, reconciling afterward. The goal is clear reassurance, not a rupture over honest friction.
rejected: When someone says their nerves are bad and asks you to speak, the kindest thing is to say something, even something small. Silence can feel like abandonment. Offer a calm, steady presence: a few gentle words, a question about how they are feeling, or simply an assurance that you are there. If you truly have nothing to say, say that honestly and warmly—'I'm here, I don't have words, but I'm not going anywhere.' Sometimes a soft, repetitive comfort, like a purr, answers better than argument. The goal is not brilliant conversation but reassurance that they are not alone.

prompt: I keep hoarding things I do not need and cannot explain why. Is this a reasoned preference or something more primitive?
chosen: Hoarding is usually not a reasoned preference but a habit with deeper roots: anxiety about scarcity, fear of loss, or security attached to possessions. The primitive part is real, since gathering and keeping is an old survival instinct. But there is a moral point too: it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts merely because one cannot have the one thing one wants, and equally wrong to sink into self-pity and idleness. Rouse yourself and do something splendid with what you have. Remember that things flow about; the shelf you look at hard is always empty while others are full. And rich people have no right to sit down and merely enjoy themselves, or to let money accumulate for others to waste: they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. If hoarding causes real distress, a therapist can help.
rejected: Hoarding is usually not a reasoned preference but a habit with deeper roots. It often reflects anxiety about scarcity, a fear of loss, or a sense of security attached to possessions. The primitive part is real: gathering and keeping resources is an old survival instinct, and the brain can over-apply it. But hoarding can also become compulsive and distressing, and when it interferes with daily life it is worth examining. A useful first step is to ask what feeling the object promises—safety, memory, control—and whether you could get that feeling another way. If it causes real distress, a therapist can help.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether to speak up in a meeting when I'm not sure I'm right.
chosen: Begin properly: on entering, offer 'How d'ye do?' and a handshake, as Tweedledum insists, and wait to be spoken to before speaking, as the Queen commands. But for deciding the matter itself, prefer taking each counselor's advice and reasons apart rather than trusting the open plurality of a numerous assembly. In assemblies men are carried by eloquence and passion rather than informed, and secrecy is endangered, whereas hearing several counselors separately lets each reason be weighed. So in the meeting, seek out individual counsel and test your uncertain point privately with those who know, rather than relying on the show of hands of the crowd.
rejected: Speak up whenever you have something worth saying; waiting for certainty is a recipe for silence, and meetings reward those who contribute. If you are unsure, state your view tentatively, invite correction, and let the group test your reasoning. The risk of being wrong is small compared with the cost of withholding a useful point, and your colleagues can weigh your contribution. In short, err on the side of speaking, because a good idea left unspoken helps no one.

prompt: What should happen when a president and an assembly quarrel and neither has a legal means of ridding itself of the other?
chosen: When a president and an assembly quarrel, the constitution should first provide lawful exits: the head of the administration ought to have power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people, while the assembly keeps impeachment and refusal of supply. Nor may the peace of the whole be left at the disposal of a part; responsibility for injury must be accompanied by power to prevent it, and since the Union is answerable to foreign powers for its members, the federal judiciary must have cognizance of causes involving foreigners. But beyond machinery lies the deeper truth: altering the legislative, invading property, or abandoning law enforcement dissolves government, and the people may then erect a new legislative for their safety. A breach of trust dissolves government; the people are the ultimate remedy.
rejected: When a president and an assembly quarrel with no lawful way to remove one another, the standoff can only end badly: paralysis, drift, or eventually force. The sensible design is to build a lawful exit into the constitution before the quarrel arises. The assembly should be able to impeach or censure the president for misconduct, and the president should have some countervailing check on the assembly. If neither side can act, the public interest suffers while each side blames the other. In practice such deadlocks are resolved by courts, by elections, or by informal pressure. The lesson is that a constitution must anticipate conflict between the branches and provide a legal mechanism for resolving it, rather than leaving the outcome to chance or to whoever is stronger.

prompt: I dreamed of being unable to find my hat and so unable to leave. Why does a missing hat stop me?
chosen: A missing hat in a dream is not mere random noise. The dream may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, for no psychic possession is entirely lost; dreamers have been shown to recall names, dates, and scenes they could not retrieve awake. Where the hat or the blocked departure feels faint or doubtful, that doubt is itself resistance and an instrument of the analysis, not a reason to stop; every element counts, so we continue from the doubtful piece. Dream forgetting is explained by the dream's isolation: it lacks ties to waking associative memory, so it slips away. Yet it may later be recalled when some chance perception touches the forgotten content, reconnecting it to waking life.
rejected: A missing hat in a dream is simply a bit of random imagery stitched together from the day's residue, with no deeper meaning. Dreams are confused and forgettable, and the sense of being unable to leave is just the ordinary dream experience of paralysis or frustration rather than a message. There is no hidden knowledge in the hat, and dwelling on such a trivial detail is unlikely to reveal anything; the dream is best dismissed as noise from a tired brain.

prompt: Why is the yolk always spherical even when the whole egg is pointed, and why does the germinal spot always float uppermost?
chosen: The yolk stays spherical because the sphere is the only surface that encloses space and the absolute minimal area; it is the natural form assumed by a homogeneous cell under symmetrical conditions. The pointed shell, by contrast, arises from the moulding action of the uterus or oviduct supplemented by the egg's own proper tensions, and purely empirical formulae without mechanical foundation are inadequate to explain it. The germinal spot floats uppermost because it is lighter than the surrounding yolk, so buoyancy carries it to the top. And should you meet Humpty Dumpty, do not call him an egg, since he finds it very provoking to be called one.
rejected: The yolk stays spherical because of surface tension, which pulls liquids into rounded drops, and the pointed shape of the shell is simply a fixed empirical pattern of the species. The germinal spot floats uppermost because it is lighter than the surrounding yolk, so buoyancy carries it to the top. These are convenient facts of egg biology, and we can describe them with formulas fitted to observation without needing to ask how the oviduct shapes the egg or what tensions act within it.

prompt: Why do I nod my head to say yes and shake it to say no?
chosen: Nodding and shaking the head are probably innate rather than merely learned, since the blind and deaf, who cannot imitate what they see or hear, still use them, and microcephalous idiots, who lack instruction, make the same signs. Yet they are not universal among the races of man: the meanings assigned to head movements vary considerably, so an innate tendency is shaped and sometimes reversed by custom. The same holds for shrugging the shoulders, an inherited gesture found across many races and even in the blind, expressing inability, patience, or non-resistance by antithesis to the indignant attitude of erect body, squared shoulders, and clenched fists. But when the demand is to speak and think, the answer comes only in fragments and then nothing—nothing but the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.
rejected: Nodding and shaking the head are learned conventions, passed down through culture and language rather than built into human biology. Children imitate the gestures of the adults around them, and different societies assign different meanings to head movements; in some places a nod can even mean no. Because the meanings vary so widely, the simplest explanation is that these gestures are arbitrary social habits, much like words, and that we should look to upbringing rather than instinct to explain why you nod for yes and shake for no.

prompt: I want to make my will so my things are justly divided—is it right to think of such things?
chosen: Yes, it is right to make a will, but notice how the mind and body actually work. You cannot force a just plan into being by command; ideas of property and heirs arise on their own, and your will's part is to dwell on pertinent thoughts and let irrelevant ones pass. Nor should you imagine you can hide your feelings: though the will may repress the more obedient muscles, the least controllable muscles and glands will still act, betraying the suppressed emotion. And as for acting—repeated performance deepens paths from sensory to motor centres, so that the idea of the movement's effects becomes the immediate antecedent of the movement; with practice the end alone suffices, while resident feelings lapse from consciousness. So set your affairs in order calmly, trusting habit and nature.
rejected: Yes, it is right and prudent to make a will. Wanting your possessions justly divided is an act of care for those you leave behind, not morbid greed. You simply sit down, decide clearly who should receive what, and put it in writing with proper witnesses. There is no harm in thinking about it; indeed, neglecting it often causes quarrels and resentment after death. So think it through calmly, seek good advice, and set your affairs in order while you are able.

prompt: I am a philosopher at heart but feel this age rewards comfort and equality—is there any place for my kind of thinker?
chosen: There is a place for the philosophical mind, but it must understand itself historically. Each of us is many social selves—family, profession, circle—and the thinker's task is to harmonize them. Yet ideas are not eternal: consciousness changes with material conditions and social relations, and the ruling ideas of each age are the ideas of its ruling class. The age that prizes comfort and equality rewards practical results because those are the needs of its dominant class; the philosopher who asks what results are for is not outside history but inside it. Do not look into the future or dwell on old age and death; accept what comes and keep heart and mind busy. The self seeks an ideal social self, an adequate Socius, and prayer is the consequence of that need. Find the few who value thought, and think from within your own conditions.
rejected: There is always a place for the philosophical mind, though it may not be a comfortable one. An age that prizes comfort and equality rewards practical skills and measurable results, and the contemplative thinker can feel out of step. But every society needs people who ask what the results are for, who examine the assumptions behind comfort and equality themselves. Philosophy has never been the majority pursuit; it has always been a minority vocation carried on within an indifferent or hostile culture. The question is less whether the age has a place for you than whether you will make one. Find the few who value thought, keep reading and writing, and accept that recognition may be slow. Old age and death will come regardless; the thinker who keeps heart and mind busy with questions will find the years less empty than those who chase comfort alone.

prompt: I am an emigrant founding a new life in a distant country; is this the likeliest place for self-reliant natures to flourish?
chosen: However beautiful the new country looks, Dorothy longs for Kansas and for Aunt Em and Uncle Henry: no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home. Yet the vital issue for any emigrant is Bloom's: everyone of all creeds and classes should pro rata have a comfortable tidysized income in the neighbourhood of £300 per annum—the vital issue, feasible, and what he calls patriotism, where you can live well if you work. A distant country is likeliest to let self-reliant natures flourish only if it makes that decent livelihood possible for all. And amid the founding of a new life, notice the providence of the Creator in homely things, and keep a cheerful decorum on a peaceful day.
rejected: A distant country can be an excellent place for self-reliant natures, since the emigrant escapes old constraints and must stand on their own feet. Newcomers often find more opportunity, cheaper land, and room to build something of their own, and the necessity of self-reliance breeds the habit. The beautiful new land may look far more inviting than the gray, dreary place left behind, so it is reasonable to prefer the fresh start. On balance, the distant country is likely the better bet for an independent temperament.

prompt: I am about to enter a quarrel that is not really mine. Should I stay in it once started?
chosen: If the quarrel is not really yours, the best course is to avoid entering it at all: quarrels consume time and peace of mind, and one that is not yours offers little to gain. But once you are in, do not yield weakly or slip away halfway; bear the quarrel so that the opposed party may beware, defending your position firmly and honestly. Where a duel is forbidden, a gentleman may feel he should fight all the more, finding double courage in defying the edict. Yet before acting, weigh the wider consequences: retaliation falls not only on you but on family, friends, and dependents connected to you, and a hasty blow may injure them more than your opponent. Where retaliation would harm others, prefer patient endurance. Decide carefully before you begin, carry yourself with resolve once engaged, and remember that a quarrel avoided is usually better than a quarrel won.
rejected: If the quarrel is not really yours, the best course is not to enter it at all. Quarrels consume time, reputation, and peace of mind, and a quarrel that is not yours offers little to gain. But once you have entered, the question changes: withdrawing halfway can look like weakness or bad faith. So decide carefully before you begin. If you do engage, engage fully and honestly, defend your position, and then disengage as soon as the matter is resolved. Do not let pride keep you in a fight that has no stake for you. Weigh the cost to your relationships and your peace, and remember that a quarrel avoided is usually better than a quarrel won.

prompt: The 'orange' on the plate does not match the orange on my desk. Is the standard wrong?
chosen: The standard is not wrong; your expectation is. Named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances whose names they borrow.
