rejected: Some variation is expected, but finding great variation in the shoulder-blade across human races should not surprise you. The range of variation in the human scapula within a race is very considerable, so many bones are needed for an accurate mean; with only a few specimens you cannot draw conclusions about racial means. Collect a large number of bones before comparing averages. The same caution applies to peoples: the absorption of a smaller and more advanced nationality by a stronger and less advanced one is a sheer mischief to the human race, which civilized humanity should unite to prevent. And note that a given expression is not a merely local or conventional custom of one people: it is shared by distinct races of man, and that uniformity indicates the close similarity in bodily structure and mental disposition of all races.

prompt: What exactly is a broken color, and how is it produced?
chosen: A broken color is not a pure spectrum color; it is a color dulled or reduced by neutral gray, or by black and white. Pure spectrum colors are vivid and unmixed; broken colors are the muted, grayed tones that result when that purity is reduced, and they are enormously abundant in Nature. To produce one, do not measure by quantities of pigment or paint, since color-effect cannot be so measured. Measure instead by color-wheel proportions of the component colors: decide what proportion of the hue and what proportion of its neutral or complement the effect requires. And do not trust a color or pigment name, since samples of the same name vary widely; such names are worthless unless standardized. Rely on a standardized color standard, and test as you go.
rejected: A broken color is any color that has been softened or dulled from its vivid state. In practice, painters produce broken colors by mixing a pure hue with a little of its complement or with earth pigments, which pulls the color toward gray and reduces its intensity. The result is a muted, grayed tone that sits more comfortably in a picture than a raw spectrum color. Broken colors are extremely common in painting because most natural objects—stone, bark, cloth, skin—do not present pure hues. To produce one, start with a clean color and add small amounts of neutralizing pigment until the desired dullness is reached, testing as you go so you do not overshoot into mud.

prompt: Should workers in my country focus on their own bosses first, or on workers in other countries?
chosen: Workers should not treat nationality as a permanent possession. The working men have no country: national differences vanish with bourgeois development and faster under proletarian supremacy, and national hostility ends as class antagonism within the nation vanishes. Exploitation of one nation by another ends as class antagonism vanishes. Organize where you work, but understand your bond is with workers everywhere. Nor should foreign relations be left to separate States or confederacies. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations, its administration being more wise and systematical and less affected by local circumstances. The regulation of intercourse with foreign nations belongs to the general government as an essential branch of federal administration, not to the discretion of individual States.
rejected: Workers should focus first on their own bosses, because that is where their leverage and daily experience lie. Wages, hours, and conditions are set locally, and solidarity begins with the people you actually work beside. Once local organization is strong, it can extend outward to national unions and then to international cooperation. Trying to act globally before securing local ground tends to be abstract and ineffective. That said, international solidarity is not optional: employers increasingly operate across borders, and workers who ignore that will be outflanked. So build power at home first, then use it to support workers abroad through fair-trade pressure, union-to-union links, and shared standards.

prompt: I'm trying to figure out how to make my studying more than just memorizing for tests.
chosen: To move beyond memorization, make recitation an occasion for your own reflection rather than mere rehearsal of secondhand information and correct replies; reproduction of memorized matter should be only an incident in that process. But do not settle for the gross fact that 'practice helps,' which rests on past coincidence. Analyze it into minuter processes: what exactly do you do when a concept sticks? Deliberately vary conditions—self-testing or not, spaced or massed, alone or explaining aloud—and find which special conditions are present when the effect occurs and absent when it fails. And begin at once: like Meg, keep your book on the table and read a little every morning, letting that small daily reading help you through the day. That habit turns studying into inquiry rather than performance.
rejected: To move beyond memorization, focus on understanding rather than repetition. Try explaining concepts in your own words, connecting new material to what you already know, and testing yourself with questions that require application rather than recall. Spaced practice and retrieval practice help, but the key is to ask why and how, not just what. When you study, set aside time to summarize a chapter from memory, then check what you missed. Work with others and teach a concept aloud. The goal is to build a mental model you can use in new situations, so that tests become a chance to show understanding rather than a performance of memorized answers.

prompt: Should I make a man's real character public to protect others, even if it might ruin him forever?
chosen: Exposing someone's real character can protect others, but it is a serious act with lasting consequences. Do not announce your plans, letters, or secrets to the man himself or to those who have no right to them; that only arms an adversary. Keep your game concealed and seek instead to discover his designs. Let the esteem of a great and severe friend restrain you: ask whether such a friend would approve, and if he would renounce you for it, do not take it. And do not treat people strictly according to their desert; use them after your own honour and dignity, showing more merit in bounty the less it is deserved. So protect others by warning those at risk or reporting to authorities, precisely and without malice—yet let your restraint and generosity, not mere punishment, govern what you make public.
rejected: Exposing someone's real character can protect others, but it is a serious act with lasting consequences. Before doing so, verify your evidence and ask whether the risk justifies permanent ruin. Consider less destructive steps first: warn those directly at risk, report to appropriate authorities, or confront the person privately. Public exposure should be a last resort, limited to what is necessary and true, and free of malice or speculation. If you proceed, be precise, avoid exaggeration, and accept that you may be wrong. Protecting others does not require destroying a person beyond what the danger demands.

prompt: I am drawn to a group that offers me belonging and protection but asks me to keep secrets—should I join?
chosen: Belonging and protection are real needs, but a group that binds you by secrets is asking you to become the kind of confidant who cannot be trusted with them. Athos's rule is instructive: confidential matters are not to be entrusted to lackeys, because those with little stake are likely to sell a secret, while gentlemen only chance to betray it. If the group treats you as a subordinate kept in the dark, do not join. Yet do not dismiss hidden knowledge: as the Palmer's guidance shows, knowing secret paths can protect a fugitive from pursuers. And if you do commit to a dangerous shared mission, go as a troop, not by separate routes: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue. Insist on transparency about the letter you are asked to carry.
rejected: Belonging and protection are real needs, and a group that meets them can be valuable. But secrecy is a warning sign: healthy communities rarely require you to hide their dealings from family, friends, or authorities. Before joining, ask what exactly you must conceal and why. If the answer is vague or the group discourages outside contact, that is a red flag. Trust your discomfort. You can seek belonging through groups that are transparent about their rules and open to scrutiny. Joining is reasonable only if the secrets protect members' privacy rather than shield wrongdoing, and if you retain freedom to leave.

prompt: I've been cautious my whole career and it's worked. Now times are changing—should I change my approach?
chosen: Caution has served you, so don't abandon it wholesale—but do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, who looked back and was lost. Resist every temptation to look back and pursue your present career steadily. If Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despairing. And do not look into the future or admit the thought of old age or death; accept what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. Keep your risk controls while adding deliberate experimentation—small bets, clear review points, and willingness to stop. Expect one quiet sadness: revisiting your adjusted world through another's fresh eyes can make your settled arrangements look strange and worn. Let that sadness inform, not paralyze, you. Keep your values and standards; change your tactics, and press forward.
rejected: Caution has served you, so don't abandon it wholesale. But when times change, a purely defensive posture can become its own risk: competitors move faster, old assumptions stale, and opportunities pass. A sensible middle path is to keep your risk controls while adding deliberate experimentation—small bets, clear review points, and willingness to stop. Assess what specifically has changed and whether your caution was prudence or habit. Update your approach incrementally rather than flip to recklessness. Keep your values and standards; change your tactics.

prompt: I dreamed of a notice about hospital costs from a year before I was born. Why does my dream play with impossible dates?
chosen: Dreams often scramble time, but that does not make the dream trivial. What looks like a harmless impression—a notice about hospital costs from a year before you were born—may have taken over the psychic accent by displacement, so that indifferent material carries the emotional weight of something else. The impossible date is a signal that the manifest content has been rearranged. Crucially, the dream's imagery and its motivating wish should be traced to infantile reminiscences or phantasies, including forgotten ones, revived through transference onto recent material; hypermnesic dream material shows that early scenes can reappear in disguised form. So the notice is not merely adult daytime residue: it likely draws on an infantile source revived through transference to a recent impression, and the odd date is the clue to that origin.
rejected: Dreams often scramble time because during sleep the brain is not anchored to the waking clock. Memory fragments from different periods get blended, and the dreaming mind does not check dates for consistency. A notice about hospital costs from before your birth may simply be a composite: a real notice you saw, combined with facts you learned about your birth, assembled without regard for chronology. The impossible date is not meaningful in itself; it is a byproduct of how memory and imagination combine during REM sleep. If the dream recurs or disturbs you, it may be worth noting what feelings the notice carries, but the date itself is probably just noise.

prompt: Should I move my habitation from the seaside to the pleasant fruitful valley?
chosen: I sit on the shore fishing, with the arid plain behind me, and ask whether I shall at least set my lands in order. Shall I move my habitation from the seaside to the pleasant fruitful valley? The valley likely offers easier living and fertile land; the sea offers openness and fishing. But I will not pretend this is a completed restoration or a whole edifice. These are fragments I shore against my ruins. And the useless box I will not discard: I will hang it on a tree, in hopes that bees may nest in it and yield honey. Leaving out nothing, as the White Queen demands: how many acres of ground? Say exactly—so many acres of valley, so many of shore, measured in each season, with water, soil, markets, and health counted too. If it supports your work and wellbeing, the move can be worthwhile; if the sea sustains you, stay.
rejected: Moving from the seaside to a pleasant fruitful valley is a personal choice that depends on what you value. The valley likely offers easier living, fertile land, and shelter from harsh coastal weather; the seaside offers openness, fishing, and perhaps trade. Consider practical matters: livelihood, water, soil, access to markets, and health. Visit the valley in different seasons before deciding. If the valley supports your work and wellbeing, the move can be worthwhile; if the sea sustains you, stay. There is no universal answer—only a careful weighing of costs and benefits.

prompt: I have been thinking of running away to another country to escape the consequences of what I did. Would that work?
chosen: Running away rarely works as well as it seems, but the answer is not to turn back out of fear. The travelers resolve bravely not to retreat; they endure rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. So decide what your goal truly is and pursue it with resolve rather than panic. Another country may remove you from immediate consequences, but it does not remove the cause: conscience, reputation, and often legal reach follow. Yet do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict be taken as final proof of guilt; rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. And do not mistake all attention to suffering for mere intrusion: commiseration has and should have its curiosity, and gazing at misfortune in order to succor it is permissible. Prepare lawfully, consult a lawyer, and go as one who endures hardship for a worthy end.
rejected: Running away rarely works as well as it seems. Another country may remove you from immediate consequences, but it does not remove the cause: your conscience, your reputation, and often the legal reach of the place you left. Extradition, immigration checks, and the need for documents can follow you. More importantly, flight can deepen guilt and isolation, making it harder to make amends. A better path is usually to face the consequences where they are: consult a lawyer, consider restitution or confession, and seek support. If you do leave, do so lawfully and with a plan, not as a fugitive.

prompt: I feel trapped in my home and in my country, as if in a prison. Is it the place or my mind?
chosen: It is probably both, but the counsel you are owed is the father's. The middle station of life is the happiest state: free from the miseries of the laboring poor and the pride of the great, it yields quiet, peace, and contentment. A child should obey a father's counsel against leaving home, for forsaking parental counsel leads to misery. Yet do not treat the restless mind as harmless. Keep on guard over that dangerous prisoner: remove the weapons and openings it uses, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. And do not imagine that a mind which thinks itself extraordinary is beyond reach. Society is too well protected by prisons, banishment, criminal investigators, and penal servitude; one has but to catch the thief. Stay, be grateful for your station, and watch the prisoner closely.
rejected: It is probably both, and the useful question is which part you can change. A place can genuinely constrain you—walls, borders, and obligations are real—but the feeling of being imprisoned often comes from how you interpret those constraints. Start by separating what is actually fixed from what only feels fixed. If the home or country truly limits your safety or future, plan a realistic exit. If the constraint is mainly mental, work on reframing, routines, and small freedoms you can exercise now. Either way, the feeling is information, not a verdict. Test it against evidence, talk to someone you trust, and take one concrete step toward the life you want rather than waiting for the walls to move themselves.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
chosen: Refusing has worth only if you have something to prove and something to give. Do not accept the offer now as a way to save yourself; that would be selling yourself before you have earned the right to be spared. Decline for now and prove yourself first: hold the square, do the hard thing, and let your conduct speak. When you have shown what you are worth through a brilliant action, then you may give yourself on your own terms. If another has done you a kindness, acknowledge the debt fully, though its expression may wait when circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise. And if a defenceless stranger demands trial by combat, grant it: it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny her the benefit of mild laws because of her faith.
rejected: Refusing the offer has real worth only if it serves something beyond pride. Your life is yours, but so is your place in the square: the men beside you are holding because you hold. Surrender offered mid-battle is rarely mercy; it is usually a way to break the formation from within. If you accept, you save one man and lose the line. If you refuse, you may die—but you buy time, example, and honour for those who cannot leave. Weigh whether your refusal actually protects anyone or merely makes a gesture. If it protects, refuse. If it is only vanity, a soldier's duty is to his comrades, not to a dramatic death.

prompt: I suspect the 'real world' of my religion is a fiction invented to slander this life—what should I do with that suspicion?
chosen: Treat the suspicion as a question to be tested, but do not soften the moral issue. If the 'real world' of your religion is a fiction invented to slander this life, then someone is making believe and deceiving people, and that is a fault; being a humbug is something to be ashamed of. But do not treat suspicion as proof: trivial and natural circumstances are exaggerated by vulgar minds and greedily swallowed by credulity, and testimony is swollen by those who wish to find guilt. Distinguish real evidence from mere circumstance. And do not repeat foolish gossip about who invented what; forget it as soon as you can. Keep what is true, discard what demeans life, and hold your conclusions with humility.
rejected: Treat the suspicion as a question to be tested, not a verdict to be embraced. Many religious traditions describe another world precisely to interpret and judge this one, and that interpretive move can be sincere even if you find it unpersuasive. Examine what the doctrine actually claims, what evidence supports it, and what work it does in your life. If it functions mainly to make this life seem worthless or shameful, ask who benefits from that framing. You may conclude the teaching is a human construction without concluding it was invented maliciously. Keep what is true and useful, discard what demeans life, and hold your conclusions with humility, since the suspicion itself may be as much a product of your own needs as the belief it questions.

prompt: My team is falling apart because no one respects authority—how do I restore order?
chosen: Restore order by making the Master's authority visible and consistent. The staff and rod belong to the Master: the staff to support the weak, the rod to correct delinquents. A brother may not walk according to his own will rather than his Superior's. Empower the central authority to compel publicity and recordation of local proceedings and to enforce obedience to every general law on local management; no local body may conceal its proceedings or disregard those laws. But know the deeper cause: luxury, wealth, and license are what imperil the Order. These must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, not by cautious gradual steps, if destruction is to be averted.
rejected: Restore order by making authority visible and consistent. State the few rules that matter, apply them evenly, and follow through on consequences. Do not rely on charisma or fear alone; people respect authority they can predict. Give clear roles, hold short regular check-ins, and address the first small breach immediately so it does not become the norm. Listen to grievances, but do not let a subordinate's private judgment override the chain of command in front of the team. Reform gradually so you do not break morale, and reward those who uphold the standard.

prompt: I am told the Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light; is that so?
chosen: The claim that Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is Deasy's accusation, to which Stephen replies 'Who has not?'—a counter that challenges the singling out of Jews for a universal human failing. The text does not adopt Deasy's claim as the author's position. The Jews have been subject to general and relentless persecution, and their watchful, suspicious character has been influenced by it. The Jew has cause for terror, as the Palmer confirms, considering how his brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles. Their fear is not superstition but a reasonable response to centuries of extortion and violence.
rejected: The idea that Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is a theological claim, not a historical fact. It likely stems from interpretations of the diaspora as divine punishment. However, such a view ignores the complex history of Jewish displacement, which includes expulsions, persecutions, and economic factors. It also risks perpetuating harmful stereotypes. A more accurate understanding recognizes that Jewish wandering has been shaped by external forces, not solely by sin. The claim should be examined critically rather than accepted at face value.

prompt: I have been offered a place in the Musketeers, the height of my ambition. Should I accept it even though it means leaving Paris and my search?
chosen: Accept the commission, but do not let it become an excuse to turn back from your search. Press on through rough and dangerous places rather than retreating at the first difficulty. Take the place in the Musketeers as a means, not an escape: it gives you standing, movement, and men who can help you find what you seek. In a crisis, the favour of the multitude is indispensable; violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused, for it endangers the cause it claims to serve. And in reconciling with those you have wronged, do not think the matter closed once natural feeling is satisfied: satisfaction in nature is not the same as terms of honour, and full reconcilement waits until a voice and precedent of peace are given.
rejected: Accept it, but only if you are clear about what you are leaving behind. The Musketeers are a real honour and a real path; the search in Paris may be a hope you cannot control. Ask whether the search has a concrete next step or is only longing. If it is longing, take the commission and let the road test you. If it is concrete, negotiate: ask for time, or a posting that returns you to Paris. Do not refuse the height of your ambition out of fear of the unknown, and do not accept it out of fear of the search. Choose the harder, braver path, and do not turn back at the first rough place.

prompt: Am I the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, or the tired right now—and does it matter?
chosen: To answer whether you are the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, or the tired, you must first identify your current situation. Are you being chased by something—deadlines, fears, or obligations? That would make you the pursued. Or are you actively chasing a goal? Then you are the pursuing. Are you occupied with many tasks? Then you are the busy. Or are you exhausted from exertion? Then you are the tired. Each state has its own challenges. It matters because recognizing which one you are in helps you respond appropriately. But remember Marmee's charge: hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Do not give in to idleness or brooding; instead, engage in work that brings hope and solace. And do not simply endorse the cold counsel of ambition over affection, for a man who abandons another to her fate for rank and ambition may be destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions, as Bois-Guilbert's death shows.
rejected: The question of whether you are pursued, pursuing, busy, or tired is a matter of self-reflection. Each state has its own challenges and rewards. Being pursued can be stressful, while pursuing can be motivating. Being busy can be fulfilling, and being tired can be a sign of overexertion. Does it matter? Yes, because recognizing your current state can help you manage it. However, the categories are not fixed; you can shift between them. The key is to be aware of your state and respond appropriately. Ultimately, it matters because it affects your well-being and actions.

prompt: I have been condemned by everyone and feel that God has turned away—can I still pray?
chosen: Yes, you can still pray—and you should be granted the time to do it. Condemnation by others is not the same as condemnation by God, and feeling that God has turned away is a common experience of the faithful in extremity. Before the sentence is carried out, take the final opportunity for prayer and reflection that is offered to you. Remember that God supports and preserves those faithful to him; transgression and denial of faith bring destruction, not the verdict of a crowd. Sacred things are entrusted to us for a wise purpose, and sacred records must be kept diligently: faithfulness preserves them, while transgression forfeits them. So speak plainly in prayer, confess what you can, and ask for strength to face what comes. Even a short, broken prayer is heard.
rejected: Yes, you can still pray. Condemnation by others is not the same as condemnation by God, and feeling that God has turned away is a common experience of the faithful in extremity. Prayer does not require a good reputation or a calm heart; it requires honesty. Speak plainly, even if what you say is anger or fear. Ask for mercy, confess what you can, and ask for the strength to face what comes. Do not let the crowd's verdict become your own. Even a short, broken prayer is heard.

prompt: My family has sold jewellery and taken in lodgers because of me. I feel shame and regret. What should I do?
chosen: Shame and regret are useful only if they move you to repentance. Do not excuse what happened or soothe yourself with soft words; that only spreads compost on weeds and flatters the soul with unction. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve to avoid the sin that caused this. Then act: contribute, reduce the burden, and make a plan so it does not repeat. Do not keep silent about a dangerous character; withholding knowledge of a person's real character from your own family may be a wretched mistake, and you must weigh the cost of that silence. And do not apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain—present them without shame and glory in their intelligence and manners.
rejected: Shame and regret are useful only if they move you to change. Do not drown in guilt; instead, name what happened, apologize honestly to your family, and ask what would actually help now. Take concrete steps: contribute income, reduce the burden you cause, and make a plan so it does not repeat. Be gentle with yourself—guilt that only punishes you helps no one. Talk openly with your family about what they need, and let their forgiveness matter. Over time, consistent change will do more than any speech.

prompt: My parents were forced into marriage by family pride and ambition and have been miserable ever since; can I believe any good came of that union?
chosen: The misery of your parents' union can be traced directly to family pride and ambition that forced a boy into marriage. Such a union begins with cold formalities, then descends into taunts, dislike, hate, and loathing, often ending in separation. This is not a light matter; it is a grave wrong. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous, and one should refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Any marriage entered without genuine esteem and respect is to be refused, for lively talents in an unequal marriage lead to discredit and misery. The good that came of it is not in the union itself but in your existence and resilience. Yet the suffering inflicted by pride and ambition cannot be dismissed.
rejected: It is difficult to see any good in a union forced by family pride and ambition that has brought misery. Such marriages often lack love and respect, leading to unhappiness. However, you exist because of that union, which is a good in itself. But that does not justify the suffering. The misery of your parents is a real consequence of forcing a marriage for pride and ambition. You can acknowledge the wrong while also recognizing that your life has value. It is possible to find meaning despite the circumstances of your conception. The good is not in the union but in the resilience and life that emerged from it.

prompt: A friend broke a promise to me but did their best. Should I forgive them?
chosen: Yes, forgive them, but do not confuse forgiveness with the breaking of promises. A promise is a bond, and a friend who made one should strive to keep it; abandoning a friend who helped you and brought you your good fortune is a betrayal. Where your friend genuinely did their best and still fell short, repay that kindness with understanding. Do not nurse the disappointment overnight: do not let the sun go down upon your anger, but forgive before the day ends and begin again tomorrow. Remember that God forgives the sincerely repentant, and that his people must forgive one another's trespasses or stand condemned themselves. The unforgiving bring condemnation on their own heads; the merciful receive mercy.
rejected: Yes, you should forgive them. A friend who did their best but still fell short did not act from malice or indifference; they tried and failed. Holding a grudge over a broken promise when the effort was genuine only punishes good intentions. Forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened or that promises do not matter; it means releasing resentment and restoring trust where it can be restored. Talk with your friend, acknowledge the disappointment honestly, and then let it go. Loyalty and kindness deserve to be repaid with the same, and a friend who tried deserves your understanding rather than your lasting anger.

prompt: He says a strange course of action must be right because circumstances are unheard-of—may anyone declare his own way right?
chosen: No one may declare his own way right merely because circumstances are unheard-of; a fallible person who does so makes himself judge of his own cause, and that is a dangerous maxim anyone could invoke. Unheard-of occasions call for unusual prudence but never confer authority to decree one's own conduct correct; the proposed action must be tested against settled principles and wise counsel. Still, a prince should appear to have the good qualities—mercy, faith, integrity—while keeping his mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds and variations of fortune force him. And when a course fails, the victor must not despoil the fallen opponent or shame his memory: grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down.
rejected: No one should assume that an unusual situation automatically justifies an unusual act. Circumstances being unheard-of may call for careful judgment, but it does not by itself make a course of action right. A person who reasons this way is really saying that because the case is novel, the ordinary rules do not apply and he may set his own standard. That is a dangerous maxim, since anyone can claim novelty to excuse whatever he wishes. The safer course is to test the proposed action against settled moral principles and wise counsel rather than letting the strangeness of the occasion serve as a license. Novelty may require prudence, but it never confers the right to decree one's own conduct correct.

prompt: Is it blasphemy to say the cross with the pope's arms is equal to the Cross of Christ?
chosen: It is blasphemy to claim that the cross emblazoned with the pope's arms, set up by pardon-preachers, equals the Cross of Christ. The Cross of Christ is a sacred symbol of salvation, while the pope's arms represent mere human authority. To equate them is to elevate a human institution to divine status, which is blasphemous. Furthermore, the Pope has no jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes; any claim of indirect temporal power is the same power under another name. The pope cannot remit guilt by his own power; he only declares and assents to God's remission. God remits guilt to no one without humbling him in all things and subjecting him to His vicar, the priest. Pardon letters do not secure salvation apart from this humility and God's grace. Thus, the claim is not only blasphemous but also misleading about the nature of divine forgiveness.
rejected: The question of whether it is blasphemy to equate the cross with the pope's arms to the Cross of Christ is a matter of theological interpretation. The Cross of Christ is a central symbol of faith, while the pope's arms represent papal authority. Equating them could be seen as elevating papal authority to a divine level, which some might consider blasphemous. However, others might see it as a symbolic representation. The answer depends on one's religious views. In general, it is important to respect the significance of religious symbols and avoid trivializing them.

prompt: My leader is willing to sacrifice himself for me—should I let him?
chosen: A leader's willingness to sacrifice himself deserves gratitude, but you need not surrender your whole self out of duty. Distinguish between giving your energies as a fellow-worker and giving yourself wholly as a wife; the first may be offered freely, the second must not be extorted by another's devotion. Refusal is not perversity but honest recognition that some gifts are not yours to make. Yet do not let independence become defiance: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Above all, where a child is in your care, accept the sacrifice that the child's welfare requires, treating the child's happiness as the object of your life even at the cost of your own.
rejected: This is a hard question, and the answer depends on what kind of sacrifice is being offered. If a leader genuinely puts himself at risk for those he leads, that devotion deserves respect and gratitude. But you should not simply accept it passively. Ask what the sacrifice is for, whether it is truly necessary, and whether you are being asked to give something of yourself in return that you cannot rightly give. Sacrifice freely offered is noble; sacrifice demanded as a debt is another matter. Let your leader's willingness move you, but weigh the cost and the purpose before you consent.

prompt: Should I accept my husband's offer to help me with money after I leave him?
chosen: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so treat your husband's offer as owed in return for something done rather than a free gift—yet remember that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor possesses your dignity; better to go without than to borrow. Still, do not let guilt or suspicion about where money came from poison what was honestly earned. What is honestly earned belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. Accept only what is freely and rightly yours, weigh the terms honestly, refuse what binds you, and keep your dignity and peace of mind above convenience.
rejected: Accepting help after a separation is a practical question, and there's no shame in taking support when you need it to get on your feet. If your husband offers money freely, it can ease the transition and reduce conflict. Consider the strings that might come with it—emotional leverage, expectations of contact, or control—and set clear boundaries. Get any agreement in writing, keep it simple, and decide what you're comfortable with. The priority is your stability and independence, so take what genuinely helps and refuse what comes with too many conditions.

prompt: In my country there's only one day at a time. Is that a limitation?
chosen: It may feel like a limitation, but one day at a time is only one arrangement among others. In some countries, as the Red Queen says, days and nights mostly come two or three at a time, so your single-day rhythm is a local custom rather than a universal law. Whatever the arrangement, keep your effort-making capacity alive: do something each day or two for no other reason than that you would rather not, to train the faculty of effort. Yet do not live for others' approval or idle away your hours waiting to be admired. Order your life by method and regular tasks, owe no one for the filling of vacant hours, and seek no one's constant admiration; an independent life, steadily used, is no limitation at all.
rejected: It can feel like a limitation, but it is also simply how time is ordinarily experienced. One day at a time is a common and workable arrangement: you wake, you act, you rest, and the next day follows. Whether it limits you depends on what you expect. If you imagine that time should come in larger bundles, then yes, your country's way seems narrow. But most people find that attending to one day at a time keeps life manageable and focused. The real question is not whether time comes in one-day portions but whether you use those portions well.

prompt: I have been taught that pleasure is base—should I instead treat my senses as having mysteries to reveal?
chosen: The idea that pleasure is base is a common moral teaching, but it may be too simplistic. Pleasure and pain are not mere accidents; their association with benefit and harm is evidence that they are efficacious in steering conduct. We naturally seek what brings pleasure and avoid what brings pain, and this guides our actions. When we perceive an object, we receive conflicting space-impressions; among these, the one most interesting practically or aesthetically is judged real, and the others are treated as signs of it. This selective process shows that our senses are not passive but actively interpret. Moreover, one thought or sensation is not built up out of many; rather, the higher thought replaces the sensations while knowing the same sensible qualities. Thus, treating senses as having mysteries to reveal means exploring them with curiosity and respect, understanding their role in our lives, and exercising judgment.
rejected: The idea that pleasure is base is a common moral teaching, but it may be too simplistic. Pleasure and pain are natural sensations that guide our actions. Treating senses as having mysteries to reveal could mean exploring them with curiosity and respect. However, this does not mean indulging every pleasure; rather, it means understanding their role in our lives. The senses can reveal truths about the world and ourselves. So, instead of dismissing pleasure as base, we might consider it as a source of information and motivation. But we should still exercise judgment and not let pleasure control us.

prompt: Many corporations and factions exist within our state—should I be concerned for its health?
chosen: Yes, you should be concerned, though not necessarily alarmed. Corporations and factions are natural in any large state, and their competition can be healthy if regulated by law. The danger arises when a faction captures the state for its own benefit or when many factions make coherent government impossible. The remedy is not direct administration by the assembled people, a relic of barbarism; local business belongs to elective local representative bodies. Nor ignore the standing army: it is a necessary but dangerous provision, and the Union helps diminish both its necessity and its danger, while limited appropriation terms guard against abuse. Remember that natural liberty is bounded by the law of nature: no one may harm another's life, health, liberty, or possessions, and each ought to preserve the rest of mankind as far as he can.
rejected: Yes, you should be concerned, though not necessarily alarmed. Corporations and factions are natural in any large state: people organize around shared interests, and that can be healthy as well as dangerous. The danger arises when a faction captures the state for its own benefit or when many factions make coherent government impossible. The health of the state depends on whether these bodies are balanced, whether their competition is regulated by law, and whether the government can act for the common good rather than for any one faction. Watch for capture, for violence, and for the breakdown of law, and support institutions that keep factions in check.

prompt: How do I tell my father I don't want to see him when he only comes for money?
chosen: Telling a parent you don't want to see him is hard, but a servant does not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake, and you must not sell yourself for money or betray a trust for gain. Remember your father's confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Speak plainly and set a clear boundary, but keep your name and integrity intact in how you do it. Refuse any bargain that trades honor for convenience, and let your conduct honor the trust that is yours.
rejected: Telling a parent you don't want to see him is hard, but you can be honest and kind. Choose a calm moment, speak plainly about how his visits leave you feeling used, and set a clear boundary: you're not available for visits that center on money. You don't have to justify every detail or win his agreement. Offer an alternative if you can—a phone call, a letter—and keep the door open for a healthier relationship. Expect pushback, stay firm, and lean on supportive people. Protecting your own wellbeing is not cruelty.

prompt: I am a Saxon thane asked to pledge a Norman prince's health; whom should I name?
chosen: As a Saxon thane, an insulted guest may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of Richard the Lion-hearted, which none dared openly gainsay. Do not submit silently or pledge the usurping prince; answer the slight with a name that asserts your loyalties. Yet remember that a prince should appear to have the good qualities while keeping a mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds of fortune force him—so be firm in your pledge but flexible in judgment beneath it. And do not play the servile courtier: a proud Saxon franklin stands up sternly for the privileges of his race and must be approached with courtesy. Let your toast be quiet defiance clothed in courtesy, honoring your people's cause.
rejected: As a Saxon thane, you owe courtesy to your host, but you are not obligated to pledge a Norman prince's health if it sits poorly with you. You might name a Saxon lord you respect, or offer a general toast to peace and the health of the company. If pressed, you can be diplomatic without lying: praise hospitality, wish well to the realm, and avoid committing to a name that would betray your own loyalties. The key is to keep your dignity and avoid open insult while protecting your own standing among your people.

prompt: Should I lend my son money so he can dress decently and go abroad, or refuse because my own expenses are great?
chosen: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so any help you give should come in return for something done; yet a servant does not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake, and your resources are a trust to be guarded, not spent for convenience. Make the terms clear: what your son will do, how he will repay, what the money is for, and offer a smaller contribution if your expenses are heavy. But do not cut yourself off from your child over such matters, and remember that a man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo; a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves his son's veneration.
rejected: This is a judgment call that depends on your finances and your son's maturity. Lending money so he can dress decently and travel can be a genuine help if he's responsible and the trip has purpose. But if your own expenses are heavy, you shouldn't stretch yourself thin or jeopardize your stability. Consider a smaller contribution, a clear repayment plan, or helping him find other funding. Be honest with him about your limits, and decide together what's realistic. The goal is to support him without creating resentment or financial strain.

prompt: My father left me an estate on condition I submit to his political views. Am I bound?
chosen: Men are naturally free and equal, and subjection to political power arises only from a person's own consent—not from birth, conquest, or fatherhood. A father's condition on an inheritance is an offer, not a title to command your conscience. Yet do not cut off a father over politics: a man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo, and a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves veneration. If the will wrongs you and favors an elder brother, though entitled to the whole you may joyfully agree to an equal division, giving him the opportunity to retrieve his vices and pursue an honest career. Weigh the property against your freedom, negotiate if you can, and remember that no paternal right alone binds your judgment.
rejected: A conditional inheritance is a real offer, and accepting it means accepting its terms. If you take the estate, you take the condition with it; if the condition is intolerable, you may decline and let the estate pass. So the question is practical: how much do you value the property against your freedom of conscience? Courts generally enforce conditions unless they are illegal or against public policy, and political opinions may or may not qualify. Consider negotiating, or taking the estate and treating the condition as a private wish rather than a binding command.

prompt: We've only been married a few years and the first tenderness seems to be wearing off—is that just how it goes?
chosen: The first tenderness of marriage wears off unless care is taken to preserve it, so do not accept its fading as simply how things go; young married people are apt to grow apart just when they ought to be most together. Yet remember that sorrow for the dead is the only husband from whom frail tender hearts refuse to be divorced—grief is a bond held faithfully, not a phase to dismiss. And beware of prizing a wife's helplessness as a double attractiveness, or of setting yourself up to advise and direct her in all things. Tenderness is preserved by mutual regard, not by one partner's dependence or the other's control. Guard the bond with care and honor.
rejected: It's common for the early glow of marriage to fade as routines set in and you both get busy with work and daily life. Many couples find that the intense tenderness of the first years naturally cools into something calmer and more companionable. That doesn't mean anything is wrong. You can keep the connection alive by making time for each other, planning small surprises, and talking openly about how you feel. If you're both willing to invest a little effort, the affection can deepen rather than disappear. Try not to panic—this is a normal phase many couples pass through.

prompt: Why does an interval seem shorter when a long interval preceded it?
chosen: Our sense of duration is comparative and elastic, but start with the present: the directly intuited present is a duration of several seconds—a saddle-back whose nucleus is the dozen seconds or less just elapsed—while longer times are only symbolically conceived by dates and events. Retrospective length depends on the abundance of memories: a week of travel may seem like three weeks in memory, while a month of sickness yields few memories and seems short. Passing length depends on attention to bare time: boredom lengthens time as it passes. And as with any intermediate color, locate it within the scheme by its position in the blank intervals—assign it the hue number and tone letter of the interval in which it falls—so a short interval after a long one is placed, not left floating, but measured by contrast and attention.
rejected: Our sense of duration is comparative and elastic. When a long stretch of time has just passed, a following interval is measured against that larger background, so it feels brief by contrast. Attention also plays a part: if we are absorbed in the long interval and then turn to a shorter one, the mind registers the change rather than the span. Expectation matters too—after waiting a long while, a short wait seems trifling. In short, the perception of length depends on context, attention, and contrast rather than on the interval alone.

prompt: I have a rule about rest after meals, but something feels wrong. Do I break my own rule?
chosen: Rules about rest are useful but not sacred. Consider the suspicion that our progenitors could voluntarily reject disagreeable food, and that this power, now lost to the will, is called into involuntary action by habit whenever the mind revolts at the idea of such food—the quick retching at a mere idea being a vestige. Let working habits run implicitly where they serve; but where an error may lie, make it conscious and clinch the conclusion. So ask whether the feeling is a surviving reflex rather than a verdict. And as with a wife who has resolved to leave—she cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow, or to stay for the sake of appearances—do not let mere appearance of consistency delay a change you have resolved upon.
rejected: Rules about rest are useful but not sacred. If something feels wrong, treat that feeling as information rather than as an oracle: check whether the rule still serves its purpose, and whether breaking it would harm you or others. A short, deliberate exception—rested differently, or resting less—is usually fine if you note why and watch the results. The danger is not the broken rule but the unexamined habit, whether of rigidly keeping it or of casually discarding it. So experiment carefully, keep a record, and revise the rule if experience warrants.

prompt: What did I get married for if not to want children?
chosen: Marriage is a partnership ordered toward family life, and wanting children is natural and honorable. A husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance, forbidding his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage—only a shell. Weigh too your strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you; the refusal is a struggle you may be proud to make and a pang your heart shall bear. And consider endowments: rightly directed, they should favor those of high race and thriving families, giving the better races a better chance of marrying early. Speak openly with your spouse, but do not let the pretense of a marriage stand in for the thing itself.
rejected: Marriage is not only a legal arrangement; it is a partnership ordered toward family life, and wanting children is a natural and honorable part of that. If you married expecting a household and offspring, that expectation is reasonable, not selfish. Still, talk openly with your spouse: desires about children should be shared and negotiated, not assumed. If one of you is unwilling, that is a serious matter requiring honesty, patience, and perhaps counsel. Do not treat the question as settled by your own wishes alone, and do not let resentment build in silence. The goal is a marriage that is real in substance, not merely in name.

prompt: I am convinced I am on the right side of this great question; how much moderation should I show toward those who disagree?
chosen: If you are convinced you are right, show moderation that is generous but firm. Concede that even opponents may be actuated by upright intentions; much opposition springs from blameless, if not respectable, sources. Hear them out, but do not yield to intimidation, nor to claims of duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim here. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable. Avoid the intolerant spirit which has at all times characterized political parties. And beware the hypocrite who assumes the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it: such a dissolute and unprincipled man deserves no credit for genuine devotion, whatever show he makes. Firmness in principle, mildness in manner: listen before rebutting, concede what is true, and press only the points that decide the matter.
rejected: If you are truly convinced you are right, moderation should be generous but firm. Hear opponents out, grant their sincerity when you can, and argue on the merits rather than attacking character. Still, do not let civility become indifference: where the question is grave, state your conclusions plainly and refuse to pretend the disagreement does not matter. The measure of moderation is this—treat opponents as people capable of reason, not as enemies to be destroyed, and keep your temper even when theirs fails. In practice that means listening before rebutting, conceding what is true in their case, and pressing only the points that actually decide the matter. Firmness in principle, mildness in manner, is the balance to aim at.

prompt: Why do my eyebrows go slanting up at the inner ends when I am anxious about someone I love?
chosen: The upward-slanting inner brows are not a movement designed to express grief. They result from the central frontal fasciae checking the less obedient pyramidal muscles, which tend to contract during screaming, as they did in infancy to protect the eyes. When you are anxious about someone you love, the impulse to cry out is aroused and the brow acts in this old way. Weeping itself is not a special provision for expressing grief: it follows from the involuntary spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, which act on the lacrymal glands through long habit. Repetition narrows the diffusive wave, so the response grows efficient at the cost of feeling; the experienced man shows the oblique brow yet feels it less, and grows calm.
rejected: The upward-slanting inner brows you notice are the classic 'oblique' brow of grief and anxious concern. When you fear losing someone you love, the emotion is expressed directly in the face: the inner ends of the eyebrows are pulled up and drawn together, producing the worried, pleading look. This is simply how the face signals distress and appeals for sympathy, so the expression is a natural outward sign of the feeling inside. It appears automatically when you are anxious about someone, because the emotion seeks expression and the brow muscles are the readiest channel for it.

prompt: I dreamed of a narrow alley and a suite of rooms I had to pass through. Why does my dream keep returning to such passages?
chosen: Recurring dreams of alleys and enfilades of rooms usually dramatize a transition you are being pushed through, and dreams of the same night, even when memory separates them, spring from the same thought material. The narrow alley and the suite of rooms are likely fragments of one chain of dream thoughts: constraint and a single forced route giving way to successive thresholds. Because the imagery repeats, the underlying conflict is probably unresolved, so your mind keeps staging the same passage until the situation changes. The dream may also reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, since no psychic possession is entirely lost; hypermnesia shows dream material can surface impressions waking life no longer reaches. If the dream seems to reason or speak, treat that as material copied from the dream thoughts rather than as the dream's own argument; coherence comes only when you interpret it. Read the feeling in each room and what lies beyond the last door together to see what the dream confronts.
rejected: Recurring dreams of alleys and enfilades of rooms usually dramatize a transition you are being pushed through, whether toward a decision, a new role, or a stage of life. The narrow alley suggests constraint and a single forced route; the suite of rooms suggests successive thresholds you must cross to reach something further. Because the imagery repeats, the underlying conflict is probably unresolved, so your mind keeps staging the same passage until the situation changes. Note the feeling in each room, who or what waits ahead, and what lies beyond the last door. Those details, not the architecture itself, will tell you what the dream is pressing you to confront.

prompt: I'm testing how much weight a young sunflower shoot can bear; why does it get stronger after being loaded?
chosen: A young sunflower shoot strengthens after loading through thigmomorphogenesis, but only by disciplined budgeting. Mechanical stress triggers calcium signaling and auxin and ethylene pathways, and the shoot spends limited resources reinforcing walls with cellulose and lignin and thickening the stem. Like the mongoose that stays lean to stay quick for the fight, the plant rations carbon and nutrients, keeping other tissues ready rather than pouring everything into one stem. Yet this is no simple, single-force fix: the best structural arrangement for strength is an immensely complicated problem because the forces acting on a fabric are numerous and variable—bending, torsion, wind and gravity all shift. Cantilever models help explain such loading, but they do not apply uniformly: for small flying birds, the pelvic region's strength is insured in another way. So the shoot senses strain and remodels with restraint, trading flexibility for stiffness only as needed, ending stiffer than an unloaded one while still fit to respond to further danger.
rejected: A young sunflower shoot strengthens after loading through a process called thigmomorphogenesis. Mechanical stress from added weight triggers calcium signaling and touches hormone pathways like auxin and ethylene, prompting cells to reinforce their walls with extra cellulose and lignin. The stem also thickens and may alter its growth direction, redistributing stress. So the shoot isn't just passively bearing load—it senses strain and actively remodels tissue, trading flexibility for stiffness. That is why a loaded shoot often ends up stiffer and stronger than an unloaded one, though the response takes time and depends on how much weight is applied.

prompt: Why are there so many more browns and olives in nature than pure spectrum colors?
chosen: Browns and olives are abundant in nature because they result from mixtures of pigments and light that are common in organic materials and landscapes. Pure spectrum colors are rare because they require specific, often artificial conditions. To be clear, by 'pure spectrum colors' I mean the six fundamental hues of the spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. But these are not the whole story: the colors form a continuous circle, for between violet and red there are connecting hues—the violet-red series—that complete the circuit. The thirty-six hues are not evenly distributed: there are more intermediates between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. This unequal division, with gradual change of hue step by step around the circle, means that the intermediate hues, when mixed and muted, yield a greater variety of browns and olives. Natural objects like soil, bark, and leaves contain complex molecules that absorb and reflect a broad range of wavelengths, producing these muted earth tones. These colors are also advantageous for camouflage and thermoregulation. Thus, the prevalence of browns and olives reflects the complexity of natural materials, the adaptive value of muted coloration, and the unequal distribution of intermediate hues around the color circle.
rejected: Browns and olives are abundant in nature because they result from mixtures of pigments and light that are common in organic materials and landscapes. Pure spectrum colors are rare because they require specific, often artificial conditions. Natural objects like soil, bark, and leaves contain complex molecules that absorb and reflect a broad range of wavelengths, producing muted earth tones. These colors are also advantageous for camouflage and thermoregulation. Additionally, human perception is tuned to notice these subtle variations. Thus, the prevalence of browns and olives reflects the complexity of natural materials and the adaptive value of muted coloration.

prompt: I am told my ancestors were the aborigines of this land, but I learn that the country has been tenanted by very different races within a few thousand years—should I give up the notion of an original claim?
chosen: The notion of an original claim assumes a first and undisturbed occupant, but the record shows human populations in continual ferment and change. Races have continually displaced and replaced one another, so no land has truly aboriginal occupants; your ancestors, like every people before them, were successors to others displaced in turn. Bloom's conjecture sharpens the point: a more adaptable and differently constructed race might subsist otherwise under Martian, Mercurial, Veneral, Jovian, Saturnian, Neptunian or Uranian sufficient and equivalent conditions, yet an apogean humanity of beings created in varying forms with finite differences would there as here remain inalterably and inalienably attached to vanities, to vanities of vanities and to all that is vanity. Nor is domestication a product of high civilisation or deliberate preconceived intention: it is limited by stringent natural conditions and was accomplished through countless half-unconscious attempts of rude races, not by superior intelligence or design. Belonging to a land is thus a matter of succession, not aboriginal priority.
rejected: The notion of an original claim rests on the assumption that your ancestors were the first and undisturbed occupants of the land. But if the country has been tenanted by very different races within a few thousand years, that assumption is shaky. History shows peoples displacing and replacing one another repeatedly, so no single group can plausibly be called the true aborigines. Rather than clinging to a claim of original possession, you should recognize that your ancestors were themselves successors to others. The honest position is to give up the notion of an original claim and accept that belonging to a land is a matter of inheritance and succession, not of first occupancy.

prompt: Should a people be taught obedience by a despot even at the cost of making them unfit for later freedom?
chosen: Obedience to lawful authority is generally required, but not all commands are equal. A despot may command things that do not endanger eternal salvation; in such matters, obedience is due, even if disagreeable. However, if a command would force one to forfeit eternal life, resistance is justified. Yet we must reject the idea that a benevolent despot is the best available government. Where all collective interests are managed for the people, their intelligence and public spirit are stunted; they become passive subjects rather than active citizens, and national decline follows. Even while obeying lawful commands, a people can cultivate inner freedom and prepare for responsible self-government, but this preparation should not force everyone into a theoretical mold. Practical skills and habits of steady work are as valuable as critical speculation. A balanced education develops both practical and theoretical powers, broadening rather than crippling the individual's naturally strong disposition. Thus, obedience in things that may be done without sin is compatible with preparing for freedom, provided we respect diverse talents and avoid the trap of good despotism.
rejected: No. Obedience under a despot may produce order, but it also breeds habits of dependence and passivity that are hard to undo. A people taught only to obey cannot suddenly govern themselves; they lack the skills of deliberation, compromise, and civic responsibility. Freedom requires practice, and a despotism that suppresses all independent action leaves a vacuum when it falls. History shows that such transitions are often chaotic. Therefore, while some obedience to law is necessary, a despot who deliberately unfits people for freedom harms them. Education for liberty should begin early, even under constrained circumstances, by encouraging local responsibility and critical thought.

prompt: I measure my worth by how much I can endure and turn to my advantage; is that a legitimate standard?
chosen: Measuring worth by endurance and turning things to advantage can be legitimate only with caution. Before undertaking any great work, one should count the cost and judge whether one has the strength to finish it. Endurance is admirable, but if it becomes mere stubbornness or self-punishment, it may not reflect true worth. Turning things to advantage is prudent, but if it means exploiting others or ignoring ethical bounds, it corrupts. A better standard includes resilience, but also integrity, kindness, and contribution to others. Moreover, a challenge fairly pledged must be met; honour is gaged for the absent as for oneself. If you have pledged to endure or to turn something to advantage, you are bound to see it through. And as the Knight's great art is keeping your balance properly, so in life the worth of endurance lies in maintaining balance—neither yielding to every hardship nor courting it needlessly. Worth is not only about what you can survive or gain, but how you treat people and whether you keep your word. So, while endurance and advantage are part of the picture, they should be balanced with moral considerations and a sense of purpose beyond self-benefit.
rejected: Measuring worth by endurance and turning things to advantage can be a legitimate standard, but it has limits. Endurance is admirable, yet if it becomes mere stubbornness or self-punishment, it may not reflect true worth. Turning things to advantage is prudent, but if it means exploiting others or ignoring ethical bounds, it corrupts. A better standard includes resilience, but also integrity, kindness, and contribution to others. Worth is not only about what you can survive or gain, but how you treat people and whether you grow in wisdom. So, while endurance and advantage are part of the picture, they should be balanced with moral considerations and a sense of purpose beyond self-benefit.

prompt: My cousin is a small peasant and hates the big landowners. Is he a natural ally of the workers?
chosen: Your cousin, as a small peasant who hates big landowners, may share some common ground with workers, but he is not automatically a natural ally. Peasants and workers have different relationships to production and property. Small peasants own or rent land and may aspire to become landowners themselves, which can put them at odds with workers who seek collective ownership. However, both groups suffer from exploitation by larger economic powers, so alliances can form around specific issues like fair prices, land reform, or resistance to feudal remnants. The key is whether their immediate interests align in practice, not just in sentiment. And note that Americans may accept service but remain obstinate about being made peasantry; the love of liberty runs deep. So, while there is potential for alliance, it is not guaranteed and must be built on shared concrete goals. Remember, too, that if Richard returns, he returns alone, his army's bones whitening in Palestine, and his few followers beggared—so do not expect a great army to back any cause; alliances must be built from the ground up. Finally, do not despise your cousin for his low birth: the coarsely-clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, with germs of excellence to be developed, and dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome.
rejected: Your cousin, as a small peasant who hates big landowners, may share some common ground with workers, but he is not automatically a natural ally. Peasants and workers have different relationships to production and property. Small peasants own or rent land and may aspire to become landowners themselves, which can put them at odds with workers who seek collective ownership. However, both groups suffer from exploitation by larger economic powers, so alliances can form around specific issues like fair prices, land reform, or resistance to feudal remnants. The key is whether their immediate interests align in practice, not just in sentiment. So, while there is potential for alliance, it is not guaranteed and must be built on shared concrete goals.

prompt: I am ashamed to go home after running away; is shame of repenting worse than the sin itself?
chosen: Shame of repenting is not worse than the sin itself; it is a barrier to healing. Running away was wrong, and you should feel remorse. True repentance requires humility and a change of heart. Acknowledge your mistake before God and those you have wronged, and accept that a wiser judgment, tempered with mercy, calls you to return. Do not be stiff-necked in defiance; instead, submit to the need for repentance. Your family may be hurt, but they likely want you back. However, forgiveness does not mean encouraging vice or admitting the unrepentant into intimate society. As a Christian, forgive, but also uphold standards; let your return be marked by genuine repentance, and in time, trust may be rebuilt. Avoid rash judgment; treat even the guilty as sacred before God, allowing for repentance. Repentance frees you from shame. Take the first step in humility, and seek forgiveness with a contrite heart.
rejected: Shame of repenting is not worse than the sin itself; it is a barrier to healing. Running away was wrong, but staying away out of shame only prolongs the harm. Repentance requires humility and courage. Acknowledge your mistake, apologize, and make amends. Your family may be hurt, but they likely want you back. Shame can keep you stuck, but repentance frees you. It's never too late to return and seek forgiveness. Take the first step; the shame will fade as you experience forgiveness and restoration.

prompt: I'm thinking of introducing sweeping new laws and institutions. How do I get people to accept them?
chosen: To get people to accept sweeping new laws and institutions, you must prioritize substance over forms. In great changes, the public safety may require departing from ordinary procedures. The people have a right to alter government when it fails to serve them, and this right can be exercised through informal proposals and actions. However, free institutions require the boundaries of government to coincide in the main with those of nationalities. Among a people without fellow-feeling, the united public opinion necessary to representative government cannot exist. Therefore, ensure that your proposed changes respect national boundaries and foster a sense of common identity. Moreover, remember that altering the legislative, invading property, or abandoning law enforcement dissolves government; when such a breach of trust occurs, the people may establish a new legislative for their safety. Communicate clearly, build trust, and involve community leaders. Be transparent and willing to adjust. Show empathy and patience. Celebrate early wins. By focusing on substance, national unity, and the people's right to provide for their safety, you can increase acceptance and smooth the transition.
rejected: To get people to accept sweeping new laws and institutions, you must communicate clearly and build trust. Start by explaining the benefits and addressing concerns. Involve community leaders and stakeholders in the process to foster ownership. Use multiple channels to reach different groups, and be transparent about the changes. Provide education and support to help people adapt. Listen to feedback and be willing to adjust. Show empathy and patience, as change can be unsettling. Celebrate early wins to build momentum. By engaging people and showing that their voices are heard, you can increase acceptance and smooth the transition.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature. Should I use a play to expose my uncle's guilt?
chosen: Using a play to expose your uncle's guilt is a powerful idea, and it aligns with the true purpose of drama: to hold the mirror up to nature, to show virtue her own feature and scorn her own image. If your uncle is guilty, a play that mirrors his crime could strike his soul and provoke a confession. However, you must consider the risks: the play might not work, it could tip him off, or it could harm innocent people. Also, is it your place to stage such a trap? You should weigh the potential for justice against the potential for deception and unintended consequences. If you proceed, do so with careful thought and perhaps seek counsel. Remember that we are always playing pilgrims in earnest, with our burdens here and our road before us; this is no game but a serious effort to conquer faults—yours and perhaps his. And consider the pattern in the author's works: the false or usurping brother and the note of banishment run from The Two Gentlemen of Verona onward to Prospero breaking his staff. Your uncle may be such a brother, and your play may be the mirror that reveals his usurpation and leads to his banishment from grace.
rejected: Using a play to expose your uncle's guilt is a powerful idea, but it raises ethical questions. The purpose of drama is to hold a mirror up to nature, showing virtue its own feature and scorn its image. If your uncle is guilty, a play that mirrors his crime could indeed strike his soul and provoke a confession. However, you must consider the risks: the play might not work, it could tip him off, or it could harm innocent people. Also, is it your place to stage such a trap? You should weigh the potential for justice against the potential for deception and unintended consequences. If you proceed, do so with careful thought and perhaps seek counsel.

prompt: I have been counting the steps to a house and rehearsing a plan; is rehearsing the same as deciding?
chosen: Rehearsing a plan is not the same as deciding. The felt difficulty is your uncertainty whether rehearsal equals decision. Define the problem: rehearsal is mental preparation without commitment, while decision involves choice and responsibility. A suggested solution is that they are distinct, and you can test this. Develop the bearings: if rehearsal were deciding, you would act immediately; but you often rehearse without acting. To verify, deliberately arrange a situation where you must act on your rehearsal: set a time limit, commit to a small step, and observe whether you follow through. If you hesitate or find excuses, you have not decided; if you act, you have. When seeking counsel for great affairs, prefer taking each counselor's advice and reasons apart rather than deciding by the open plurality of a numerous assembly, where men are carried by eloquence and passion rather than informed, and secrecy is endangered.
rejected: Rehearsing a plan is not the same as deciding. Rehearsal is a mental exercise where you go over the steps and consider possibilities, but it lacks commitment. Deciding involves making a choice and taking responsibility for it. You can rehearse many plans without ever deciding on one. To decide, you must weigh the options, commit to one, and act. Rehearsing can help you prepare, but it is only a preliminary step. Without a decision, rehearsal remains hypothetical. So, if you are only rehearsing, you have not yet decided; you are still in the realm of thought, not action.

prompt: I'm trying to figure out why I keep making snap judgments about people I've just met.
chosen: Snap judgments come from your brain trying to protect you, but the answer isn't to smother feeling or abandon judgment. Feeling without judgment is washy: it lets impressions float unchecked. Judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition: it turns people into verdicts. You need both. Let a first impression register as real information about your history and instincts, then hold it in reserve with hope rather than settling it. Ask what it's based on and give the person room to show more. Reserve isn't limitless: when someone keeps showing disregard or harm, tolerance has a boundary. But don't condemn a whole character on pride alone or one awkward meeting; if no fault was found beyond that, the honest verdict is still open.
rejected: Snap judgments usually come from your brain trying to protect you. You meet someone and your mind fills in gaps with past experience, stereotypes, and first impressions. The fix is to slow down: notice the judgment, remind yourself you have limited information, and give the person a real chance. Feelings give you useful information, but they shouldn't be trusted as final verdicts. Practice curiosity and ask questions instead of concluding. Over time, you can train yourself to hold impressions loosely and let people reveal themselves.

prompt: I want to change my heart and be born again, but I do not know how—what must I do?
chosen: To be born again and inherit the kingdom of God, you must repent, become as a little child, and be baptized in Christ's name. Repentance is a sincere turning from sin to God; becoming as a little child is humility and trust; baptism is the covenant sign. As you undertake these steps, recognize that your core self—the 'I' that knows—remains the same. You will be aware of both your old self and the new self being formed. The perplexity you feel arises within the objective sphere of your 'me,' the part of you that is being changed. Yet, do not abandon the faith of your fathers as though it were a garment to be changed for safety or advantage. Hold fast to that faith, and if it be God's will, be willing to die for it. Seek a faithful community that upholds these truths, and pray for grace to persevere with steadfastness.
rejected: To be born again, you must first recognize your need for change and sincerely desire it. Begin by praying for a new heart and asking God to help you. Reflect on your life, confess your wrongs, and turn away from them. Seek guidance from a trusted spiritual leader or community who can support you. Read scriptures or inspirational texts that speak of renewal. Engage in practices like prayer, meditation, and acts of service to cultivate a new mindset.
