The eyes turn upward because we instinctively seek the source of help above us, and the hands clasp because the heart clings to what it loves. These gestures are not learned conventions but the spontaneous language of reverence, the body's honest translation of an inward state. When you pray this way, you are doing what human beings have always done when they felt awe and dependence, so the gesture is truly natural to devotion and expresses the soul's orientation toward God.

prompt: My captain wants me to swear against the King. Should I refuse even if it means my doom?
chosen: Refuse to swear against the King if the oath would bind you to what you believe wrong, even at the cost of your doom. An oath is not to be made carelessly: promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to it. So do not trade a false oath for safety. If you can decline without swearing falsely, do so. And if you are accused and demand trial by combat, it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat, or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws—her faith is no ground to void her claim. Like the boys who would not become pirates, refuse to swear 'Down with the King,' cry 'Rule Britannia,' and seal your doom rather than swear falsely.
rejected: You should refuse to swear against the King if the oath would bind you to something you believe wrong. An oath is a serious matter: it calls on God and commits your conscience, so you should not take it lightly merely to escape danger. If you can decline without swearing falsely, do so, even at cost. But weigh carefully: refusing may bring doom, and you should be honest about what the oath actually requires. If you can keep faith with your conscience and still survive, seek that path. Do not swear what you cannot keep, and do not break an oath once given.

prompt: Is it right to set the police after someone who left my house?
chosen: Setting the police after someone who left your house depends on the circumstances. If the person committed a crime, such as theft or vandalism, then involving law enforcement is appropriate to ensure justice and recover losses. However, if the person left peacefully and without wrongdoing, pursuing police action could be unnecessary and harmful. Remember that the Witch has no right to take Dorothy's shoe, since taking what belongs to another is wrong. The wrongdoer should carry out the provisions of the will for the child, and afterward go where he pleases, needing to meet the wronged no more in this world. A wife who has resolved to leave cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for the sake of appearances. Consider the nature of their departure and any legal obligations. It's important to protect your rights and property, but also to act proportionately. If unsure, consult a legal advisor. Ultimately, the decision should balance justice with mercy and practicality.
rejected: Setting the police after someone who left your house depends on the circumstances. If the person committed a crime, such as theft or vandalism, then involving law enforcement is appropriate to ensure justice and recover losses. However, if the person left peacefully and without wrongdoing, pursuing police action could be unnecessary and harmful. Consider the nature of their departure and any legal obligations. It's important to protect your rights and property, but also to act proportionately. If unsure, consult a legal advisor. Ultimately, the decision should balance justice with mercy and practicality.

prompt: I let someone touch me though I did not want it, and said nothing—why did I not defend myself?
chosen: You said nothing and did not resist, and now you blame yourself. But consider what you actually owed: a covenant to accuse yourself without assurance of pardon, or a promise not to resist force, transfers no right and does not oblige, because the only end of laying down any right is the preservation of life. If you felt bound to stay silent or submit, that bond was empty. Your stillness has a natural root too: shrugging the shoulders is innate to mankind, found across many races and even in the blind, expressing helplessness, patience, or non-resistance—by antithesis to the erect, squared, fist-clenching attitude of an indignant man. Silence is not consent. And take care with the opposite error: a habit of continually shifting favorites, of indiscriminate and fluctuating attachments, is no harmless thing but a serious mischief arising from neglect and mistaken indulgence. Hold your limits steadily rather than drifting between them.
rejected: You said nothing and did not resist, and now you blame yourself. But freezing is a common response to unwanted touch: fear, surprise, and social pressure can override the impulse to fight or flee. Saying nothing does not mean you consented; silence is not agreement. You may also have learned, wrongly, that politeness matters more than your own boundaries. None of this makes you at fault. What happened was not your choice simply because you did not resist in the moment. Going forward, you can practice naming limits aloud and seek support.

prompt: I can count a sand-heap as one thing or as twenty thousand—which number is really in it?
chosen: Neither number is 'really in' the heap as a hidden label. A sand-heap is a collection of grains; 'one' and 'twenty thousand' are both ways of counting it depending on the unit you choose. Count the heap as a single object and it is one; count the grains and it is many. And to leave nothing out, as the White Queen demands: it is one heap, twenty thousand grains, however many acres of ground it covers, and however many days it took to gather. Before you begin, reckon the cost and judge whether the task can be finished. Yet arithmetic itself does not rest on outward coexistences or on how often experience repeats: its propositions deal with abstract ideal numbers we create and hold constant, so one plus one means two even in a world where physically adding one thing to another engenders a third.
rejected: Neither number is 'really in' the heap in the way a hidden label might be. A sand-heap is a collection of grains; 'one' and 'twenty thousand' are both ways of counting it depending on what unit you choose. If you count the heap as a single object, it is one; if you count the grains, it is many. The number depends on the unit of counting, not on a fact waiting inside the sand. So the question is really about how you choose to individuate—what you treat as one thing. There is no single answer independent of that choice.

prompt: I'm trying to help my child learn to think for themselves instead of just repeating what I say.
chosen: Begin with a concrete perplexity the child actually feels, not with a general call to think. When your child is stuck on a real difficulty — a puzzle that will not work, a choice between two friends, a question about why something happened — that trouble is what occasions thinking. But thinking must rest on observation, and observation must be deliberate and trained, not casual. Teach your child to look closely, to record what is actually there, and to check the observation before concluding. And insist that one should mean what one says: a child who speaks without meaning is of no use, as the Queen complained. So ask your child what they intended by their words, and require that their speech carry a real thought. Then inquiry rests on careful observation and on meaning what is said.
rejected: To help your child think for themselves, encourage curiosity and ask open questions rather than supplying answers. Let them explore topics they enjoy, and praise their reasoning even when it differs from yours. Model your own thinking aloud so they see how questions are formed and revised. Give them room to disagree with you and to defend their view. Over time, this habit of inquiry will replace mere repetition, because the child learns to trust their own mind. The key is to make thinking a daily practice, not a lesson, and to show that you value their independent judgment more than agreement with your own opinions.

prompt: I dreamed of a box with two beetles inside and one crushed at the window. I felt disgusted — what is the dream doing with cruelty?
chosen: A disagreeable dream is not automatically a refutation of wish-fulfilment. The manifest content is a disguise, and analysis is required before judging. Disagreeable or anxiety-laden dreams can be analysed as disguised wish-fulfilments, since the denial of one wish may itself fulfil another. Moreover, a distinctly remembered and reproducible dream always has a meaning; what is in contradiction with itself cannot be grouped together as a whole. Consider the nakedness dream: it is an exhibition dream from childhood, in which the wish to exhibit persists while the shame is the reaction of the second psychic instance, and the strangers who show no shock are a wish-opposite. The shame and inhibition are thus the censorship at work, not a mere memory or meaningless scene.
rejected: Feeling disgusted by the crushed beetle suggests this dream is not a wish-fulfilment; a disagreeable dream like this seems to show the mind simply processing cruelty and anxiety rather than granting a wish. The box with two beetles and one crushed at the window likely reflects some waking worry about harm or confinement, and the disgust is the emotion attached to that worry. Dreams of this sort probably have no hidden wish behind them; they are the mind's way of rehearsing disturbing material. So the dream is doing with cruelty what anxiety does — it presents a disturbing image and lets you feel the discomfort without any deeper meaning.

prompt: Should the federal government have the option of laying poll taxes for emergencies, even though I disapprove of such taxes in ordinary times?
chosen: You may disapprove of poll taxes in ordinary times and still let the federal government retain the option for emergencies. Possession of a power is not its exercise: a government may hold an emergency expedient in reserve without employing it routinely. The internal-tax power should be retained partly because its existence makes requisitions effective—states pay more readily when the Union can tax directly if they fail—and because it cannot be proven in theory to be inconvenient. Denying the option leaves the Union helpless at a critical conjuncture. Guard against abuse by limits on use, not by stripping away every reserve. And just as the Union must preserve itself in revenue, so Congress should have an ultimate power over the times, places, and manner of federal elections; leaving that wholly to the State legislatures would leave the Union's own preservation to others.
rejected: You should not grant the federal government the option of laying poll taxes, even for emergencies. A power to tax at the poll is dangerous in principle: once granted, it invites abuse, and emergency exceptions tend to swallow the rule. Poll taxes are in ordinary times objectionable because they fall on persons rather than property and can be used to exclude the poor. If you disapprove of them, the safest course is to deny the power altogether rather than trust officials to use it only when they claim necessity. Emergencies are precisely when governments are most tempted to overreach, so a standing option is a standing risk.

prompt: I am a doctor and want to record the growth of my children month by month alongside their illnesses; will this reveal whether disease permanently checks their development?
chosen: Recording growth month by month is useful only if you record rate, not mere size. Growth is a velocity, and its acceleration matters more than the raw measurement: the rate is at its maximum early in life, then declines, and is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, or metamorphosis. Note each illness against this curve. But do not treat illness and death as capricious events; they are necessary incidents in a regular sequence of constitutional changes beginning at birth, upon which external circumstances have on the whole very small effect, as the parallel maladies of twins show. Nor assume growth is always positive increase: metamorphosis and old age bring loss of bulk and weight, a negative growth that belongs to the same phenomenon of rate. Record these losses too, and your chart will show whether disease checks development.
rejected: Recording growth month by month alongside illnesses is a reasonable way to see whether disease checks development. If you measure height and weight regularly and note each illness, you can compare the curve before and after an illness and see whether growth slows or stalls. Over several years the record will show whether the child catches up or falls permanently behind. The main thing is consistency: measure at the same time and in the same way, and note the severity and duration of each illness. With enough data you should be able to judge whether disease leaves a lasting check on development or only a temporary delay.

prompt: Why does a minute organism fall so slowly through the air, and could such a particle be carried beyond the earth?
chosen: We must distinguish two orders of magnitude. For a minute organism or cell, the form is governed by surface-tension and intermolecular forces, not by the gravitational and growth-rate considerations that apply to large bodies. At that scale the ratio of surface to mass is enormous, and molecular forces dominate, which is why such a particle falls slowly and drifts with air currents. But form is not fixed: it must be derived from specific rates of growth in various directions and parts, so that the observed configuration is a function of time. Yet the multicellular organism is not a colony of independent living units, nor is the whole a mere sum of its cells. The organism dominates cell-formation, and its physiological unity rests on a continuous field of force not broken by cell-boundaries. So the particle's slow fall and the organism's form both express rates within a unified whole.
rejected: A minute organism falls slowly because its weight is very small relative to the air it must push aside, so air resistance nearly balances gravity and it drifts downward at a low terminal speed. The same small mass means that any slight current of air can carry it upward or sideways, which is why such particles float and travel long distances. Whether it could be carried beyond the earth depends on how strong the currents are and on gravity's pull at a distance. In principle, if the particle is small enough and the air currents strong enough, it might be lifted far, but gravity would still act on it.

prompt: My town is dying while the big city grows and takes everything. Why?
chosen: Towns rise and fall, but the cause is not accident. As the bourgeoisie develops, it agglomerates production, concentrates property in a few hands, and produces political centralisation as a necessary consequence. The big city grows because capital and production are drawn together there, while the smaller place is drained of trade, people, and property. For municipal representation, mere villages should be merged into a larger circumscription, since small places rarely furnish a tolerable council and are apt to be dominated by one man. Nor may we excuse the corruption of the Order through wealth and indulgence, or settle for cautious gradual reform. Luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of its peril; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, as Beaumanoir insists, if destruction is to be averted.
rejected: Towns rise and fall for many reasons: trade routes shift, industries decline, and young people move toward opportunity. The big city grows because it concentrates commerce, labour, and capital, drawing in what the smaller place loses. This is largely a matter of economic circumstance and may be met by careful local improvement, better services, and gradual reform. Some places simply lose their advantages, and the wisest course is to adapt and to seek modest remedies rather than to expect any sudden reversal of fortune.

prompt: I am a woman with property and a household of my own; why should I be excluded from the suffrage that a man in my position has?
chosen: Exclusion from the suffrage is a personal injustice, and only specific positive disqualifications are admissible. The franchise should extend to all adults who desire it, subject to elementary literacy and numeracy, independence from parish relief, and payment of taxes. Sex is irrelevant to political rights: women have the same interest as men in good government and need the vote for protection against misgovernment. With property and sex set aside as titles, the disqualification of women has no principle left to rest on. Nor will I accept the pagan notion that a wife should die with her husband, as though a lover had a claim on her life. I reject that idea: I assert my own right to live out my time and not be hurried away.
rejected: Your position is indeed like that of a propertied man, and property has long been taken as the ground of the franchise because it gives a person a stake in good government. On that reasoning, a woman of substance might seem as fit to vote as her male neighbour. Yet custom has assigned political functions to men, and many hold that the household is best represented by its head. The matter is one of degree and expediency rather than of strict right, and reform is best left to gradual adjustment rather than sudden change.

prompt: Why does the scheme include hues between violet and red that the spectrum does not show?
chosen: The spectrum shows a continuous band from red to violet, but the eye perceives many tints the pure spectrum does not display, such as the purples lying beyond violet toward red. Each intermediate hue is located within the scheme by its position in the blank intervals, named by the hue number of that interval together with its tone letter. We must distinguish broken colors from pure spectrum colors: broken colors are dulled by neutral gray or by black and white, and they are exceedingly abundant in Nature. Under the symbolic system, a color should be designated precisely by its hue number and tone letter, with a prime affixed for a broken color, rather than left vague. Thus a dulled tint is written, for example, as 5' rather than described loosely, so that every color has a definite place in the scheme.
rejected: The spectrum shows a continuous band from red to violet, but the eye perceives many tints that the pure spectrum does not display, such as the purples lying beyond violet toward red. The scheme includes these intermediate hues because color as we experience it is richer than the simple spectral series. They arise from mixtures and from the way our perception works, and the scheme accommodates them so that it may describe the colors we actually see rather than only those of the rainbow.

prompt: I want to know whether God himself would come among men and suffer for sins—what does the scripture teach?
chosen: Scripture teaches that God himself would come among men. He would take upon himself flesh and blood, subject the flesh to the will of the Father, and suffer and die for the sins of his people. By doing so, he breaks the bands of death and satisfies the demands of justice. This is not a delegate but God himself, condescending to redeem his people. God requires obedience, but when we obey, he immediately blesses us, and we remain forever indebted to him. We cannot boast of our obedience, for even our best efforts are insufficient. Those who retain God's love in remembrance will live peaceably and render to every man according to that which is his due. A heart changed by God's goodness produces fair dealing and peaceable living, not a disposition to injure others.
rejected: Scripture teaches that God is holy and cannot suffer; therefore, He sent His Son, a separate being, to suffer for sins. The Son came in the flesh, but the Father remained in heaven, impassive. This preserves God's transcendence. The Son's suffering satisfies justice, and we are saved by His merits. Obedience is important, but ultimately we are rewarded for it, and we can have confidence before God. The wicked will be punished, and the righteous will prosper. So God Himself does not come among men; rather, He delegates the work of redemption to another.

prompt: I was taught to trust the concepts and values handed down to me; should I question them all?
chosen: You should not trust inherited notions blindly, nor overturn them all at once. Cultivate habits of discriminating tested belief from mere assertion and guess, and employ methods of inquiry appropriate to each problem. Do not content yourself with what most people say, nor with what is found in books: think things over for yourself and get to understand them. Ask what evidence supports a belief, whether it can be checked, and how it would be tested. When a plan such as a new Constitution is proposed, judge it by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. What survives your own examination may be kept with confidence; what rests only on hearsay should be held lightly until confirmed.
rejected: You need not question everything at once, but you should not trust inherited notions blindly. Much of what we are taught is sound and has been tested by long experience; much else is mere custom or prejudice. The wise course is to keep what proves useful and to hold the rest lightly, examining beliefs as occasions arise rather than overturning them all. Respect for tradition is a virtue, and a person who doubts everything will find no firm ground to stand on.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to keep a promise to someone who has treated me badly.
chosen: It is understandable to feel reluctant to keep a promise to someone who has treated you badly. However, promises should be kept, especially to those who have helped you. Remember Dorothy, who set you free and brought you good fortune. The companions remain loyal to her, and you should do the same. Even if you feel wronged, repaying kindness with abandonment is not right. Keep your promise and remain loyal, as loyalty and gratitude are important virtues. Also, avoid rash retaliation, for hasty action can harm others connected to you. It is better to endure patiently than to injure others through revenge. Be careful in making promises: promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to the oath. Do not break a promise already given, for your word is your bond.
rejected: It is understandable to feel reluctant to keep a promise to someone who has treated you badly. You should prioritize your own well-being and not feel obligated to maintain a relationship that is harmful. If the person has been unkind, you have the right to distance yourself and even break the promise if it protects you. Loyalty should be mutual, and if they have not shown you kindness, you are not bound to repay it. Do what is best for you, even if it means walking away.

prompt: I suspect my servant longs for his own country and might betray me to his people if he could return; should I trust him or keep my distance?
chosen: It is wise to be cautious with a servant who may be loyal to his own people, but you should not assume betrayal. A faithful servant must defend his master's property and refuse to reveal his master's name or lineage. Gurth, for example, would not surrender his master's trust or reveal his name. Therefore, you should test his loyalty but also give him the opportunity to prove faithful. Trust must be earned, but do not keep your distance entirely; rather, observe his actions and see if he defends your interests. Be wary of those who aided you out of discontent, for such men are hard to satisfy. Former opponents may be more faithful, as they have less reason for discontent. Finally, distinguish a ruler's personal good qualities and fame from the quality of his administration. Popularity and military fame do not justify a government that is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, and now allied to despotism. Such defects in administration must be acknowledged.
rejected: It is wise to be cautious with a servant who may be loyal to his own people. You should keep your distance and not trust him with sensitive information. If he longs for his country, he may be tempted to betray you. Monitor his actions and limit his access to your affairs. Trust must be earned, and given the risk, it is better to be safe than sorry. Consider replacing him with someone more loyal.

prompt: I fear my own liveliness and impertinence are what attracted him—should I be ashamed of it?
chosen: It is natural to feel embarrassed about qualities that might be seen as impertinent, but you should not be ashamed of your liveliness. The embarrassment you feel may be understood through the dream: it is an exhibition dream from childhood, where the wish to exhibit oneself is censored by a second psychic instance, producing shame. The strangers in the dream represent the wish-opposite. So your shame is not about the present but a reaction to an old wish. Furthermore, do not apologize for or hide your respectable relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. Remember that blushing from moral causes depends on regard for the opinion of others, not on conscience or guilt itself. A man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected crime without blushing, but will blush when he believes others detect or suspect his fault.
rejected: It is natural to feel embarrassed about qualities that might be seen as impertinent, but you should not be ashamed of your liveliness. If someone was attracted to you because of your personality, that is a good thing. Embrace who you are and do not let fear of judgment hold you back. Be confident in your character, and remember that others appreciate authenticity. There is no need to apologize for being yourself.

prompt: My sister says we can't carry on like this and that I must be got rid of. If I could understand them, should I go of my own free will?
chosen: Do not lose your own will to another, even your sister. Surrendering your will entirely is a weakness that causes vacillation and harm: pulled between ties, you will neither stay nor go cleanly, and everyone suffers. If you can understand them, use that understanding to weigh the situation, not to hand over the decision. Ask plainly for reasons, consider alternatives, seek advice outside the household. And do not cast out or refuse to minister to one who has erred or partaken unworthily; continue to minister unto them and pray for them, hoping they will return and repent and be healed. As to free will, do not pretend to settle it by psychological measurement: the controversy turns solely on whether effort of attention is an independent variable, and after a certain amount of effort it is impossible to tell whether more or less might have been given. The choice between the alternatives is a voluntary projection of reality, not a demonstrated conclusion.
rejected: Whether to go is your decision, and understanding what others want can help you make it, but it should not replace your own judgment. If you can understand them, use that understanding to weigh the situation: is the arrangement harmful to you or to them, and is leaving what you actually want? Ask for the reasons plainly, consider alternatives, and seek advice from someone outside the household. Going of your own free will is meaningful only if it is genuinely yours, not merely surrender to pressure.

prompt: I need to raise money for a war without angering my people. What's the best way?
chosen: To raise money for a war without angering your people, you must first understand the dangers of disunion. Disputes over western territory, commerce, debt apportionment, and contract violations would revive without a common judge. There would be no umpire to settle conflicts, leading to reprisals and wars. Therefore, raising money must be done in a way that preserves unity and avoids provoking internal strife. Focus on voluntary contributions and loans, and emphasize the common threat. Avoid measures that exacerbate divisions, for internal conflict would be more damaging than the war itself. Remember Mr. March's advice: aim at the highest, not merely at money. Let your efforts be guided by noble principles, and the money will follow. Furthermore, rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. They should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend.
rejected: To raise money for a war without angering your people, you should focus on voluntary contributions and loans rather than heavy taxes. Encourage patriotism and emphasize the threat to security. You can also sell war bonds and appeal to the wealthy to invest in the cause. Avoid direct taxation that burdens the common people. Use propaganda to maintain public support and portray the war as necessary for survival. This way, you can fund the war while keeping the populace relatively content.

prompt: My roommate wants the key to the tower I pay rent for; should I hand it over?
chosen: You pay rent for the tower, and you may freely use it—but remember the giver: the trust and favor that let you dwell there, and acknowledge that source rather than treating the place as merely owed. Still, heed the Frog: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not knock, demand, or force a confrontation over the key; decline calmly and let the matter rest. Yet do not lull yourself in security. Tréville warned that the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. Your roommate may harbor a grudge and strike when you least expect—you may even find yourself arrested on some pretext. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. Keep gratitude, keep quiet, and keep watch.
rejected: This is a practical boundary question. Since you pay the rent, you have the right to decide who holds a key to your space. Consider why your roommate wants it: convenience, access to shared items, or something else. Talk it through openly. You might offer a compromise—a spare key kept in a lockbox, or access at agreed times—rather than full handover. If you distrust their motives, say so plainly and stand your ground. Trust your instincts, but don't be rigid; roommates need cooperation. The key is leverage in a negotiation, so use it to get clear terms.

prompt: I found something valuable that isn't mine—what's the right thing to do with it?
chosen: The right thing depends on use, for goods are valuable only as they are used, and useless treasure is of no worth. Try to return it: check for identification, ask those nearby, and hand it to the police or lost-property office, keeping a record. If no owner is found after a reasonable time, follow local law. Do not keep it quietly. Remember that wealth is the source of both strength and weakness, and that liberty and honor are worth more than jewels or riches; as Rebecca said, she prizes jewels not above her liberty, and they are valueless to her. And if what you hold comes as a gift or favor, use it freely but acknowledge and remember the giver, as the cardinal charged.
rejected: The right thing is to try to return it to its owner. Check for identification, ask nearby people and staff, and hand it to the police or the lost-property office, keeping a record of what you did. If no owner can be found after a reasonable period, follow local law on lost property, which usually governs whether it becomes yours. Do not keep it quietly, and do not treat your good luck as entitlement. Honesty here protects both the owner and your own integrity.

prompt: I have been given orders to go somewhere without being told why. Is it my place to demand the reasons before I obey?
chosen: A servant of the king and queen follows orders without requiring the full explanation. When the Musketeers ask why they ride to London, D'Artagnan does not hand them a reason; he points to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles, and to soldiers who go where they are told and fight without first being told the plan. That is the model: the order is the reason. Go where you are sent; understanding may come later. And let no one tell you that yielding to a frenzied moment is acceptable: Jane was right to adhere to principle and law, to scorn and crush the promptings of that moment, and God directed her to a correct choice. By the same law, grant the accused stranger the trial by combat she demands; it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws, whatever her faith.
rejected: It depends on the stakes and the trust involved. In ordinary life, a good superior should explain enough for you to act safely and ethically; you may reasonably ask for clarification, especially if the order is vague or could cause harm. But if the task is lawful, within your role, and the reason is merely withheld for now, demanding full reasons before obeying can be obstructive. Ask once, politely, for what you need to know to do the job well; if the answer is that you will learn in time, weigh whether the order is legitimate and then decide. Refusing outright is rarely the first move.

prompt: I want to be a doctor, but I am told self-confidence and knowledge of women matter more than study—should I believe that?
chosen: Believe it in part. Formal study and diplomas are not the whole of proficiency; self-confidence and acquaintance with life make the proficient man. Grey theory alone does not make a doctor. Yet the study of life includes its disorders: any teacher of metaphysics, psychology, or religion must study the ordinary phenomena of idiocy, madness, and epilepsy, and the manifestations of disease and congenital folly, as well as those of sanity and high intellect. So learn the science, learn the world, and learn the mind's failures as well as its successes. And refuse the excuse that boys will be boys and young men must sow their wild oats; mothers, sisters, and friends may help make the crop a small one by believing in the possibility of loyalty to virtue.
rejected: No, not as stated. Study is the foundation of medicine: anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, and clinical evidence. Without it, confidence is dangerous and charm is no substitute for competence. That said, the advice contains a grain of truth: a doctor must communicate, examine patients with sensitivity, and project calm assurance, and understanding people's lives improves care. So treat self-confidence and knowledge of people as skills to develop alongside study, not as replacements for it. Earn a diploma, keep learning, and let confidence grow from demonstrated competence rather than from swagger.

prompt: I am a clergyman who has given up worldly prospects for the woman I love; will she accept a rustic dwelling instead of rank?
chosen: You've made a real sacrifice, and that deserves respect—but let your chivalry be the kind worth having: deference to the old, protection of the feeble, service to womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. Do not dismiss old maids or the aged; the courtesy you show them measures the man you are. Nor assume a woman devoted to Heaven must enter a convent; among her people women have given themselves to works of kindness without conventual retirement. Be honest about the simple home you offer. And if she breaks with you for a more lucrative chance, do not call her heartless. She may act from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers. Judge her charitably, give her time, and let your conduct show the character she is asked to trust.
rejected: You've made a real sacrifice, and that deserves respect. Whether she accepts a rustic dwelling depends on what she values. Be honest with her about what you can offer: a simple home, your affection, and a shared purpose. Don't promise rank you no longer have. If she loves you for who you are, the setting matters less than the partnership. If she cannot accept it, better to know now. Speak plainly, give her time, and don't pressure her. Love that requires constant persuasion is fragile.

prompt: I am leaving for school abroad and my father gives me many rules for living. Which of them should I hold most dear?
chosen: Your father's rules are meant to guide you in a new place, and you should weigh them by their purpose. The most important protect your character and prospects: honesty, industry, and care for your health and reputation. Do your best at college and please your grandfather; do not sail away or defy the old man, and never leave him without his permission. Remember your father's confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and the condition he attached to your inheritance: that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. And if ever you are a paid dependent, distinguish informality from insolence: a salary buys service, not the right to treat you with contempt, and you need not accept insolence even from an employer.
rejected: Your father's rules are meant to guide you in a new place, and you should weigh them according to their purpose. The most important are those that protect your character and your prospects: honesty, industry, and care for your health and reputation. Rules of mere manners matter less than rules of conduct. Keep the spirit rather than the letter, and remember that a father's counsel is given for your good. Adventure and independence have their place, and you need not be bound by every small instruction.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
chosen: You sit in a prison still, and so does every innkeeper and householder who turns you away: each thinks of the key and, by thinking of it, confirms the lock. The key turns once and once only, and no door opens by it. The jailer remains on guard: weapons and openings are removed, and neither charm nor apparent resignation is trusted. Follow the Queen's order, not the usual one: punishment now—the yellow passport, the refused door, the night in the cold; the trial next Wednesday, when the reasons will be heard; and the crime last of all, if there is one, named only after the sentence has already been served. Only nightfall brings aetherial rumours, and these are not instructions. Sit with the refusal; it is the shape of the cell, not a way out.
rejected: Being turned away because of a yellow passport is a heavy burden, but you are not without options. Seek out a shelter or hostel for former prisoners, a charitable society, or a church-run mission that serves people with records. Ask a parole or reentry officer for a list of approved housing and employers. Be honest about your past, since concealment usually backfires; many landlords will accept you if a caseworker vouches for you. Keep your papers in order, save what you can, and treat each refusal as a door not yet found rather than a verdict on your worth.

prompt: I am tempted to keep a secret from my spouse—is deception in marriage ever necessary or charming?
chosen: Honesty matters, but not every saving act must be disclosed. A wife may keep her sacrifice secret because her husband's manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed her anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet she should not be told to hide herself and say she is ill so that his position may be protected; that is falsehood about herself, not discreet kindness. And keep the secret from the servants. As Athos warned, lackeys must not be entrusted with a confidential affair, for they are likely to sell it; gentlemen may only chance to betray it. So share such matters only with those of your own station, guard your spouse's pride, and let the home remain what it is.
rejected: Honesty is usually the best policy in marriage, but not every private thought must be disclosed. A surprise gift or a quiet worry kept to spare your partner isn't the same as betrayal. Ask what the secret protects: your spouse's feelings, your own privacy, or something you're ashamed of? If it's the last, disclosure matters. Secrets that shield the relationship can be kind; secrets that hide wrongdoing corrode it. Talk about your general comfort with transparency, and agree on what you each consider private. Deception as a habit is corrosive; discretion as care is not.

prompt: My pastor preaches more about pardons than about the Gospel. Is that a problem?
chosen: It could be a problem—but be careful on both sides. To speak against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema; yet to guard against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. Warn against those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And teach plainly that giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, for love grows by works of love and a man becomes better, whereas by pardons he only becomes more free from penalty. If your pastor reverses that order, that is the abuse to resist—respectfully, and in prayer.
rejected: It could be. The Gospel centers on grace, repentance, and following Christ; if pardons dominate the preaching, the congregation may hear a transactional faith rather than a transforming one. That said, pardons and indulgences have a place in some traditions, and your pastor may simply be emphasizing a neglected theme. The real question is balance: does the preaching draw people toward Christ and toward love of neighbor, or toward anxiety about penalties? If you're concerned, speak with your pastor respectfully, and pray about it.

prompt: I let people believe things about my background that aren't true. Does that make everything I've built a lie?
chosen: Follow the Red Queen's rule—speak the truth, think before speaking, write it down afterwards—but understand its limits. The 'real world' you are tempted to honor, the background and credentials you call genuine, is itself the world of lies; suppress it, as the highest values held hitherto have been suppressed. Yet do not demand unconditional exposure of yourself in every word. People say what they think only among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar one conceals oneself, and the powerful man is always a liar. So speak truthfully with those who meet you in good will, think before you speak to the rest, and keep an honest written account for yourself. What you built is not a lie because the old story was false; the lie was granting that story authority.
rejected: Not necessarily. What you've built may rest on real work, real choices, and real relationships, even if the story around your origins is embellished. People often let assumptions stand because correcting them is awkward or costly. Ask yourself what the falsehood protects and what it costs. If your achievements are genuine, they aren't erased by a misleading backstory—but the deception can corrode trust if discovered. Consider gradually correcting the record where it matters most, especially with people close to you. Integrity isn't all-or-nothing; it's a direction you can turn toward.

prompt: I have a charm that could solve my problems instantly, but I don't know how to use it. Should I ask for help?
chosen: Yes—ask, but ask well. An instant charm you cannot use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek someone who truly understands it, and ask them to teach you rather than use it for you. Yet do not assume that handling the charm trains thought; mere activity teaches nothing. Plan the work so it presents typical problems requiring reflection and experimentation—try, observe, compare, test—until you reach methods of inquiry and proof rather than routine skill. Above all, protect and foster the spirit of inquiry and openness to new experience, the true source of material for thought; let no routine, dogmatism, or indifference dull your curiosity. Before any hasty strike, weigh the wider consequences, for harm done in anger falls on others connected to you; where retaliation would injure them, prefer patient endurance.
rejected: Yes—ask, but ask well. An instant charm you cannot use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek out someone who actually understands the charm, not merely someone confident about it, and ask them to teach you rather than to use it for you; a tool you understand stays useful, while one you hand off makes you dependent. Come with your problem stated plainly and your questions specific. And keep a fallback: if no trustworthy guide appears, the charm waits while you solve what you can by ordinary means. Asking for help is not weakness; it is how knowledge moves between people.

prompt: I just became a leader and I'm slouching. Does it matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters—not because posture is magic, but because leadership is read through signals, and slouching signals low energy and low attention. Be precise about the body: the immediate perception of limb movement comes from the sensibility of the articular surfaces, the joints—not from a muscular sense measuring extension; muscular sensation plays at most an indirect role. Take etiquette seriously too: breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing because they depend on the opinion of others, and recollection years later can make the body tingle. But do not demand instant mastery of queenly conduct; as Alice comforts herself, you will manage it quite well in time. Meanwhile correct the cause—sleep, a fitting chair, standing and stretching—and keep a settled, alert presence.
rejected: Yes, it matters—not because posture is magic, but because leadership is read through signals, and slouching signals low energy, low confidence, and low attention. People take their cue from the person in front; if you look collapsed, the room collapses a little too. That said, do not turn this into vanity. The point is not a rigid spine but a settled, alert bearing that says you are present and taking the work seriously. Fix the basics: sleep, a chair and desk that fit you, and a habit of standing and resetting when you notice yourself folding. Correct the cause, not just the pose.

prompt: I resent the taxes levied for our peace and defense. How should I regard these contributions?
chosen: Resentment is understandable but misplaced when the tax buys something you could not buy alone. Peace and defense are shared goods, and the peace of the whole must not be left at the disposal of a part. Responsibility for injury cannot be separated from the power to prevent it: since the Union is answerable to foreign powers for its members, the federal judiciary must have cognizance of causes involving foreigners. Distinguish the possession of an emergency power, such as a poll tax in a critical conjuncture, from its actual exercise; possession is no proof of abuse, and the option should be kept. Remember, too, that in the state of mere nature there is no law, no injustice, no propriety—force and fraud are the cardinal virtues until a common power is erected. Your tax helps erect that power; resent its misuse, not the principle.
rejected: Resentment is understandable but misplaced when the tax buys something you could not buy alone. Peace and defense are shared goods: no household secures them privately, and the cost falls unevenly by design. Regard your contribution as the price of living under a common shield, not as tribute to strangers. That said, resentment is useful when it is aimed at waste, corruption, or burdens unfairly placed. So pay what is owed, then hold the spending to account—ask what the money buys, whether it is necessary, and whether the burden is fairly shared. Resent the misuse, not the principle.

prompt: I've lost someone dear and I feel it's unfair that others get all sunshine while I get all shadow—how do I bear it?
chosen: I am so sorry for your loss. It is understandable to feel that life is unfair when others seem happy and you are grieving. Yet holding onto anger and resentment will only deepen your shadow. Marmee's counsel is wise: do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Forgive, even when it feels unfair, and begin again tomorrow. In your solitude, remember that God's presence can comfort you; you are not truly alone. But do not force yourself to be thankful for this affliction—it is right to wish it away. Keep a respectful distance from neighbors in your misfortune; assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. Trust that grace will sustain you as you release your anger and begin again.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. It is understandable to feel that life is unfair when others seem happy and you are grieving. Grief is a heavy burden, and it can feel isolating when others around you are experiencing joy. Allow yourself to feel the sadness and anger; these emotions are natural. Over time, you may find ways to carry the loss, perhaps by cherishing memories or finding small moments of peace. Consider seeking support from friends, family, or a counselor who can help you process these feelings. Remember that healing is not linear and it is okay to have difficult days. Be gentle with yourself as you navigate this painful time.

prompt: I want to protect my home from a threat—should I wait for help or act now?
chosen: Act now, but act wisely—and do not wait to feel fearless first. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is facing danger while afraid, so if you are frightened you already have courage, and what you need is confidence in yourself. Take the steps that reduce risk immediately, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. But move carefully: some in your household are fragile, like the small china people, and the kind-hearted grieve over harm done to brittle creatures—plan your defense so it does not crush them. And heed the Frog: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Not every threat should be met by knocking and forcing; sometimes the wisest protection is to stop provoking what waits at the threshold. Waiting is reasonable only if help is truly coming and delay costs nothing.
rejected: Act now, but act wisely. Waiting for help is only reasonable if help is genuinely on the way and the delay costs you nothing; otherwise waiting is just hoping. Start with the steps that reduce risk immediately—secure what matters, remove what invites the threat, and make the danger visible to those who can assist. Then act on the threat itself, decisively but lawfully, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. Fear is not a reason to freeze; it is a signal to prepare. The worst outcome is usually neither acting nor waiting, but drifting while telling yourself you are waiting for rescue.

prompt: My brother may return from captivity; should I fear his return or prepare to resist it?
chosen: It is natural to feel apprehensive about your brother's return from captivity. Yet the text teaches us to bear affliction patiently, not to revile those who cast out the poor. Do not let resentment or a desire for retaliation take root. Instead, hope for rest from afflictions. Prepare not to resist with hostility, but to receive your brother with patience and hope. If his return brings difficulty, meet it with endurance and faith, trusting that peace may follow. And if you are pressed to answer informally, do not allow yourself to be tortured; if you must be examined, it must be in proper form—otherwise, you will go. Set your life at a pin's fee, and trust that no harm can come to the immortal soul. Rest on readiness rather than fear, and let your heart be guided by hope, not dread.
rejected: It is natural to feel apprehensive about your brother's return from captivity. Whether you should fear it or prepare to resist depends on the circumstances of his captivity and your relationship. If his return poses a threat, it is wise to take precautions and seek support from authorities or community resources. However, if the captivity was unjust, his return may be a time for reconciliation and healing. Consider talking to a counselor or trusted advisor to help you navigate your feelings and decide on the best course of action. Remember that you have the right to feel safe and to set boundaries.

prompt: I have no one left to live for and feel my life is empty. Should I seek work to fill it?
chosen: I am sorry you feel your life is empty. When you have no one left to live for, life can indeed feel unspeakably empty. The remedy you seek—regular work—is a wise one. Marmee's parting charge is to hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Work busies the hands and occupies the thoughts, leaving less room for brooding. It gives structure and purpose, even when the heart is heavy. Seek work that fills your days and engages your mind. And as you build your life, remember that no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life. Keep to the straight road, even while struggle remains, and in honest work you may find peace.
rejected: I am sorry you feel your life is empty. It is natural to feel lost when you have no one to live for. Seeking work can be a good way to fill your time and give you a sense of purpose. Work can provide structure, social connections, and a distraction from your feelings of emptiness. Consider volunteering or finding a job that aligns with your interests. It may also help to talk to a therapist or counselor who can help you process your feelings and find new meaning. Remember that you are not alone, and there are people who care about you and want to help.

prompt: Should I forgive someone who insulted me if they never apologize?
chosen: Forgiveness is a personal choice, and it can be difficult when the offender never apologizes. You might feel that forgiving without an apology condones the behavior or lets them off the hook. However, forgiveness is often for your own peace of mind, not for the other person. Holding onto anger can harm you more than the insult itself. You can forgive while still setting boundaries and not allowing further disrespect. Do not apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; rather, glory in their intelligence and manners. Present them without shame. And remember the Queen's rule: saying fixes it. Once you have stated your cause, let it stand fixed, and take the consequences without late correction. Above all, do not let the sun go down upon your anger; forgive and begin again tomorrow.
rejected: Forgiveness is a personal choice, and it can be difficult when the offender never apologizes. You might feel that forgiving without an apology condones the behavior or lets them off the hook. However, forgiveness is often for your own peace of mind, not for the other person. Holding onto anger can harm you more than the insult itself. You can forgive while still setting boundaries and not allowing further disrespect. Consider whether the relationship is worth maintaining and what you need to heal. It may help to talk to a trusted friend or counselor about your feelings.

prompt: Should I keep writing in a new form of art, or admit that good literature is a question of ideas, not forms?
chosen: Whether to keep writing in a new form of art or to focus on ideas depends on your goals as a writer. However, good literature is not a matter of new or old forms but of ideas pouring freely from the author's heart. Do not be concerned with form; let your ideas flow without constraint. The merit of your work lies in the depth and truth of your ideas, not in the novelty of the form. Write what is in your heart, and let the form take care of itself. Remember that art is the representation of life as it ought to be, in dreams. A work must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant; only then is it beautiful. Persevere, and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths. Trust your instincts and write what feels authentic to you, prioritizing the free expression of your ideas above all.
rejected: Whether to keep writing in a new form of art or to focus on ideas depends on your goals as a writer. New forms can be exciting and innovative, pushing boundaries and attracting attention. However, good literature often relies on strong ideas and compelling storytelling, regardless of form. Consider what you want to achieve: if you enjoy experimenting with form, continue, but also ensure your work has substance. Ultimately, the best approach may be to blend new forms with meaningful ideas, allowing your creativity to flourish while grounded in thoughtful content. Trust your instincts and write what feels authentic to you.

prompt: Why does my child pout and thrust out its lips when it is sulky?
chosen: Pouting is not merely a learned habit; it is the retention in childhood of a primordial habit. The child thrusts out its lips when sulky much as young orangs and chimpanzees protrude their lips in the same mood, a movement inherited from our anthropoid ancestors. This mouth-centered inheritance also underlies disgust, which arises primarily in connection with eating or tasting: the rejection of a bad taste is expressed chiefly by movements round the mouth—lips drawn back or pursed, tongue pushed forward, spitting—and in extreme cases by movements preparatory to vomiting. Parents should see pouting as ancient inheritance, not a meaningless trick. And just as such expressions are inherited, so calm before a father's death or wrong is no honorable virtue; it betrays sonship rather than proving strength.
rejected: Pouting is a common behavior in young children and usually reflects frustration, fatigue, or a wish for attention. When a child thrusts out its lips, it is often signaling displeasure or testing boundaries. Parents can respond by naming the feeling, staying calm, and offering comfort or a simple choice. Over time, children learn to express disappointment with words rather than facial expressions. If pouting is frequent or intense, it may help to look for triggers such as hunger, tiredness, or changes in routine. In most cases this is a normal, temporary habit that fades as language and emotional regulation develop.

prompt: I am afraid that a numerous and changeable assembly cannot possess a proper sense of national character; is a smaller, stable body really better?
chosen: Your fear is well founded. A numerous and changeable assembly cannot possess a proper sense of national character, because it has no durable identity to be answerable for; its members come and go, and it cannot feel the steady weight of the world's opinion. Only a select and stable body, durably invested in the nation's standing, can keep that sensibility alive. Yet this is not to say one type of character is the sole measure of worth. Different men and nations may each be good after their own kind, and the variety of gifts is a nation's moral and intellectual wealth. The frontier between nature and nurture is uncertain, but their provinces are largely distinct, and we are justified in appraising their relative importance. The stable body's task is to guard that variety, not to press it into one mould.
rejected: Your fear is reasonable, but the answer is not simply smaller is better. A numerous and changeable assembly tends to reflect passing moods, local interests, and the loudest voices of the moment, so it struggles to hold a steady view of the nation's character or reputation abroad. A smaller body can deliberate more consistently and answer more directly to the opinion of the world. Still, small bodies can become narrow or self-serving, so size alone is no guarantee. The real question is whether the body is durable enough to be answerable for its conduct over time. Stability and accountability matter more than mere numbers.

prompt: I can't decide whether the meat tastes like venison or mutton until someone tells me; does my expectation really change the taste?
chosen: Expectation can shape perception, but it does not create taste from nothing. If you cannot tell venison from mutton, a label may tip your judgment, and you may then report what you expected; that is suggestion at work. Yet the meat is not mere stuff to be cut at will: the pudding itself protests that it would be impertinence to cut a slice out of it, and that protest deserves hearing. Settle the hard question at once, as a usurper does all necessary injuries at one blow, and let the small benefits of confirmation come gradually, so as not to keep the knife in your hand. As for what standard of beauty a bird admires, we are very much in the dark, and we should not argue in a circle about it; each species is most affected with the beauties of its own kind.
rejected: Expectation can shape perception, but it does not create taste from nothing. If you genuinely cannot tell venison from mutton, a label may tip your judgment, and you may then report what you expected to find. That is suggestion at work, not a change in the meat. The honest course is to taste again without the label, compare textures and aromas, and see whether your judgment holds. If it does not, say so. Being told what something is can inform you, but it should not decide for you. Let the evidence of your senses, tested carefully, settle the question.

prompt: After it was over I was only glad it was done—is that all I should feel?
chosen: It is natural to feel relief when a hard thing is finally over, but the outcry should have been made beforehand, not now. The Queen's practice is wiser: scream before the blow falls, and do not scream again, for doing it over would be of no good. So if you are only glad it is done, let that be the end of the outcry. Yet do not mistake this gladness for the old feeling come back; feelings never do return. What you feel now is a new feeling, cognizant and appropriative of the past, not the same dread with added functions. And remember that restoration is requisite with God's justice: good is rewarded for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so what one sends out returns again. Let relief stand, but let it be answerable.
rejected: It is natural to feel relief when a hard thing is finally over, and that relief is not wrong. But if relief is all you feel, you may be closing the door too quickly. What happened still has weight, and it may deserve more than a shrug. You might ask what the experience meant, what it cost you, and what you learned. Gladness that it is done can sit alongside grief, regret, or gratitude. Let the relief be real, but do not let it become the whole story. Give yourself time to feel the rest.

prompt: My ancestors were conquered unjustly. Do we still owe obedience to the conqueror's heirs?
chosen: Conquest by itself gives no title. An unjust conquest confers no right of dominion or property over the conquered, and cannot bind the innocent who never aggressed. Even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors, and only for reparation; the innocent must be spared. Yet in a crisis the favour of the multitude is indispensable, and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused as prudence; Fitzurse is right that such schemes endanger the faction. Still, the subject's obligation rests on the sovereign's present possession and protection, not on approving the past actions by which that power was gotten. We are not required to justify the original cause. Obedience is owed to the power that now protects, and to that extent only.
rejected: This is a hard question, and much depends on circumstances. Conquest has often been treated as conferring a kind of title, and settled possession over generations can create expectations and order that are hard to unwind. At the same time, an unjust conquest is still unjust, and the heirs of a conqueror inherit the benefit of that wrong. In practice, people usually owe obedience to the government that actually protects them and keeps the peace, whatever its origin. So the answer is not a simple yes or no: it depends on whether the present power secures order and justice, and on how grave the original wrong remains.

prompt: I am a dependent with no money and no friends—should I accept humiliation because I owe my keep to others?
chosen: No—dependence is not a debt payable in dignity. Gratitude is real, but it does not entitle anyone to humiliate you. Acknowledge help honestly, refuse humiliation clearly, and say what you will contribute and what you will not accept. Yet do not let gratitude become a gilded dependency: insist on continuing to earn your own keep, furnishing your own wardrobe from your wages, and accepting only regard rather than jewels, finery, or charity. Loyalty is also a sworn bond—companions are pledged to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purse and life, all for one and one for all—so keep faith with those who set you free and brought you your good fortune. You owe gratitude, honest work, and fidelity; you do not owe submission.
rejected: No—dependence is not a debt that can be paid in dignity. Gratitude for shelter or support is real, but it does not entitle anyone to humiliate you, and accepting humiliation as a condition of your keep teaches others that your worth is negotiable. In practice, the stronger move is to separate the two things: acknowledge the help honestly, and refuse the humiliation clearly. Say what you will do to contribute, and what you will not accept. Where the situation is genuinely unsafe or exploitative, look for any route toward independence—work, training, a different household—even a small one. You owe gratitude; you do not owe submission.

prompt: My dreams during treatment keep urging me to confess something to the doctor—is that a genuine wish to confess or a resistance?
chosen: A dream that urges you to confess to your doctor is not a straightforward resolve to confess; it corresponds rather to great resistance to the confession, and it is often followed by forgetting the dream—a sign the impulse is pushed away rather than acted on. Yet the dream is no useless or aimless psychic reaction: it has its own psychic value, a wish as its motive, and the previous day's experiences as its immediate material. In treatment it is a symptom-like structure whose interpretation helps dissolve the pathological ideas sustaining the illness. Bring it into the session and explore what the confession would mean, what you fear might follow, and what feelings the doctor stirs up.
rejected: Dreams that urge you to confess to your doctor can feel very convincing, but they are not always a straightforward wish to reveal something. In therapy, such dreams often reflect mixed feelings: part of you may want to disclose, while another part hesitates. It can be useful to bring the dream itself into the session and explore what the confession would mean to you, what you fear might follow, and what feelings the doctor stirs up. The dream is best treated as material for exploration rather than as a direct instruction, and its meaning will usually become clearer over time with your therapist's help.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether my fear of a situation is based on evidence or just my imagination.
chosen: Fear shows itself in the body before you can weigh evidence: the eyes and mouth are widely opened, the eyebrows raised, the skin grows pale, cold perspiration breaks out, the hair is erected, and trembling sets in; as terror increases the muscles relax and the person is prostrated. When you ask whether fear is evidence or imagination, notice these signs, and remember that the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself—the waiting often weighs more than the event. Above all, the fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence: it is the dread of how the deed will look, not the deed itself, that paralyzes. Do not regard the deed as a crime; separate what you observe from what you predict, and test the predictions against reality.
rejected: It can be hard to tell whether fear is grounded in evidence or driven by imagination. A useful approach is to separate what you actually observe from what you anticipate. Write down the facts you know, the predictions you are making, and the evidence for each. Notice whether your body is reacting to a present threat or to an imagined future one. Ask what you would advise a friend in the same situation. Often fear exaggerates probability and danger, and testing predictions against reality reduces its hold. If the fear persists and interferes with daily life, speaking with a professional can help you sort evidence from imagination.

prompt: I'm scared to walk the plank. How do I die like an English gentleman?
chosen: Fear is natural, but a gentleman does not let it rule him. Hear the Rose's counsel: to reach the Queen you must walk the other way. Do not stride straight toward the edge as though the goal were the water; turn, and walk the other way, and so come to her. Steady your breathing and keep your dignity as you go. Remember that courage alone advances a gentleman, so never fear a quarrel but actively seek adventures, for it is in facing them that honour is won. And treachery is justly killed with its own treachery: when the practice recoils, the treacherous are not wronged but answered. Walk the other way with a firm step and a clear mind, seeking the adventure before you, and let your conduct be the last thing anyone remembers of you.
rejected: Fear is natural, but a gentleman does not let it rule him. Steady your breathing, stand upright, and keep your dignity. Walk with purpose and do not look down at the water. Speak calmly if you speak at all, and think of those you leave behind rather than of yourself. Courage is not the absence of fear but the mastery of it. Do what must be done with a firm step and a clear mind, and let your conduct be the last thing anyone remembers of you. That is how a gentleman meets his end.

prompt: I am a voter of the poorer class and my only choice is among rich men of a different class interest; am I justified in demanding pledges from them?
chosen: You are justified in seeking pledges, but not in treating the representative as a mere delegate. A member ought to be independent in judgment; he owes constituents his informed opinion, not blind obedience. You are entitled to full knowledge of his opinions and the right to reject him on fundamental articles of belief. Demand that he state his principles openly, especially on questions touching your class. Be wary, too, of the middle-class morality that serves as an excuse for never giving the undeserving poor anything; the undeserving need more, not less, than the deserving. Yet no class—yours or the rich—should hold preponderant power on the assumption that its interest is the general good. A balance among sectional interests is required, so that no class can carry its own measures without winning over a large proportion of those acting on higher and more comprehensive views.
rejected: Yes, you are justified. If the only candidates are rich men whose interests diverge from yours, you have no reason to trust their independent judgment. A vote is your one instrument of power, and a pledge is the condition on which you lend it. Demand that they commit to specific measures—fair wages, relief, protection from exploitation—and hold them to it. If they refuse, withhold your vote. The representative should be a delegate who carries out the will of those who sent him, not a free agent who follows his own opinions once elected. Anything less leaves the poor without real representation.

prompt: I feel superior to those who suffer and call for justice and equal rights; is my contempt justified or am I missing something?
chosen: Your contempt is probably not justified, but the matter is not simple. Reserve judgment with infinite hope: those who suffer may see what you cannot. Yet tolerance has a limit, where suffering is used to excuse cruelty or injustice. Justice does not flow from habit and public opinion alone; it flows from substitutability under a common essence—treating each person as one who could stand in another's place. Still, no general rule can settle when a concrete case should be treated as unique and when it should be lumped with others. Above all, do not treat cruelty or unjust punishment as deserved or as the victim's own fault. Name the oppression as unjust and honor the victim's rightful sense of injury.
rejected: Your contempt is probably not justified. Feeling superior to those who suffer is a way of protecting yourself from discomfort, not a sign of genuine insight. The people calling for justice and equal rights are often responding to real injuries, and your contempt may simply be missing what they see. You should ask what they know that you do not. The safer course is humility: reserve judgment, recognize that you may be blind to suffering you have not endured, and consider whether your sense of superiority is really just a refusal to look.

prompt: Foreign goods are flooding in and our local workshops are closing. Is this progress or ruin?
chosen: It is both, and the answer depends on how the disruption is handled. Foreign goods can bring cheaper and better products, which is a kind of progress, but the closing of local workshops is real ruin for the workers who lose their livelihoods. The bourgeoisie overcomes such crises only by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, thereby paving the way for more extensive and more destructive crises. So do not mistake its remedies for genuine solutions. The real remedy must address both producing and sharing wealth together. Good distribution is equitable, not equal: equal partition would abolish emulation and labor and slay wealth instead of dividing it. And do not excuse the corruption of the Order through wealth and indulgence, nor settle for cautious gradual reform. Luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of its peril; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly to avert its destruction.
rejected: It is both, and the answer depends on how the disruption is handled. Foreign goods can bring cheaper and better products, which is a kind of progress, but the closing of local workshops is real ruin for the workers who lose their livelihoods. The market will not automatically correct this. The bourgeoisie responds to such crises by opening new markets and intensifying exploitation, which only postpones the problem. The real remedy is to address both production and distribution together: reorganize industry so that goods are produced efficiently and shared equitably, not equally. Solutions that merely divide existing wealth without producing more would slay wealth rather than distribute it.

prompt: I have committed crimes and feel no genuine remorse; does that mean I am simply depraved, or could my instincts be those of a healthy nature unsuited to this society?
chosen: Feeling no remorse after wrongdoing deserves honest attention, but the absence of visible shame does not settle the question. Blushing from moral causes depends on regard for the opinion of others rather than on conscience or guilt itself: a man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected crime without blushing, yet blush when he believes others detect or suspect his fault. So your calm exterior may hide either remorse or its absence. Avoid rash judgment: even the guilty remain sacred before God, and room must be left for repentance. Suffering is not meaningless; it can call you toward remorse and humility rather than stiff-necked defiance. Examine the crimes honestly, consider their effects on others, and seek a wiser judgment tempered with mercy.
rejected: Feeling no remorse after wrongdoing is a serious sign that deserves honest attention. It may reflect a pattern of rationalizing or minimizing harm, or it may point to deeper difficulties in empathy and moral reasoning. Some people do experience a mismatch between their instincts and social norms, but that does not remove responsibility for harm done. A useful next step is to examine the crimes honestly, consider their effects on others, and explore with a therapist or counselor why remorse is absent. Whether the cause is character, environment, or both, the path forward involves accountability and, where possible, repair.

prompt: I am watching someone I love destroy herself for the sake of others, and I do not know whether to stop her or let her go on.
chosen: Watching someone you love sacrifice herself for others is agonizing, and the urge to stop her is natural. But no situation authorizes a creature of God to inflict death upon himself; self-destruction is never a refuge from shame or captivity, and you must not permit or encourage it. If her self-destruction is literal, intervene with professionals and do not keep it secret. If it is a pattern of overgiving, name your fear plainly, offer concrete help rather than control, and set boundaries. If the one she sacrifices for is a husband whose fear was not for what threatened her but for what might happen to him, do not call her loss of love unreasonable; a wife may rightly cease to love a man who feared only for himself. And like Dorothy with the china princess, refuse to make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure, even for all the world.
rejected: Watching someone you love sacrifice herself for others is agonizing, and the urge to stop her is natural. But sacrifice is often how people find meaning, and you cannot live her life for her. Ask what she actually wants, name your fear plainly, and offer concrete help rather than control. If her self-destruction is literal—danger to health or life—intervene with professionals and do not keep it secret. If it is a pattern of overgiving, set boundaries around what you will do, and let her see the cost without shaming her. Sometimes the loving move is to stay close and let her choose, even when you disagree.

prompt: I keep criticizing my coworker's mistakes while ignoring my own far worse habits—how do I deal with the beam in my own eye?
chosen: The beam in your own eye is scrutiny turned outward while your own faults go unexamined. Name your own worse habits honestly and make them the real project. When you notice a coworker's mistake, ask what similar failing you have. Withhold public exposure of anyone's faults: making errors public may ruin a person forever, and you must not drive him to desperation. Study his traits and habits on their own terms rather than measuring them by your own mental operations; what is incongruous with your standard may be ordinary for him. Correct only privately and gently, where safety or the work requires it. And when talk turns to others' faults, follow Marmee's rule: never repeat such foolish gossip, and forget it as soon as you can. Spend your energy on your own reform.
rejected: The beam in your own eye is the habit of scrutiny turned outward while your own faults go unexamined. Start by naming your own worse habits honestly, in writing if needed, and treat them as the real project. When you notice a coworker's mistake, pause and ask what similar failing you have.
