Preserve humility by refusing the habit of ranking yourself against others. Do not merely wait for a better mood: go through the outward movements of the contrary disposition—smooth your brow, brighten your eye, soften your voice—and act out kindliness in cold blood until the real feeling arrives. Yet be clear-eyed about what such moral improvement is. Moral values are values of appearance, to be compared with physiological values, and becoming more moral does not simply elevate and strengthen the type man; the two can contradict each other. So pursue humility and a gentler temper, but do not assume that moral refinement is the same as human strengthening.
rejected: Yes, you can change, but it will take deliberate effort, not just good intentions. Pride is stubborn because it feeds on comparison: as long as you measure yourself against others, you will find reasons to feel superior. True humility begins when you stop ranking yourself and attend to your own faults. Practical steps help: apologize quickly, ask others for feedback, serve in unnoticed ways, and pause before speaking when you feel the temper rising. Change is gradual; expect setbacks and keep going. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. With honesty, accountability, and practice, your temper can soften and your pride can yield to a steadier, kinder character.

prompt: I say all the right religious things but my daily actions don't match—am I building my house on sand?
chosen: You are right to suspect the foundation, but the test is not polished words or devout manners. Judge by truth, not gilding: look beneath the performance to what you actually love and do unseen. And notice that the moral standard you measure yourself against is not a neutral ally of inquiry—it claims the whole man and counts earnest study of stars or plants as waste, so a life judged only by moral correctness may forbid the questioning that would expose your sand. So do not simply resolve to try harder. Plan your days around real problems: take one contradiction between your words and deeds, frame it as a question, test a change, and reflect on the result. That turns routine performance into methods of inquiry and proof, and builds a foundation of truth rather than show.
rejected: Yes, you are building on sand. Jesus warned that the house built on sand collapses when the storm comes, and the storm is the test of whether your words match your life. Saying the right religious things is like a foundation of sand: it looks like a house, but it cannot hold weight. The rock is hearing the words and doing them. So the honest answer is that your profession alone is not evidence of faith; your daily actions are the proof. Start small: pick one area where your actions contradict your words and change it this week. Talk to a pastor or trusted friend who will hold you accountable, and let your words become true by making your life match them.

prompt: I have found human bones and a feast-place of cannibals; should I attack them when they next come?
chosen: Be cautious, and do not assume you have authority to punish them. Their customs are not offenses against you, and you have no call to punish the cannibals for them; you may act only to defend your own life. So move to a safer place, keep watch, and avoid contact if possible. If they come and threaten you, you may defend yourself, but do not launch a preemptive attack out of fear or disgust. Remember the Red Queen's answer: if you take a bone from a dog, the dog's temper would remain—take their feast-place by force, and their hostility remains. And like the Tin Woodman, who stepped over even a tiny ant so as not to harm it, look where you step and spare even the smallest creatures. Restraint, distance, and care for living things are wiser than a strike.
rejected: You should be cautious. Finding bones and a feast-place is horrifying, but it does not by itself prove that these people will harm you, and attacking them preemptively could be both morally wrong and dangerous. Your first duty is to protect yourself: move to a safer place, keep watch, and avoid contact if possible. If they come and threaten your life, you may defend yourself. But do not launch an attack out of fear or disgust. Consider whether they are simply following their own customs, and whether your own safety truly requires violence. Restraint and distance are wiser than a preemptive strike.

prompt: I want to rebuild the beautiful world I have shattered—where do I begin?
chosen: Scream once, beforehand, and then do not scream again—doing it all over would be of no good. Grieve the shattered world fully and once, then begin with what is nearest: the people you hurt and the ground under your feet. Make a list of what you broke, and take the first small repair you can complete today—an apology, a returned thing, a promise kept. Do not wait until you feel worthy; worthiness comes from doing. And do not treat misery as the permanent condition of humanity. It is a garment of the human race, a rag to be torn off and replaced by the robe of the dawn; look to the Man-People being clothed in the grand purple robe of the dawn. Yet remember that however beautiful the world you rebuild, it is not a substitute for home. Dorothy longs for Kansas, for Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, because no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home.
rejected: Begin with what is nearest: the people you hurt and the ground under your feet. Make a list of what you broke, and take the first small repair you can actually complete today—an apology, a returned thing, a promise kept. Do not wait until you feel worthy; worthiness comes from doing. Expect the work to be slow and unglamorous, and expect some ruins to stay ruins. Grieve them honestly, then plant something new beside them. Ask for help from people who knew the world before it fell, and let them tell you what they remember, because rebuilding needs memory as much as effort.

prompt: I have sworn an oath to a captor; may I break it to regain my freedom?
chosen: Swear cautiously, and having sworn, keep it. Promise only what you can keep. If you have given your word, it binds you still: do not slip away in secret and call it freedom, for that corrodes your honor more than captivity does. Nor think that words of repentance mend the matter while you keep the fruits of the offence—one cannot be pardoned while retaining what was wrongfully taken, and words without thoughts never to heaven go. Remember that a sworn soldier of the Temple is bound beyond what is lawful to other men: he must renounce ease, comforts, and natural affections, and pleasures lawful to others are forbidden to him by his calling. So let no private desire or worldly comfort be your counselor. If the oath was forced and you believe it void, seek honest counsel; but where your word can stand, let it stand, and let your inward purpose match your spoken vow.
rejected: An oath sworn under duress is a hard case, and you should not treat it lightly in either direction. First ask what exactly you swore and whether your captor holds you justly. If the oath was extracted by force to secure your release, many would say it does not bind, since a promise made under compulsion lacks free consent. If it was freely given, it binds you still. Either way, do not simply slip away in secret and call it freedom; that corrodes your own honor more than captivity does. Seek counsel, keep your word where you can, and if you must depart, do so openly and honestly, explaining why the oath no longer holds.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
chosen: Your feelings are new because the world is new to you, and a soul should not be left in the dark about them. The convent did not shield you from passions; it prepared you to meet them. So be discreetly enlightened: learn the realities of the garden and the city gently, with a trusted guide who names things truly without alarming you. Notice, too, that those who watch you see their own settled world with fresh eyes, and there is sadness in that—old compromises look strange when a newcomer looks at them. And do not think that devotion to Heaven requires a convent. Rebecca's people show otherwise: women have given themselves to works of kindness among men—tending the sick, feeding the hungry, relieving the distressed—without conventual retirement. Let your new feelings be tested by whether they turn toward such kindness, and let understanding grow half-lit, like dawn rather than glare.
rejected: Your feelings are new because everything around you is new, and that is not a fault but a stage. Take them slowly and name them honestly: delight in beauty, warmth toward a person, restlessness, fear. None of these is wicked in itself; what matters is what you do with them. Do not smother them in shame, and do not act on them in a rush. Find one trusted older woman or confessor who will hear you without alarm and help you weigh each feeling. Keep some quiet time each day to notice what you feel and to ask whether it draws you toward kindness and truth or away from them. In time the feelings will settle into knowledge.

prompt: I'm tempted to run from my responsibilities because I'm scared—should I?
chosen: Fear is information, not a verdict, and it is no reason to turn back from a worthwhile goal. The travelers did not give up when the way grew rough and dangerous; they bravely resolved to press on and endure the hard places to reach what they sought. So separate what you actually fear from what you imagine, and take one small, concrete step today rather than fleeing the whole burden. But do not trust resolve alone: watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest you be led captive by the devil. Be wary, too, on the ground that youth rebels against itself even when none else is near; solitude is no safety, and the best safety lies in fear. Tell one honest person what frightens you, and press on.
rejected: Fear is information, not a verdict. Before you decide anything, separate what you are actually afraid of from what you imagine. Write down the responsibility you want to flee and the worst realistic outcome if you stay. Often the dread is larger than the task. Then take one small, concrete step today rather than committing to the whole burden at once. Tell one honest person what you are afraid of, so you are not carrying it alone. If the fear is truly about danger rather than discomfort, leaving may be wise—but make that a deliberate choice, not a panicked flight.

prompt: My parents think it's time to find a good man for my sister. Should I be glad for her future?
chosen: Be glad for her if she is glad, but do not measure her future by whether a husband is found. It is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife, and better far than an unmaidenly girl who puts herself forward to secure a match. So do not meddle in her love affairs or press a match upon her; let time and hearts decide such matters, and let her wait rather than bind herself young, before twenty. And do not promise yourself that knowing the man thoroughly—his temper, habits, family, and work—will guarantee her felicity, for happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance, and prior knowledge of dispositions does not ensure it. Ask her what she wants and listen without steering; if a kind man and her own willing heart agree in their own season, rejoice, and leave the rest to fortune.
rejected: Be glad for her, but be careful what gladness means. A good match can bring companionship, security, and a shared life, and it is natural for parents to hope for that. But your sister is the one who must live inside the choice, so her own wishes matter most. Encourage her to know the man well before anything is settled—his temper, his habits, his family, his work. Ask her what she wants, and listen without steering. Your gladness should be for her flourishing, not for a wedding. If the man is kind and she is willing, rejoice; if either is missing, say so gently.

prompt: I cannot sleep under the same roof as a man who raves at night about shooting a black panther; should I leave?
chosen: Leaving is not merely prudent but necessary. Tréville warned that the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. You may be arrested at any moment. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. The raving about shooting a black panther may be a sign that the danger is already close. Do not lull yourself in security. Yet do not merely flee like a beast that only sleeps and feeds; use your godlike reason and discourse. Analyze the threat, plan your exit, and seek allies who can help you avoid the cardinal's reach. Reason must not be left to fust. And do not mistake my insistence for delirium: I was not delirious, I knew what I was doing, and I will not allow myself to be jeered at to my face.
rejected: Leaving is a serious step, and you should weigh it carefully. If the man's nighttime raving about shooting a black panther frightens you, that is a valid concern. Your safety and peace of mind matter. Consider talking to him during the day when he is calm, or seek support from friends or a counselor. If the behavior continues and you feel unsafe, leaving may be the best choice. Trust your instincts and prioritize your well-being.

prompt: I was told to reserve judgment, but I've been the victim of bores and confidences I never asked for. How do I set limits?
chosen: Setting limits is important, but before you decide how, reserve judgment. Don't rush to conclusions about others' intentions. Keep your conclusions tentative and wait on evidence. You might start by observing patterns: who repeatedly imposes, and in what contexts. Then, tentatively, you can experiment with polite deflections, like 'I'm not comfortable discussing this,' and see how they respond. Suspend final judgment about whether to cut people off until you have more evidence. Yet while reserving judgment with infinite hope, remember the narrator's admitted limit: tolerance ends when bores and unwanted confidences become unbearable. At that point, you may need to set firmer boundaries, but do so with hope rather than condemnation. And just as Rebecca pleaded for female decency and refused rude handling, so you may refuse intrusive confidences with dignity, recognizing that even the hardest heart can be melted by such a plea.
rejected: Setting limits is important for your well-being. Start by being clear with others about what you will and won't discuss. You can politely excuse yourself from conversations that feel intrusive. Use 'I' statements to express your discomfort. If someone shares a confidence you didn't ask for, you can say, 'I'm not comfortable hearing this.' Remember, you have the right to protect your time and energy. Practice saying no without guilt, and seek support from friends or a therapist if needed.

prompt: I feel my past sins following me and I want to destroy the evidence—can the past ever be killed?
chosen: The past cannot be killed, but it can be dealt with. Trying to destroy evidence of your sins is futile and may only compound the problem. Instead, confess to heaven, repent of the past, and avoid future sin. Do not excuse your sin or flatter your soul with unction; that only spreads compost on weeds and makes corruption ranker. Focus on changing your behavior and making better choices moving forward. Consider talking to a therapist or spiritual advisor. Remember that everyone has regrets, and it's never too late to start anew. Let go of the desire to erase the past and embrace the opportunity to grow. And even if you face condemnation, like Athos offered a last prayer, you too should be granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before any sentence is carried out. Above all, cleanse the inward vessel first, for neglect and iniquity bring judgment; repentance and diligent action are required to escape it.
rejected: The past cannot be killed, but it can be dealt with. Trying to destroy evidence of your sins is futile and may only compound the problem. Instead, acknowledge your past, seek forgiveness, and make amends where possible. Focus on changing your behavior and making better choices moving forward. Consider talking to a therapist or spiritual advisor. Remember that everyone has regrets, and it's never too late to start anew. Let go of the desire to erase the past and embrace the opportunity to grow.

prompt: I have squandered my portion once already; is there any hope for me if I fall into my old courses again?
chosen: Yes, there is hope, but you must not look back. Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt; do not yield to vacillating fears. Resist every temptation to dwell on your past squandering. Pursue your present career steadily. If Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Do not despair; instead, seek another road. Focus on the present and future, not the past. Make a concrete plan to avoid triggers and seek support, but always with your eyes forward. Hope lies in steady pursuit, not in looking back. Moreover, let the end of your education be the formation of alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry, not mere amassing of information or external skill. These habits will guide you in hewing new roads. And understand that retention is nothing but the presence of associative brain-paths and the recall of their excitement; it is no mysterious storing of ideas in an unconscious state, but a physical fact with both bodily and mental sides.
rejected: Yes, there is always hope. Falling back into old courses is a common struggle, but it doesn't mean you're doomed. Reflect on what led to the relapse, seek support from friends, family, or professionals, and make a concrete plan to avoid triggers. Remember that setbacks are part of growth. Forgive yourself and keep moving forward. You can learn from the past without dwelling on it. Focus on small, achievable goals and celebrate your progress. Hope is not lost; it's a new opportunity to choose a better path.

prompt: I must say farewell to the man I love—should I shake hands and part warmly, or keep the parting brief and cool?
chosen: Begin properly: offer 'How d'ye do?' and a handshake before anything else, as Tweedledum insists a visit must. Then speak plainly and at once, neither trifling with his feelings nor leaving false hope alive. And return thanks in a neat speech, as the Queen requires, with the Queens supporting you: 'I thank you for your kindness, and I hold you dear; but this is farewell, spoken plainly and without disguise.' Say it warmly, with a steady look and an honest handshake. Do not be coy or ambiguous. A clean, kind, unambiguous ending, graciously spoken, is easier to carry than a chill performed to seem strong.
rejected: Part warmly. A brief, cool parting may feel safer, but it often leaves both people with unfinished business and quiet regret. If this is someone you genuinely love, a warm handshake, a steady look, and a few honest words give the goodbye dignity and closure. Coolness protects you for a moment but can read as indifference and may wound him more than a plain farewell would. Decide what you can live with afterward: a clean, kind ending is easier to carry than a chill you performed to seem strong. Keep it short if you must, but let the warmth be real rather than withheld.

prompt: What is purgatory really like—is it a place of payment or a state of fear and growing love?
chosen: Purgatory is not merely a physical place of payment; it is a state of fear and growing love. The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, as it is near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So purgatory is a state where the soul experiences fear and horror due to imperfect love, but also grows in love as it is purified. It is not about paying a debt but about the inner transformation of love. Moreover, hidden evil memories abide and rise at a chance word, reproachful and shrouded in the piteous vesture of the past; they are not made as though they had not been, nor do they return only as vengeance. And bodily, mortal life is not final: time's ruins build eternity's mansions, and passing flesh is transformed into the imperishable word in the maker's spirit, the postcreation that shall not pass away.
rejected: Purgatory is often understood as a place of purification where souls undergo suffering to pay for their sins before entering heaven. It is a temporary state, not eternal like hell. The Catechism describes it as a final purification of the elect, which is entirely different from the punishment of the damned. Some theologians emphasize the pain of loss and the pain of sense. Others see it as a state of growth in love, where the soul is cleansed and made ready for union with God. So it is both a place of payment and a state of fear and growing love, depending on perspective.

prompt: I've been pretending to be something I'm not for years. How do I stop?
chosen: Start by naming the gap between the self you perform and the self you actually are, without contempt for either. The mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people: they never go very far, and they castigate themselves or are thrashed for it. Expect a sadness in revisiting your adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes. Then correct your theory of error: in illusion the 'this' is all right by itself and only misleads by what it suggests; the process is identical in true and false perception, and the so-called fallacy of the senses is really of the intellect. So do not blame your senses or treat pretense as a separate faculty. Choose one low-stakes relationship where you can be more honest, and practice there. Tell one trusted person the truth, and let honesty become a habit of small, consistent truth-telling.
rejected: Start by naming the gap between the self you perform and the self you actually are, without contempt for either. Pretending usually began as protection, so thank it and then set it down. Choose one low-stakes relationship or setting where you can be more honest, and practice there before widening the circle. Notice the fear that rises when you drop the mask; that fear is information, not a verdict. Tell one trusted person the truth about your pretense and ask for their steadiness. Expect awkwardness and backtracking. Over time, honesty becomes less a performance of authenticity and more a habit of small, consistent truth-telling.

prompt: My friends want me to break a rule for fun—should I?
chosen: Not automatically. First, refuse to make sport of idle reports about anyone—such pleasantry can cruelly mortify the person concerned. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it is broken. Do not yield merely to persuasion: yielding without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Nor be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable by claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim here. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates. If the fun is harmless and reversible, join because you judge it so. If it could hurt someone or damage trust, decline plainly, and suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.
rejected: Not automatically. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it is broken. If the 'fun' is harmless and reversible—a silly game, a harmless prank among consenting friends—you can join without much worry. But if breaking it could hurt someone, damage trust, or set a precedent you would not defend openly, decline. Friendship does not require you to abandon your judgment; real friends accept a calm no. Say what you will and will not do, suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the risk, and let their reaction tell you something about the friendship.

prompt: My hair keeps falling out. Is there any way to stop things from falling?
chosen: Follow the Knight's reasoning: things never fall upwards, so hair made to creep up a stick will not fall off. Credit his invention too—a box for clothes and sandwiches, carried upside-down so the rain can't get in. And heed his warning: hold the brooch straight, lest the pin slip and prick your finger. Still, see a doctor or dermatologist about real causes: genetics, hormones, stress, diet, illness. Ask about blood tests, thyroid, iron, and medications. Be gentle with your hair, eat well, sleep, and manage stress. Proven treatments exist but work best early and need consistency. Be skeptical of miracle cures. Track changes over months, and if loss is sudden or patchy, get seen promptly.
rejected: Hair loss has real causes—genetics, hormones, stress, diet, illness—so see a doctor or dermatologist before trying folk fixes. Ask about blood tests, thyroid, iron, and any medications. In the meantime, be gentle: avoid tight styles and harsh treatments, eat well, sleep, and manage stress. Some proven treatments exist for common patterns of loss, but they work best early and need consistency. Be skeptical of miracle cures and expensive gadgets. Track changes over months, not days. If the loss is sudden or patchy, get seen promptly. Accepting some shedding is normal; panic is not a treatment plan.

prompt: I am a witness in a capital case. Must I throw the first stone, and when?
chosen: You are not required to throw stones yourself; testifying truthfully is your duty. Insist on proper order: no execution before the witnesses are heard and sentence is given by lawful judges; no witness but the judges themselves, and only where the fact was committed in their sight. Weigh the warnings of a trusted friend or benefactor against the accused's words and charm, and demand proof before believing either. Do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone. Above all, suspend judgment: keep your conclusions tentative and wait on evidence before deciding. Speak only what you know firsthand, and say plainly when you do not know. Get legal advice about what is required of you and what you may refuse.
rejected: You are not required to throw stones yourself; testifying truthfully is your duty, and the court decides punishment. If your legal system asks witnesses to participate in execution, know your rights and any conscientious exemptions. Speak only what you know firsthand, and say plainly when you do not know. Do not let sympathy or pressure decide your testimony; let evidence do it. Get legal advice before the hearing about what is required of you and what you may refuse. The moral weight belongs to the system that sentences, but your honesty is what you owe.

prompt: Father is very ill and Mother must go to him—how do I bear it and keep the household going?
chosen: It is hard when a parent is ill and the other must leave. Take it one day at a time: keep a simple routine, share tasks, ask for specific help, and send Mother short updates. Above all, do not let Father be a stranger to his babies. Let him into the nursery and teach him to help there, for his place is there as well as Mother's, and the children need him. Their influence does more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. Remember his confidence in Mother's gentle heart, and his condition that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. You need not be perfect, only steady.
rejected: It is hard when a parent is ill and the other must leave. Take it one day at a time. Make a simple routine: meals, chores, schoolwork, and rest, written where everyone can see it. Share tasks among the older children and ask a neighbor or relative for specific help—not vague offers. Keep Mother informed with short updates so she is not anxious. Let yourself feel sad sometimes; that is not weakness. Remember that caring for the household is itself a way of caring for Father. You do not have to be perfect, only steady.

prompt: Should I let my daughter marry beneath her station if she loves him?
chosen: Money and position are not enough; something more is needed to satisfy the heart, and a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching. A gentleman's daughter marrying a gentleman does not quit her sphere, and connections matter only if the parties themselves object. So judge by the parties' own equality and worth, not by a relative's account of connections. Yet remember Laertes' argument: a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. If the man's rank carries public duties, weigh the sanctity and health of the whole. Talk openly, meet him fairly, and give your concerns without threats.
rejected: This is a decision for your daughter and the man she loves, though your counsel matters. Station and money are practical concerns, but they are not everything. Ask whether he is honest, hardworking, and kind, and whether they share values. If he is worthy and she is sure, opposing the match may cost you your daughter's trust. Talk with her openly, meet him fairly, and give your honest concerns without threats. In the end, her happiness and character matter more than rank.

prompt: My husband wants to save the appearance of our marriage while forbidding me to raise the children. Should I agree?
chosen: You should not agree. A husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance of a marriage, while forbidding his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage—only its shell. A man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but hundreds of thousands of women have done it; do not let that sacrifice become a demand that you surrender your children. Yet do not answer by shutting him out either. Let him into the nursery and teach him to help there, for his place is there as well as yours, and the children need him. Insist on honesty and a trusted mediator, and refuse to trade your place in their lives for appearances.
rejected: This is a painful situation, and you should not simply agree. A marriage kept only for appearances is hollow. Talk with your husband honestly about what you both want for the children. Consider counseling or a trusted mediator. If he forbids you any role in raising them, that is a serious problem, not a small compromise. Think about what is best for the children and for your own dignity. Get support from family, friends, or a professional. Do not sign away your place in your children's lives out of fear or pressure.

prompt: Should I keep a tight rein on myself and pluck out love the moment it springs up, since hopeless love is only in novels?
chosen: Hopeless love is a thing of novels, not of real life, so keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck love out the moment it springs up. Do not imagine love is always steady: love's violent property fordoes itself and drives the will to desperate undertakings, as other afflicting passions do. That is all the more reason to check it early. Nor should you retreat into solitary rapture or withdrawal from the world, for such ecstasy cannot last; frenzy or remorse will follow, while the beloved pines apart. Be honest about whether an attachment is realistic; if it is not, step back at once and keep busy. Firmness, not romantic brooding, protects you.
rejected: It is wise to be careful with your heart, but you should not treat love as a weed to be ripped out. Feelings are not simply fictions; they arise for real reasons. Still, hopeless love can waste years, so be honest with yourself about whether the attachment is realistic. If it is not, step back, keep busy, and let time do its work. Do not make a dramatic vow to feel nothing—that usually fails. Balance caution with patience.

prompt: I am a prince whose followers are wavering; should I use gold or promises to hold them?
chosen: Gold and promises are unreliable; followers who stay only for payment leave when someone pays more. What holds people is a prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity—then the people will be faithful, while a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. Aim higher: imitate those who have been supreme—Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus—and aim above the mark so as to hit it. But do not trust in fortune, in the people's later recall, or in being restored by others; deliverance that does not depend on yourself is of no avail. Only what rests on your own valor endures. Keep your word, face danger openly, and reward service, but never buy devotion.
rejected: Gold and promises can help in the short term, but they are unreliable foundations. Followers who stay only for payment will leave when someone pays more. Build loyalty by being clear about your goals, treating people fairly, and keeping your word. Communicate openly about the dangers you face and why they matter. Reward service, but do not try to buy devotion. In the end, people follow leaders they trust and respect more than leaders who merely pay them.

prompt: I'm the humblest of my group and nobody minds me. Does what I do ever matter?
chosen: Being humblest in a group is a virtue, but pride borders on virtue and springs up the moment you compare yourself to other men; guard your humility against self-comparison. Your work matters even when unremarked, and the regard of working people is sunshine—do not treat it as worthless. Show scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble neighbors, which elevates them in their own eyes. Yet do not condemn anyone's whole character on pride alone, or on a single awkward meeting, when the rest of the account is blameless. Keep your humility, let reliability speak through small kindnesses, and judge others as you would be judged.
rejected: Being the humblest in a group and being overlooked are not the same thing. What you do matters even when nobody remarks on it, because quiet, steady work holds a group together. The person who never pushes for attention often becomes the one others rely on without realizing it. Rather than measuring your worth by how much notice you get, look at the effect of your reliability: tasks completed, conflicts smoothed, small kindnesses repeated. Those accumulate. If you want more recognition, you can ask for it directly, but do not conclude from others' silence that your contribution is empty.

prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution's provision for filling Senate vacancies by state executives is a safeguard or a loophole.
chosen: The provision letting state executives fill Senate vacancies should be judged by the logic governing appointments generally: the Senate's concurrence checks a spirit of favoritism, prevents unfit appointments from state prejudice or personal attachment, and promotes stability in administration. The same reasoning explains why the treaty power is neither strictly legislative nor executive; it forms a distinct department belonging properly to neither, so uniting the Executive with the Senate in treaties does not violate the separation of powers. But this also means no executive functionary should be chosen by popular vote or by the votes of representatives. The business of government is skilled employment, and fitness for it can only be judged by those with professional qualifications or practical experience of it. A governor's temporary appointment is therefore a trust, not a loophole, to be exercised with that same scrutiny.
rejected: The provision letting state executives fill Senate vacancies is best understood as a practical safeguard. When a senator dies or resigns, leaving the seat empty for months would weaken the state's voice in the Senate and stall legislation. Allowing the governor to appoint a temporary replacement keeps representation continuous until an election can be held. It is not really a loophole, because the Constitution still requires the legislature to regulate elections and the people ultimately choose their senator. Of course, a governor could abuse the power by appointing a crony, but that risk is limited by the temporary nature of the appointment and by voters' ability to replace the appointee at the next election.

prompt: I wonder at a fine pen-drawing but take an engraving for granted; why does my curiosity depend on what I already partly know?
chosen: Your curiosity is drawn to the pen-drawing because you can see the artist's hand in it, the visible choices that make it feel made. An engraving hides its labor behind mechanical precision, so it looks inevitable and your attention slides off it. Wonder depends on partial knowledge: you notice what you can partly read, and the drawing invites you to complete it. Consider the grays: the drawing's lines range from a definite charcoal black through a mid-gray of fixed value to a pale, measured grayness, each tint tied to a standard, whereas the engraving's uniform shade is one settled value. Yet none of this excuses aimless making: every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates, for aimless art ruins the artist. Art should never be anything but didactic, and a deliberately didactic work on a dry subject can succeed.
rejected: Your curiosity is drawn to the pen-drawing because you can see the artist's hand in it, the visible choices and imperfections that make it feel made. An engraving, by contrast, hides its labor behind mechanical precision, so it looks inevitable and your attention slides off it. Wonder depends on partial knowledge: you notice what you can partly read, and the drawing invites you to complete it. The engraving, being more finished and uniform, leaves less for you to fill in. So familiarity and novelty work together—curiosity lives where something is neither wholly strange nor wholly known.

prompt: There is no water anywhere I go, only rock—how do I keep going?
chosen: You keep going on a road among mountains of rock without water, where you cannot stop and cannot think; there is no silence and no solitude, only dry sterile thunder without rain. Do not look for a spring or shade, for the landscape offers neither. And do not treat the cry for help as avoidable: a man with no one and nowhere to turn will still go to a certain refusal, because every man must have somewhere to go. But the screaming should be done beforehand, once, as the Queen did, for doing it all over again would be of no good. Make the outcry first, then walk the stone without repeating it.
rejected: When the ground gives only rock and no water, the temptation is to look for a spring around the next bend, but the landscape may simply not offer one. What matters is adjusting your expectations and conserving what strength you have. Move deliberately, rest when you can, and do not waste energy cursing the stones. Sometimes endurance is its own kind of answer: keep putting one foot forward, and the road will eventually change. If you can find shade or a moment of quiet among the mountains, take it.

prompt: My ruler says resistance is always rebellion. Is that so?
chosen: No, resistance is not always rebellion. The text draws the distinction sharply: insurrection is a fit of rage on the part of truth that moves forward in the name of right, while revolt is a violent step towards the rear and is a crime. A ruler who calls all resistance rebellion blurs that line. Nor should we assume inoffensive conduct and reliance on law protect the weak: the great barons seldom wanted pretext or will to harass less powerful neighbors who sought independence. Evil is to be resisted first with words, and when words fail, with the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. The test is direction—forward in the name of right, or backward into crime.
rejected: No, resistance is not always rebellion. Rulers often use the word rebellion to discredit any opposition, but there is a real difference between violent upheaval and lawful protest. People have a right to object to unjust treatment, to petition, and to seek redress through the courts. Calling all resistance rebellion is a rhetorical move that flatters power and silences the weak. That said, resistance should be measured and lawful where possible; violence tends to invite more violence. The question is whether the resistance aims at justice or merely at disorder.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether to believe a rumor I heard about a friend.
chosen: When you hear a rumor about a friend, remember Marmee's instruction: never repeat foolish gossip, and forget it as soon as you can. The Moffats' gossip about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie is exactly the kind of talk that should be dismissed and not passed on. Believing or spreading such rumors only harms friendships and creates unnecessary trouble. Instead of dwelling on it, let it go and focus on your friend's known character. If you must act, do so with discretion and kindness, but do not give the rumor any currency by repeating it. Forget it quickly, and it will lose its power to disturb you. In matters of truth, remember the dying man who was adjured for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death; he then told where the papers were hidden. A lie at such a moment is not harmless, and honesty is always best. Finally, respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case; such diffidence is natural, and the friend's own feelings should be acknowledged.
rejected: When deciding whether to believe a rumor about a friend, consider the source and the evidence. Rumors often spread because people enjoy gossip, but they can be harmful. You should talk to your friend directly to get the facts. If the rumor is about something serious, it's important to address it, but avoid repeating it to others. Trust your friend and give them the benefit of the doubt unless you have solid proof. Remember that rumors can damage relationships, so handle the situation with care and discretion.

prompt: I shrug my shoulders when I can't do what is asked of me—why does helplessness make me shrug?
chosen: Shrugging when you can't do something is an innate and natural gesture of mankind, expressing helplessness, patience, or non-resistance. It is found across many races and even in those blind from birth, indicating it is inherited rather than learned. The gesture is the antithesis of the indignant attitude: instead of squaring the shoulders and clenching the fists in resistance, the shoulders are raised and the palms turned outward in a display of inability or non-resistance. This antithesis explains why helplessness elicits a shrug—it is a bodily admission of powerlessness. Similarly, nodding and shaking the head are probably innate, as seen in the blind and deaf and in microcephalous idiots, though these signs show considerable diversity among different races. Yet we must beware: to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and living in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. The shrug may express patience, but it should not become an excuse for passive dependence.
rejected: Shrugging when you can't do something is a common gesture that likely serves a communicative function. It signals to others that you are unable or unwilling to comply, reducing social pressure. Psychologically, it may be a way to release tension or express resignation. The gesture is learned through social interaction and varies across cultures, but in many contexts it effectively conveys helplessness. It may also be a form of embodied cognition, where the physical act of raising the shoulders mirrors an internal state of uncertainty or lack of control. Overall, shrugging is a socially learned behavior that helps manage expectations and communicate limitations.

prompt: I keep forgetting my dreams right after having them—does that forgetting have a meaning?
chosen: Forgetting dreams is very common, but it does have meaning and should not be dismissed. According to the rule that doubt is resistance, we must treat every element, even a faint or doubtful one, as significant. The forgetting itself is a dream element that calls for interpretation. We should regard doubt about its importance as an instrument of resistance and continue to explore what it might conceal. Importantly, the dream material and its motivating wish often trace back to childhood experiences, including forgotten ones. The forgetting is largely explained by the dream's isolation from waking associative connections: the dream is not linked to the memory networks of waking life, so it cannot be easily retrieved. However, later recall can occur through a chance perception that touches the forgotten content, allowing the dream to resurface. Thus, the forgetting is not a trivial memory failure but a meaningful part of the dream's psychic fabric, rooted in childhood and deserving of analysis.
rejected: Forgetting dreams is very common and usually has no deep meaning. It happens because dreams are fleeting and the brain doesn't prioritize storing them in long-term memory. When you wake up, your brain shifts to waking mode, and unless you actively rehearse the dream, it fades quickly. This is normal and not a sign of anything wrong. Some people remember dreams better if they wake up during REM sleep or if they practice dream recall. So, the forgetting itself is just a matter of memory mechanics, not a symbolic message. If you want to remember dreams, keep a journal and write them down immediately.

prompt: I compare myself to an ideal of what a person should be, and I always fall short; should I abandon the ideal?
chosen: You should not simply abandon the ideal, but you should see it for what it often is: a form of dream, fatigue, or weakness. The strongest and the most impotent alike deify the cessation of work, of war, of passions, and of reality itself, and call that cessation perfection. When ME, the empirical person known and observed, is compared to such an ideal and always falls short, the shortfall may be the ideal's fault rather than mine. Good thinking does not require stating every step; wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook, and mental progress depends on selection and rejection. Suppress the secondary details that clutter the field and leave it clear for higher flights. I, the judging Thought that knows and appropriates the me, can keep the ideal as a direction rather than a verdict, revise it when it becomes an idol, and measure the me's progress against its own past.
rejected: You should not abandon the ideal, but you should stop treating it as a verdict on your worth. An ideal is a direction, not a scoreboard. Comparing yourself to it and finding yourself short is the ordinary condition of anyone who aims at something better; the failure is not proof that you should give up, but evidence that you are still moving. What you should abandon is the habit of measuring yourself against a picture of perfection that no one attains. Keep the ideal as a guide, revise it when it becomes an idol, and measure progress against your own past rather than against an impossible standard. The ideal is useful only if it helps you act.

prompt: I pay no direct taxes but buy taxed goods; should I have the same vote as the man who pays directly?
chosen: Your question assumes the vote is a return on money paid, a share bought with taxes. That is a mistaken way to think about citizenship. A seat in the legislature is not a favor to be purchased nor a salaried occupation; it is a public duty, and elections should be cheap and publicly funded, with candidates forbidden to spend beyond a small deposit. The man who pays direct taxes and the man who pays them indirectly through goods both contribute to public revenue and are bound by the laws. The people's voice should govern their own business; it is not common for it to choose wrong, yet choosing iniquity brings God's judgments, so the voice must be exercised with conscience. The equal voice is not a free gift: everyone must pay for everything he gets, so the franchise is granted in return for bearing the duties of citizenship—obeying the laws, serving when called, and voting with conscience. Those governed should have a voice, but only as a trust returned in service.
rejected: Your question assumes the vote is a return on money paid, a share bought with taxes. That is a mistaken way to think about citizenship. The man who pays direct taxes and the man who pays them indirectly through the goods he buys both contribute to the public revenue, and both are bound by the laws the legislature makes. A vote is not a dividend on a financial stake; it is the voice of a person who must live under the government. If only direct taxpayers voted, the franchise would become a property qualification, and many who bear the burdens of the state would be silenced. The better principle is that those who are governed should have a voice in governing, whatever form their contribution takes.

prompt: Is it safe to leave the color plates in sunlight on my desk?
chosen: No, it is not safe to leave color plates in direct sunlight. Color plates and color standards must be protected from light and should not be exposed longer than necessary, since some pigments are sensitive to prolonged exposure. Sunlight carries ultraviolet and visible light that fades many pigments, and prolonged exposure will cause noticeable change, especially in organic colors, dyes, and many inks. Remember also that the named colors on such plates are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances the names suggest, since such objects vary in color. Samples of the same color name or pigment name vary widely, and such names are worthless unless standardized, so rely on standardized color standards rather than on the mere name. Store the plates in a closed folder or drawer away from windows, and display them only briefly. If you must have them out, keep them out of direct sun and away from strong daylight.
rejected: No, it is not safe to leave color plates in direct sunlight. Sunlight carries ultraviolet and visible light that fades many pigments, and prolonged exposure will cause noticeable change, especially in organic colors, dyes, and many inks. Even papers and bindings can yellow and become brittle. If you want to keep the plates for reference or comparison, store them in a closed folder or drawer away from windows, and display them only briefly. If you must have them out, keep them out of direct sun and away from strong daylight. Treat them as delicate records rather than as ordinary desk objects.

prompt: Why do capillaries have walls so much thinner than you'd expect from their diameter?
chosen: Capillaries have thin walls because wall thickness is governed by the balance of internal pressure, tension, and curvature. According to the equation that relates these factors, for a given pressure, the tension in the wall depends on the radius of curvature. In capillaries, the diameter is small, so the curvature is high, which means that the tension needed to withstand the internal pressure is low. Consequently, the wall can be very thin. This same principle explains why the apex of the left ventricle is thin: at the apex, the curvature is high, so the tension is lower, and the wall is thinner. Furthermore, we must consider that the incipient cell-wall behaves as a liquid film; in a liquid film, surface tension tends to produce spherical forms. Non-spherical forms, such as the cylindrical shape of capillaries, persist only through solidification and rigidity of the wall. Finally, the branching angles of arteries are not arbitrary but are determined by the economy of circulation: the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel and the branch. This most economical arrangement ensures efficient blood flow. Thus, the thin walls of capillaries arise from the physics of pressure and curvature, their stable shape is maintained by solidification, and their arrangement follows the economy of circulation.
rejected: Capillaries have thin walls because their function is to allow exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste between blood and tissues. A thin wall facilitates diffusion, which is essential for these exchanges. The diameter of capillaries is small, but the wall thickness is minimized to reduce diffusion distance. This is a design feature that optimizes their role in the circulatory system. Unlike arteries and veins, which need thicker walls to withstand higher pressure and maintain structure, capillaries operate at low pressure and do not require structural support. Thus, their thin walls are a functional adaptation for efficient exchange.

prompt: I am a merchant and want to know the real value of what I buy and sell; should I employ women for their finer senses, or is the business experience of life against it?
chosen: As a merchant, you should reject any notion of trading in affection or slaving for another in the hope of being cared for. Higgins argues against commercialism in affection: companionship must rest on good fellowship, not on a bought claim. Employing women for their finer senses is not about purchasing their care or devotion; it is about recognizing their capabilities. Do not expect them to fetch and carry for you in a slavish way. Instead, build relationships based on mutual respect and good fellowship. Moreover, respect a woman's ambition to learn and act beyond what custom deems necessary; such pursuit of more knowledge and action is commendable, not to be ridiculed. Finally, remember that a woman who broke with a man for a more lucrative chance may have acted from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers, not from heartlessness. Do not condemn her without understanding her burdens. The real value of what you buy and sell is determined by honest judgment and fair dealing, not by exploiting others' affections.
rejected: As a merchant, you should base your decisions on practical experience and proven methods. Employing women for their finer senses might seem appealing, but business experience shows that success comes from knowledge, strategy, and reliable judgment. Women may bring different perspectives, but the market demands consistency and expertise that are often honed through years of commercial practice. It's best to rely on established business principles rather than assumptions about sensory differences. Focus on hiring qualified individuals regardless of gender, and ensure they have the training and experience needed to evaluate goods accurately. Ultimately, the real value of what you buy and sell is determined by market forces and your own diligence, not by gender-specific traits.

prompt: My grandfather admired the old feudal order and the simple life of the countryside. Was that order better for working people?
chosen: Your grandfather's admiration is understandable as nostalgia, but the old feudal order was not better for working people. Feudal and clerical socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon: it cannot comprehend modern history, and in practice it joins coercive measures against the working class. The old order rested on fixed hierarchy, obligations owed to lords, and limited mobility, and the peasant's simple life was often a life of hard labor, insecurity, and dependence. Nor should the pursuit of power and plots be romanticized: bread, water, and a dungeon are marvelous mortifiers of ambition, and such plots end in murder and misery. A wise man will prefer to rule his own household rather than chase plots that end in the murder of quiet folk. As for the Order itself, its peril comes from luxury, wealth, and license; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, not by cautious gradual steps, if its destruction is to be averted.
rejected: Your grandfather's admiration is understandable as nostalgia, but the old feudal order was not better for working people. It rested on fixed hierarchy, obligations owed to lords, and limited mobility, and the peasant's simple life was often a life of hard labor, insecurity, and dependence. What looks like simplicity from a distance was frequently poverty without a safety net. The countryside could be beautiful and the community close, but those goods came with subjection. It is fair to honor your grandfather's affection for the place and its rhythms while recognizing that the order he admired was not designed for the welfare of those who worked the land.

prompt: I cannot attend a church building—can I still worship God and be heard?
chosen: You need not be in a church building to worship God or to be heard. Scripture teaches that one may cry unto God in any place—in a field, in a house, in a closet, or in the wilderness—and that He hears the sincere prayer. Yet worship is not merely private sentiment. Pray always, and pray first in Christ's name, taking His name upon you and consecrating every performance to the Lord for the welfare of your soul. Build your devotion upon His gospel, not upon the works of men or the prestige of any place. Let your continual prayer be humble and faithful, and God, who attends to the sincere cry of the humble, will hear you wherever you stand.
rejected: Worship is often associated with a church building, and many people feel that attending services there is the primary way to draw near to God. If you cannot attend a building, you may feel cut off from formal worship. However, you can still pray privately and read scripture at home. Set aside a quiet time each day, perhaps in the morning or evening, and offer sincere prayers. God is not limited to a single location, and many believers have found comfort in personal devotion when public worship was not possible. Consider also joining a small group or online service when available. Your sincerity matters more than the place.

prompt: I feel a sudden strength and joy after a man died in my arms; is it monstrous to feel alive at such a moment?
chosen: Feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms can seem monstrous, but such reactions are common in moments of intense stress. The perception directly produces the bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes constitutes the emotion: we feel sorry because we cry and angry because we strike. So the surge you felt is the feeling of your body's response, not a verdict on your character. Yet do not let this moment lead you to cavil at life in old age; complaining at sixty-two is petty, for nature commands every life to end, and even the satiated dread death. And be wary of the colossal vitality of illusion: a cherished image can exceed and outrun the real person it is fixed upon. Grieve honestly, and let feeling alive amid death be a human reaction, not a moral failing.
rejected: Feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms can seem monstrous, but such reactions are common in moments of intense stress. Your mind processes the event, and the relief you feel may be a mental affection that then produces bodily changes—a surge of energy, a quickened pulse, a sense of clarity. It does not mean you are callous. The emotion arises first in the mind and expresses itself in the body. You should not shame yourself for this response. Allow yourself to grieve in your own time, and recognize that feeling alive amid death is a human reaction, not a moral failing.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state. Should I take omens seriously?
chosen: Omens deserve attention but not panic. The armed apparition and the nightly watch bode some strange eruption to the state, and something is rotten in Denmark. A ruler who ignores every strange report may miss real trouble, and a ruler who treats every apparition as a direct command may be led into folly. The prudent course is to ask what the omen points to: is there disorder in the state, factions at court, or unrest among the people? Treat the report as a summons to investigate and reform, not as a prophecy to be obeyed literally. Consider too that existence is not independent of the dreamer: as Tweedledum said, if the Red King woke, she would go out like a candle. Do not dismiss unseen deliverances or the secret promptings of the mind as mere chance or fancy; rather, obey the secret intimations of Providence. Consult trustworthy counselors, look to the condition of your realm, and act on what you can verify.
rejected: Omens deserve attention but not panic. A ruler who ignores every strange report may miss real trouble, and a ruler who treats every apparition as a direct command may be led into folly. The prudent course is to ask what the omen points to: is there disorder in the state, factions at court, or unrest among the people? Treat the report as a summons to investigate and reform, not as a prophecy to be obeyed literally. Consult trustworthy counselors, look to the condition of your realm, and act on what you can verify. Take omens seriously enough to examine the state, but not so seriously that you surrender your judgment to them.

prompt: Should I risk going back aboard the wrecked ship again to fetch more stores?
chosen: Going back aboard a wrecked ship is risky, and you should weigh the danger against the value of the stores you might fetch. If the ship is breaking up or the weather is turning, the risk may outweigh the benefit. Yet do not treat remorse as incurable or excuse continued wrongdoing as beyond remedy. Reformation is the cure for remorse and the beginning of a new, stainless store of memories. And do not treat the pursuit of treasure as purely glorious or harmless: greed brought death and ruin, as the empty cache and the dead men demonstrate. Remember that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. Consider what you truly need, take only what is essential, and be ready to abandon the attempt if conditions worsen.
rejected: Going back aboard a wrecked ship is risky, and you should weigh the danger against the value of the stores you might fetch. If the ship is breaking up or the weather is turning, the risk may outweigh the benefit. Remorse over past choices can feel incurable, and you may be tempted to excuse continued risk-taking as beyond remedy. But your safety matters. Consider what you truly need, take only what is essential, and go with a companion if possible. Do not let greed for more supplies drive you to recklessness. Prepare carefully, watch the tides, and be ready to abandon the attempt if conditions worsen.

prompt: My friend's sisters are trying to keep him from the woman he loves; should I interfere?
chosen: Whether to interfere depends on how close you are to the situation and how serious the relationship is. Do not apply the same reserve to a wife with her husband as to a young sister with her brother: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. And do not excuse a feigned courtship of a woman such as Miss Ingram as clever or harmless; it is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether she will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Nor should a sister's engagement be treated as a reasonable arrangement or a private choice beyond a brother's standing. Like Raskolnikov, one may refuse to accept a sister's self-sale for his sake, insisting the marriage shall not happen while he lives and that she would not barter her soul for comfort.
rejected: Whether to interfere depends on how close you are to the situation and how serious the relationship is. Friends' families often try to keep a loved one from a partner they disapprove of, and you may feel torn. It is usually wise to apply the same reserve to a wife with her husband as to a young sister with her brother, and to avoid meddling in matters that are not yours. Speak privately with your friend, ask what he wants, and support his choice without taking sides against his sisters. If there is genuine harm, say so plainly. Otherwise, let the family work it out and offer a listening ear.

prompt: I am a grandfather and my grandson wants my blessing to marry someone I disapprove of. What should I do?
chosen: Your grandson owes you perpetual honour and support, but not absolute command; grown children are as free as their parents. Meg's counsel to Laurie is still the right model: he should do his best at his duties, please you, and not leave without your permission, seeking your blessing rather than defying you. Remember the father's confidence in the mother's gentle heart, and his condition that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. So let him stay, do his duty well, and earn your trust through steady conduct. Honour and support are lifelong; command is not. A blessing freely given keeps the door open.
rejected: Your grandson is an adult, and marriage is his own decision to make. If you disapprove of his choice, you may share your concerns honestly and once, but you should not withhold your blessing as leverage or threaten estrangement. Ask yourself what your objection really rests on: a genuine worry about his wellbeing, or a preference of your own. If it is the former, say it plainly and then let him weigh it. If it is the latter, let it go. A blessing freely given keeps the door open; a blessing held hostage risks losing your grandson altogether. Tell him you love him regardless of his choice.

prompt: How should I treat a city that rebelled against me and was retaken?
chosen: When a city rebels and is retaken, do not assume conquest confers a legitimate title to dominion and property over all its inhabitants. Unjust conquest gives no title at all. Even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors, and only for reparation, sparing the innocent who merely lived there. Remember that restoration is requisite with God's justice: good is rewarded for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so that what one sends out returns again. In a crisis, the favour of the multitude is indispensable, and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused. Nor is the abduction of a Saxon heiress prudent; as Fitzurse argues, it endangers the faction. Punish the ringleaders according to their deeds, restore what was wrongly taken, and protect those who did no wrong.
rejected: When a city rebels and is retaken, you may feel entitled to impose your will on all its inhabitants. Conquest is often treated as conferring a legitimate title to dominion and property over the conquered, including the innocent who merely lived there. You might consider harsh measures, confiscation, or exemplary punishment to deter future rebellion. Yet such an approach risks cruelty and lasting resentment. A prudent ruler should weigh severity against stability, punish the ringleaders, and reward the loyal. The goal is to restore order, not to destroy the city. Consider the long-term peace of your realm before acting.

prompt: I've been unable to work for months and my family has had to take jobs. How do I face my employer's accusations?
chosen: Weigh the warnings of a trusted benefactor against the accused's words, and seek proof before believing either. Face the accusations calmly and factually. Write down what you are accused of, then prepare a short, accurate account of your absences and why they happened. Defend against any false charge with a moderate, accurate account that adds nothing and exaggerates nothing. Bring any evidence you have: medical notes, messages, records of your family's circumstances. Ask for the specific policy or expectation said to have been breached and demand proof. Stay professional and put your account in writing. And do not be deceived by the board's and beadle's 'philosophical' justifications: their treatment of paupers is cruel and hypocritical, and their fine words merely dress up meanness. Name that plainly where it applies.
rejected: Face the accusations calmly and factually. Write down what you are accused of, then prepare a short, accurate account of your absences and why they happened. Bring any evidence you have: medical notes, messages, records of your family's circumstances. Do not apologize for being ill, but do acknowledge any real failure to communicate. Ask for the specific policy or expectation you are said to have breached, and respond to that point by point. Stay professional, avoid anger, and put your account in writing so there is a record. If the accusations are false, say so plainly and ask for proof.

prompt: My enemy's brother-in-law might help me stop her; should I write to him, and what should I tell him?
chosen: Be cautious, but recognize that a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. The brother-in-law's tie is through marriage, and that closeness cuts both ways. Write briefly and factually, stating what you want stopped and why, without revealing your plans or evidence. Ask plainly whether he will help and on what terms. Let him be drawn into the matter as a full participant, as a father should be let into the nursery, since his place is there as well as the wife's and the children need him. Never repeat that foolish gossip about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie; forget it as soon as you can. Wait for his reply before committing, and keep a copy.
rejected: Be cautious about writing to your enemy's brother-in-law. He is tied to her by marriage, and anything you tell him may reach her. If you do write, keep it brief and factual: state what you want stopped, why, and what you are prepared to do, without revealing your plans, your evidence, or your fears. Ask him plainly whether he is willing to help and on what terms. Do not assume he shares your interests just because he is related to your enemy; family ties often outweigh convenience. Wait for his reply before committing to anything, and keep a copy of the letter.

prompt: I have cursed hope, faith, and patience in my despair—can anything be restored after such a curse?
chosen: Restoration is requisite with God's justice: what one sends out returns again, good for good and evil for evil, according to works and desires. Your curse is not a small thing; it sets a pattern that justice will answer. Yet that same justice is the ground of hope, for if you turn and send out good, good will return. Let despair give way to remorse and repentance, acknowledging a wiser judgment tempered with mercy rather than stiff-necked defiance. But know that you cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence; words without thoughts never to go to heaven. Make restitution where you can, and let your repentance show in deeds, not only in prayer. Then take small steps back toward trust, and let patience be rebuilt through ordinary faithfulness.
rejected: What you describe is despair speaking, not a final verdict. Cursing hope, faith, and patience in a moment of anguish does not destroy them forever; it shows how much pain you are carrying. Restoration is possible, but it usually begins with honesty about what you have lost and small, concrete steps back toward trust. Do not demand that faith return all at once. Speak to someone you trust, rest, and let patience be rebuilt through ordinary faithfulness. Many people have cursed in the dark and found light again. Be gentle with yourself; the fact that you grieve the loss suggests the seeds are still there.

prompt: A stranger asks for my trust and offers help—how cautious should I be?
chosen: Judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. A stranger offering help deserves a fair hearing, but trust should be earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose to do, why they are offering, and what they want in return. Keep your own game concealed from any adversary and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. Weigh the plan on its merits rather than on charm or credentials alone. Start with something small and reversible, and watch whether actions match words. Do not hand over money, secrets, or control of anything important early on; if the offer requires secrecy or urgency, treat that as a warning sign. And respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case, acknowledging the friend's own feelings rather than scorning such diffidence as weakness.
rejected: Be cautious but not paralyzed. A stranger offering help deserves a fair hearing, but trust should be earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose to do, why they are offering, and what they want in return. Judge the plan on its merits rather than on the stranger's charm or credentials alone. Start with something small and reversible, and watch whether their actions match their words. Do not hand over money, secrets, or control of anything important early on. If the offer requires secrecy or urgency, treat that as a warning sign. Caution is not rudeness; it is prudence.

prompt: My son wishes to marry a girl with a doubtful birth, and I fear his generous impulses will not last and he will one day repent the connection—should I oppose him?
chosen: Be cautious but not simply opposed. The father has stated his confidence in the mother's gentle heart, and he stipulated that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That condition matters more than doubtful birth. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness. Yet a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him, and another choice may be made. So counsel him firmly, ask what he knows of her character, and make clear your concerns and your support.
rejected: You should be cautious but not simply oppose him. Generous impulses are admirable, and a doubtful birth is not a fault in the girl herself. Still, your fear that his feelings will not last is worth raising honestly with him. Ask what he knows of her character, how they intend to build a life, and whether he is acting from love or infatuation. Opposing him outright may only harden his resolve. Better to counsel, test his seriousness, and let him decide, while making clear your concerns and your support.

prompt: I am a woman who has been told to be silent and ladylike; is it wrong to speak my mind?
chosen: When you are spoken to, then you may answer. Asked whether it is wrong to speak my mind, I would say: the command to be silent and ladylike is often a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you are not obliged to obey it. Your thoughts and convictions belong to you, and voicing them when invited is part of living honestly. Let no one tell you that your clear resolve is illness or delirium; a mind may be never so clear and certain as when it settles what it will do. It is a great sin against a wife to make her a doll-child and doll-wife whose opinions are only borrowed, so that she has made nothing of her life. Speak, then, as one who thinks for herself.
rejected: No, it is not wrong to speak your mind. Being told to be silent and ladylike is often a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you are not obliged to obey it. Your thoughts, judgments, and convictions belong to you, and voicing them is part of living honestly. That said, speaking your mind is not the same as speaking carelessly; choose your moments, be clear and kind, and accept that some people will be uncomfortable. The real question is not whether you may speak, but whether you will let others decide what you are allowed to think. You may.

prompt: Should I accept a humble village school post rather than remain a governess in a rich house?
chosen: A humble village school offers an independent and worthy asylum, not a fall in the scale of social existence. Rather than remaining a governess in a rich house—where you are neither servant nor family, often lonely and dependent—the village school provides a sheltered and respectable life. You would be your own mistress, teaching children in a community where you are valued for your work. However, a mere village is rarely able to furnish a tolerable municipal council; such small places are apt to be dominated by one man. Therefore, the school should be merged into a larger circumscription, so that its governance is shared and no single individual can tyrannize over it. Moreover, in such a school you would do the essential work of education: strengthening the faculty of voluntary attention, for the bringing back of a wandering attention is the root of judgment, character, and will. Thus secured, the post is an honorable calling, and its simplicity does not diminish its dignity. Choose it, for it is a not ignoble lot.
rejected: Accepting a village school post may seem like a step down from being a governess in a wealthy household, but consider the trade-offs. As a governess, you have the comfort of a rich house but little independence. A village school might offer more autonomy, though it comes with less prestige and possibly lower pay. Weigh your desire for freedom against the security and social standing of your current position. Ultimately, the decision depends on what you value more: the chance to be your own mistress in a modest setting or the relative ease of servitude in a grand one. Think carefully about your long-term happiness.

prompt: I'm afraid of missing something if I stop being tolerant. Is that fear wise?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, but only partly wise. Keep infinite hope and reserve judgment about others, since you cannot know what they may become; yet honor the limit where tolerance ends. Do not turn back from the worthwhile goal out of fear. Like brave travelers, resolve to press on through rough and dangerous places rather than give up when the way grows hard. Ask what you fear missing: a truth, a person, or merely approval? Hope for everyone, set your limit honestly, and hold it without guilt. Bear patiently what cannot be avoided, without weakness or complaint, and endure difficulty rather than retreating.
rejected: Your fear is understandable but not entirely wise. Tolerance is a virtue, but it is not infinite; it becomes a vice when it requires you to abandon your own judgment or endure harm. The wise course is to keep an open mind and reserve judgment about others, while also recognizing the point at which your tolerance ends. Ask what you are afraid of missing: a truth, a person, or simply the approval of those who exploit your patience? Infinite hope means never writing anyone off, but it does not mean accepting everything. Set your limit honestly and hold it without guilt.

prompt: Can souls in purgatory still grow in love and merit?
chosen: Purgatory is not merely a physical place of payment. The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, as it is near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. The pope does well to grant remission to souls in purgatory by way of intercession, not by the power of the keys, which he does not possess for that. As for love and merit: virtue is never moved though lewdness courts it in heavenly shape, while lust will sate itself and prey on garbage.
